detail.abstract: For decades, market stability relied on the "diversity of opinion." In 2026, that diversity is being replaced by a digital monoculture. This paper explores the phenomenon of Algorithmic Convergence-the trend where financial institutions, driven by the pursuit of "optimal" performance, deploy AI models that are fundamentally identical. By analyzing the shift from rule-based systems to Large Language Models (LLMs) and Reinforcement Learning agents, the study identifies a critical paradox: while AI increases micro-efficiency, it creates catastrophic macro-fragility. The research argues that shared training datasets (Data Incest) and concentrated cloud infrastructures have created a "Mirror Trap." When a market shock occurs, these synchronized algorithms react in unison, evaporating liquidity and triggering "flash crashes" that traditional circuit breakers are ill-equipped to handle. The paper concludes by proposing a "Diversity Mandate" for financial regulators to prevent a total systemic blackout.

title: Why the S=F Structure of Credit and Currency Has Been Hidden in English
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Why the S=F Structure of Credit and Currency Has Been Hidden in English
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the S=F Linguistic Visualization Theory , demonstrating that the identity S = F (Stock = Flow) constitutes the foundational structure underlying accounting, credit creation, currency issuance, and modern financial operations. Despite its universality, this structure has remained largely unrecognized within English-language economics. The reason is not economic but linguistic. English disperses the components of S=F across multiple lexical items-stock, flow, asset, liability, collateral, reserve, issuance, creation-fragmenting what is originally a single integrated mechanism. In contrast, Japanese possesses a 2×2 → 16 multiplicity structure, enabling multiple semantic layers to coexist within a single expression. This structural multiplicity preserves the integrative nature of S=F and makes its underlying mechanism intuitively visible. This paper presents a mathematical model of linguistic multiplicity and formally demonstrates why S=F could not be discovered under the lexical-segmentation constraints of English. It concludes that the "difficulty of discovering S=F" arises not from economics but from linguistic structure.

detail.abstract: Traditional macroeconomic models, relying on log-linearization, systematically fail to predict inflation under regimes of high volatility and external restriction. This technical note presents a rigorous derivation based on vector differential calculus that integrates the monetary identity with national accounts. Key Finding: It is mathematically demonstrated that inflationary sensitivity is inversely proportional to the economy's size (Y). Consequently, stabilization policies that contract aggregate demand (recessionary) may, counterintuitively, increase price instability by shrinking the denominator of the system's state equation.

title: Understanding the Flattening Phillips Curve in China: The Role of Central Bank Communication and Inflation Expectations

detail.title: Understanding the Flattening Phillips Curve in China: The Role of Central Bank Communication and Inflation Expectations
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the New Keynesian Phillips Curve (NKPC) and its flattening slope in China, focusing on the role of inflation expectations and central bank communication. Using forecasts and surveys' quarterly data from 1993 to 2025, we construct a latent expectation index as an inflation expectation proxy. With Large Language Model (LLM), we develop novel text-based indices of the People's Bank of China's Monetary Policy Reports. IV-GMM estimates show that inflation dynamics are dominated by expectations, while the NKPC slope becomes insignificant after 2013. Subsample and rolling analyses reveal a structural shift: before 2013 both expectations and demand contributes to inflation, while afterward demand effects weaken and inflation becomes expectation-driven. Communication indices further explain expectations: aggregate stance and forward-looking guidance reduce expectation level, financial stability concerns raise them, and forward guidance strength and structural policy focus enhance anchoring effect. Overall, the evidence suggests that conventional demand-based mechanisms have weakened. Inflation dynamics and policy transmission are now central to communication on inflation in China.

title: Absurdity and Human Existence in Yusuf Idris's The Farafir: A Philosophical Reading in Light of Existentialism ‬

detail.title: Absurdity and Human Existence in Yusuf Idris's The Farafir: A Philosophical Reading in Light of Existentialism ‬
detail.abstract: This paper examines The Farafir, a seminal play by way of Egyptian playwright Yusuf Idris, through the lens of existential philosophy, with precise recognition of the standards of absurdity, freedom, and alienation. The examinee argues that Idris employs the dynamic relationship between Farfour (the fool) and the Master to dramatise existentialist concerns, such as those explored by Western philosophers, including JeanPaul Sartre and Albert Camus. Drawing on textual evaluation and existentialist principles, the paper illustrates how Idris’s portrayal of human war, the absurd, and entrenched social hierarchies reflects a well-known human quest for meaning. The research highlights the approaches in which Idris’s characters grapple with questions of self-determination, the anxiety among characters' will, societal constraints, and the inevitability of human isolation. By situating The Farafir inside both its Egyptian cultural context and the wider existentialist tradition, the play looks at how well-known shows the play’s ability to transcend nearby socio-political critique, supplying a profound philosophical inquiry into the absurd situation of human lifestyles. In doing so, it underscores Idris’s function in bridging Arabic theatre with international highbrow movements.

title: Beyond Human Capital: The Human Resonance Systems (HRS) Framework and the Ontological Turn in Organizational Science

detail.title: Beyond Human Capital: The Human Resonance Systems (HRS) Framework and the Ontological Turn in Organizational Science
detail.abstract: Beyond Human Capital: The Human Resonance Systems (HRS) Framework and the Ontological Turn in Organizational Science The human capital paradigm has failed. Organizations spend hundreds of billions annually on HR infrastructure, talent development, and employee engagement programs. The result: employee engagement is stagnant or declining; burnout is epidemic; institutional collapses are accelerating. This is not a knowledge gap. This is a paradigm failure. The Human Resonance Systems (HRS) framework offers a fundamental reorientation. The problem is not human capacity. The problem is institutional structure. Organizations fail not because people lack capability, virtue, or motivation. Organizations fail because institutional structures do not enable sustainable expression of human faculties under the demands being imposed. The framework rests on three foundational pillars: 1. Fitrah: Eight universal human faculties (somatic, processing, discernment, affective, relational, conative, axiological, and teleological) that constitute human capacity independent of role or context. These faculties are cross-culturally invariant, developmentally grounded, and measurable without surveillance or psychological reduction. 2. Institutional Authority Constitutional Mechanics (IACM): Eight irreducible institutional domains (Zeus, Hera, Athena, Artemis, Hermes, Ares, Nemesis, Hades) that either enable or constrain faculty expression. All eight domains are necessary; none individually sufficient. The Minimal Viable Constitution theorem demonstrates their necessity empirically. 3. Resonance Theory: The Master Resonance Axiom formalizes how institutional value is created through sustained alignment between human readiness and structural support: V = ∫ R × S_align dt - C_distortion. This integration explains why high-readiness individuals underperform in misaligned structures, and why well-designed institutions enable ordinary people to achieve extraordinary results. The framework specifies Evidence-Based Behavioral-Cognitive Assessment (EB-BCA)-an eight-engine measurement architecture that assesses faculty readiness without reification, surveillance, or psychological reduction. Assessment focuses on capacity under specified conditions, bounded by explicit evidence sources, and subject to individual epistemic agency. Application across diverse institutional contexts (manufacturing, nonprofit, technology, education, healthcare) demonstrates that structural intervention reliably produces institutional improvement without requiring changes to personnel. The pattern is consistent: when institutional domains are present and functional, faculty expression occurs naturally. When domains are absent or compromised, faculty atrophy is predictable. The framework's validation pathway spans four years of prospective research designed to test falsifiable predictions about faculty degradation under structural constraint, domain necessity and sufficiency, and readiness-performance relationships.Critically, the ethical architecture is foundational: six hard constraints against surveillance protect human sovereignty and ensure assessment informs structural change rather than individual control. The framework is designed to diagnose institutional failures structurally and enable intervention with human dignity preserved. The paper concludes by establishing HRS as foundational for artificial intelligence governance. AI systems will inherit institutional design failures unless institutions are first fixed. The Human Resonance Systems framework provides the specification for institutional structures capable of enabling both human flourishing and trustworthy artificial intelligence.

title: Impact of Prognostic Score-Based Paired Randomization on the Operating Characteristics of Clinical Trials with Continuous Outcomes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Padua University - Department of Cardio-Thoraco-Vascular Sciences and Public Health and Padua University - Department of Cardio-Thoraco-Vascular Sciences and Public Health

detail.title: Impact of Prognostic Score-Based Paired Randomization on the Operating Characteristics of Clinical Trials with Continuous Outcomes
detail.abstract: BackgroundRandomized controlled trials often suffer from limited power and inefficient use of prognostic information. The use of a prognostic score estimated from historical data has been proposed to increase efficiency at the analysis stage. We propose PROMATCHER, a prognostic score-based paired randomization strategy leveraging historical information via machine learning to reduce within-pair outcome variability and increase power.MethodsWe developed prognostic models using linear and non-linear models (random forest, extreme gradient boosting, and a super learner ensemble) trained on historical data. Prognostic scores were used to match participants within predefined distances and then randomized within pairs. Simulation studies assessed the impact of different models, analysis strategies, caliper settings, and sample sizes on the trial's operating characteristics. Analytical formulas were derived for power and sample size estimation. The PROMATCHER approach is applied retrospectively on two twin RCTs in knee osteoarthritis.ResultsThe method showed an absolute power gain of 15-25% across well-specified models. Gains were about 2-7% under model misspecification. However, moderate inflation of Type I errors, particularly with large calipers and unadjusted analysis, was found with a maximum of 7%. XGBoost provided the best balance between power and type I error and outperformed other methods when models were mis-specified. The case study showed a treatment effect that was not observed with standard analysis, especially with XGBoost-based scores.ConclusionMatching on prognostic scores can improve efficiency by reducing variability within pairs. Model selection and calibrations are critical for balancing power gains and type I error.

title: How Managed Care Networks Reduce Medical Spending: Evidence on Provider Behavior and Patient Selection
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Lucerne, University of St. Gallen and University of Bern

detail.title: How Managed Care Networks Reduce Medical Spending: Evidence on Provider Behavior and Patient Selection
detail.abstract: We examine the effects of managed care within a physician network on health spending, medical practice, and quality of care in Switzerland. When primary care physicians join the network, annual medical spending for their existing patients falls by roughly CHF 800 per patient, equivalent to about 15% of pre-network costs. These savings are driven by reductions in outpatient and medication spending. We find no evidence of a cost-quality trade-off: visit frequency, consultation time, inpatient spending, and the use of high-value preventive services remain unchanged. Network enrollment also systematically alters patient composition, as physicians attract younger and healthier patients with lower baseline costs. Observed spending differences therefore reflect both the causal effects of managed care on medical practice and advantageous patient selection.

detail.abstract: Religion occupies a central position in the social, political, and cultural life of Sub-Saharan Africa. While existing scholarship has examined its moral authority, social capital, and political influence, its economic role remains marginal in mainstream development analysis. This paper reconceptualises religious institutions as economic institutions that mobilise resources, accumulate capital, shape labour relations, and influence household and national development outcomes. Drawing on political economy and institutional economics, the study introduces the Religious Economic Complex (REC) framework, which explains how faith, trust, and cultural legitimacy are transformed into sustained economic power. Using a mixed-methods approach combining household survey data (N ≈ 45,000), crosscountry development indicators, and qualitative case studies from Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa, the paper demonstrates that religious institutions operate as quasi-market actors largely outside formal regulatory oversight. The findings indicate that religious economic activity is associated with significant opportunity costs for households and is linked to long-term development trajectories, particularly industrialisation and productive investment. By repositioning religion at the centre of economic analysis, the paper contributes a novel institutional perspective to development studies and highlights the importance of incorporating religious economic activity into development frameworks.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into military command and control systems to enhance decision speed, situational awareness, and operational efficiency. While these technologies promise tactical and strategic advantages, their incorporation into high-stakes military decision-making introduces new risks of inadvertent escalation, particularly in crisis and conflict scenarios involving peer competitors. This paper examines how AI-enabled decision support and autonomous systems may compress decision timelines, amplify automation bias, and generate a false sense of certainty from probabilistic or incomplete information, thereby increasing the likelihood of rapid and unintended escalation.

Drawing on recent experimental studies, military wargaming, and doctrinal analysis, the paper develops a conceptual framework describing how tightly coupled human–machine command structures can evolve from advisory “centaur” models toward more autonomous “minotaur” configurations under operational pressure. It argues that while high levels of autonomy may be necessary in narrow domains such as missile defense and hypersonic intercept, their application in ambiguous, politically sensitive, or nuclear-adjacent contexts undermines crisis stability. Comparative analysis of United States, Chinese, and Russian approaches to AI-enabled command authority highlights how differing institutional structures and strategic cultures shape these risks.

The paper introduces the concept of "Strategic Latency" the deliberate preservation of time, human judgment, and organizational friction within AI-mediated command systems as a stabilizing design principle. It concludes by outlining policy and governance measures to ensure meaningful human control, reduce escalation incentives, and mitigate the risk of AI-driven “flash wars” in great power competition.

title: From Subjective to Objective: Validating Patient Satisfaction in Facial Surgery Through Psychometrics

detail.title: From Subjective to Objective: Validating Patient Satisfaction in Facial Surgery Through Psychometrics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None declared.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract: Patient satisfaction sits at the heart of aesthetic surgery, yet measuring how well outcomes meet patient expectations has always been difficult. Rather than relying on the surgeon's impression, we synthesized research on Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) in facial aesthetics. Our work focuses on the FACE-Q instrument and explores newer technological applications. We reviewed studies on facelifts (563 patients across 10 studies), injectable treatments (2292 patients in 23 studies), and rhinoplasty (937 patients across 10 studies). Our original data came from a Dutch cohort at Clinique Rebelle in Amsterdam—259 patients undergoing facial procedures, supplemented by Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) simulation research. The FACE-Q scales demonstrated strong psychometric properties—Cronbach's alpha between 0.885 and 0.951—and successfully captured differences between patients that traditional photos miss. CAT methods reduced questionnaire length by roughly 71% without sacrificing measurement accuracy (r = 0.98 with complete surveys). Looking ahead, machine learning shows real potential for forecasting patient satisfaction outcomes. Routine PROM collection in aesthetic practice makes sense on multiple fronts: better patient selection, benchmarking quality across surgeons, protecting against medicolegal concerns, and aligning with value-based healthcare models. We also discuss how AI and 3D imaging might reshape outcome assessment going forward.

title: Payments and Competition in a Digital Economy
affiliations: Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University) and Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University)

detail.title: Payments and Competition in a Digital Economy
detail.abstract: This submission to the Australian House of Representatives Inquiry into Schemes, Digital Wallets and Innovation in the Payments Sector examines competition in payments through a dynamic, institutional lens. Rather than treating payment systems as static markets to be optimised through fee controls or scheme regulation, we argue that payments infrastructure shapes entry, experimentation, and economic coordination over time. Digital wallets, stablecoins, and machine-mediated exchange enable new institutional forms that compete by expanding economic capabilities, not merely by lowering prices. Interchange fees are best understood as governance mechanisms within complex payment networks, not simple monopoly rents. We caution against ex ante controls that risk entrenching incumbent systems and foreclosing institutional experimentation, and argue for payments regulation that supports contestability, innovation, and institutional evolution in a digital economy.

title: Is the Golden Ticket Tainted? Testing Standardized Tests with AI
affiliations: University of Cincinnati

detail.title: Is the Golden Ticket Tainted? Testing Standardized Tests with AI
detail.abstract: Standardized test scores are signals in college admissions, yet the measurement properties of these instruments receive little empirical attention. This paper uses large language models (LLMs) as stable external benchmarks to audit item-level changes in the SAT math section from 2011 to 2023. Estimating a pooled item response theory model on 1291 math items evaluated by 20 LLMs, I find a downward drift in item difficulty beginning in 2017, with discrimination remaining broadly stable. This shift moves test information towards lower ability regions, reducing signal precision at the upper tail where selective institutions screen applicants. These diagnostics suggest that where the SAT is most informative has changed over time, with implications for efficiency of student institution matching and the distributional consequences of admissions policies.

title: The Sleep-Aging-Motor Memory Triad: A Systematic Review of Task-Dependent Consolidation and Neuroplasticity

detail.abstract: Motor learning includes a set of processes linked to practice and experience that are crucial for gaining new skills and altering behavior as time progresses. Proficiency in motor skills is crucial for maintaining autonomy and enhancing quality of life in older adults. Nonetheless, recent findings indicate that alterations in sleep patterns due to aging may greatly hinder the consolidation of motor memory, thus speeding up the decline of motor abilities. In this context, motor learning is modulated/affected not just by internal neural processes but also by the quality and organization of sleep, especially the preservation of slow-wave and REM sleep. Interruptions in these sleep stages seem to hinder the neurological changes required for enduring enhancements in motor skills. This synthesis emphasizes the importance of recognizing the relationship among sleep, aging, and sensorimotor plasticity, while suggesting effective intervention strategies like improving sleep or specific therapies to alleviate age-related motor deficits. These findings originate from a preregistered systematic review of 21 research articles extracted from 740 sources indexed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. We investigated these effects on motor learning and whether these effects vary by task type, complexity, sleep effect, and age. This review seeks to enhance our comprehension of age-suitable empirical studies on sleep-related motor memory consolidation among healthy groups by synthesizing results from various research projects.

title: Public-Private Partnerships in the Energy Sector of the Gulf States: Digital Transformation as a Factor Aligning the Interests of the Economy and Private Investors

detail.title: Public-Private Partnerships in the Energy Sector of the Gulf States: Digital Transformation as a Factor Aligning the Interests of the Economy and Private Investors
detail.abstract: Gulf countries increasingly rely on public-private partnerships (PPPs) to modernize energy infrastructure and advance economic diversification objectives. Digital transformation improves the efficiency and transparency of projects, but also introduces new requirements for data governance and cyber-risk management. This paper reviews the institutional foundations of PPPs across the six GCC states; discusses key project areas (renewables, thermal generation and desalination, and smart grids); and considers socioeconomic effects, including employment, localization, and technology transfer. Policy recommendations are proposed to improve regulatory frameworks and implementation practices in line with the digitalization of the energy sector.

title: Beyond Targeting Women: Intrahousehold Contexts and the Effectiveness of Food Vouchers
affiliations: Kyung Hee University, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Economics and Washington State University

detail.title: Beyond Targeting Women: Intrahousehold Contexts and the Effectiveness of Food Vouchers
detail.abstract: Many transfer programs target women based on evidence that mothers are more likely than fathers to allocate resources toward child welfare. However, findings on gendered impacts remain mixed—likely because parental knowledge, preferences, and household decision-making roles differ across contexts. In this study, we experimentally vary the intrahousehold context itself through a randomized controlled trial in rural Ethiopia. Specifically, employing a factorial design, we cross-randomize two key dimensions: (1) which parent receives nutrition behavior change communication (BCC)—neither, mother only, or both; and (2) which parent receives a household food voucher—mother or father. We find that vouchers are more effective at improving child-feeding practices if given to mothers than fathers, but only when fathers do not receive BCC. This maternal advantage disappears when fathers also receive BCC. We provide suggestive evidence that when mothers have both knowledge advantage and control over resources, they are better able to mobilize paternal support in childcare and household labor. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for intrahousehold dynamics, not just recipient gender, when designing nutrition interventions.

title: A Holonic Economic-Legal Manifest (HELM) for Diagnostic Analysis of Financial Systems Migrations. Conceptualising Holons, Helmprints, and State Transitions in Financial Infrastructure
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Holonic Economic-Legal Manifest (HELM) for Diagnostic Analysis of Financial Systems Migrations. Conceptualising Holons, Helmprints, and State Transitions in Financial Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Success of financial systems migrations is commonly evaluated through delivery milestones, functional completeness, and reconciliation outcomes. While necessary, such measures are insufficient to determine whether a migrated system continues to represent the same underlying economic-legal reality as its predecessor. This paper introduces the Holonic Economic-Legal Manifest (HELM), a conceptual framework that reframes financial systems migration as a transformation of economic-legal state rather than a purely technical deployment. Within HELM, a financial system is treated as representing a holon: the coherent economic-legal state the system is responsible for managing in operation, encompassing legally enforceable agreements, positions, obligations, and their evolution under market and regulatory events. Structural representations of this state are defined through canonical forms termed helmprints, and migration correctness is expressed through preservation of invariants as that state is subjected to future events. Building on this foundation, the paper presents a set of diagnostic archetypes that explain recurring classes of migration failure as violations of holonic state invariants. HELM provides regulators, system architects, and practitioners with a shared conceptual language for assessing migration risk at the level of financial infrastructure rather than implementation detail.

title: The Substantiation Gap AI-Mediated Record Formation Under Administrative Law

detail.title: The Substantiation Gap AI-Mediated Record Formation Under Administrative Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I founded CiviQs B.V. and co-founded CivAI B.V. Both develop and deploy AI systems for EU public bodies and educational institutions. The procedural analysis applies equally to systems I develop or deploy.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
When administrative acts are contested, the authority must demonstrate what was considered and why. Where AI mediates record formation without preserving case-bound traces, that demonstration fails: the authority cannot show what information was available, how it was framed, or what the official adopted, regardless of output quality or human review. The result is a substantiation gap: a structural inability to demonstrate lawful procedure in the individual case.

The gap originates in epistemic delegation: where AI mediates retrieval, summarisation, or drafting, what information reaches the official is determined not by the official's engagement with primary sources but by systems whose per-case operation is not preserved in reconstructible form. Two diagnostic instruments follow. The Decision-Grounding Use (DGU) trigger specifies when AI use becomes procedurally relevant. The Decision Provenance Bundle (DPB) defines the evidentiary minimum: retrieval logs, configuration snapshots, and adoption records, retained through challenge periods and producible as case documents. Existing governance instruments audit the processing infrastructure; they do not show what flowed through it in the individual case.

While grounded in Dutch administrative law (Awb), the logic extends to any jurisdiction where contested administrative acts must be substantiated. The argument clarifies what administrative law already requires; it does not propose reform. It applies only where deployments cannot produce a case-bound DPB under ordinary operational conditions; where they can, the thesis does not hold for that deployment.

title: Risk Acceptance in Critical Infrastructure Cyber Incidents: A Retrospective Analysis of the Colonial Pipeline Ransomware Attack

detail.title: Risk Acceptance in Critical Infrastructure Cyber Incidents: A Retrospective Analysis of the Colonial Pipeline Ransomware Attack
detail.abstract: The May 2021 Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack represents a watershed moment in critical infrastructure cybersecurity, highlighting fundamental tensions between operational imperatives and security best practices. This article examines the incident through the lens of risk management theory, analyzing both the long-term risk acceptance decisions that created vulnerability conditions and the crisis-time risk calculus that led to ransom payment. Drawing on retrospective analyses published between 2022 and 2026, we construct a comprehensive framework for understanding risk acceptance in critical infrastructure contexts, where private operators make decisions with broad public consequences. Our analysis reveals that Colonial Pipeline's decision to pay $4.4 million in ransom, while operationally expedient, reflects systemic failures in pre-incident risk governance and raises fundamental questions about who should determine acceptable risk levels when critical infrastructure security has national security implications. We propose a multi-stakeholder governance model that balances operational autonomy with public accountability, supported by quantitative risk assessment matrices and decision trees specifically calibrated for critical infrastructure environments. title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Literature Reviews
affiliations: , The University of Sydney - Business School, University of Virginia, University of Virginia and HEC Montreal

detail.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Literature Reviews
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), based on large-language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, has taken organizations, academia, and the public by storm. In particular, impressive GenAI capabilities such as summarization of large text corpora, question-answering, data extraction, and translation, carry profound implications for the conduct of literature reviews. This impacts science, organizations and the general public, as all can benefit from GenAIsupported literature reviews. Building on the technical foundations of GenAI and grounded in established methodological discourse, this work outlines approaches for conducting literature reviews using both general-purpose (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) and specialized GenAI tools (e.g., Consensus, Elicit). We provide illustrative examples of prompts and suggest methodologically-sound literature review strategies. Throughout this perspective paper, we adopt a balanced approach considering both the opportunities and the risks of relying on GenAI in the conduct of literature reviews. We conclude by discussing philosophical questions related to the effects of GenAI on long-term scientific progress, and also present fruitful opportunities for research on improving the core of GenAI's technology-its architecture and training data-and suggest open issues in GenAI-based literature reviews methodology.

title: Designing Context-Aware Referral Artifacts in Social Commerce: The Crowding-Out Effect of Incentives via Metacognitive Inference
affiliations: National Taichung University of Science and Technology, Soochow University and Feng Chia University

detail.title: Designing Context-Aware Referral Artifacts in Social Commerce: The Crowding-Out Effect of Incentives via Metacognitive Inference
detail.abstract: Referral Reward Programs (RRPs) are pivotal digital artifacts in social commerce, yet their efficacy in high-involvement contexts remains an empirical puzzle. Drawing on Social Capital Theory and the Persuasion Knowledge Model (PKM), this study investigates the interplay between community structure and incentive mechanisms. Using a multi-method approach in the New Energy Vehicle (NEV) market, Study 1 (N=408) demonstrates that in high-involvement social commerce, referral sharing is intrinsically driven by altruism, whereas economic motives exert a diminishing effect. Study 2 (N=160) further identifies a causal "crowding-out" mechanism: high monetary rewards trigger motive skepticism (metacognitive inference) within strong-tie networks, significantly impairing sharing intentions. In contrast, such rewards function as effective economic signals within weak-tie interest groups. These findings redefine RRPs as context-sensitive artifacts, suggesting that platforms should dynamically adapt incentive designs—masking economic cues in social graphs while emphasizing them in interest graphs—to reconcile the conflicting social and economic logics of digital communities.

title: How to Regulate the Cloud: A Blueprint to Address the Market Failures and National Security Risks of Cloud Computing

detail.title: How to Regulate the Cloud: A Blueprint to Address the Market Failures and National Security Risks of Cloud Computing
detail.abstract: Cloud computing is a market worth hundreds of billions of dollars that underpins modern AI systems, critical infrastructure, and vast swaths of the digital economy, yet it remains largely unregulated. Three hyperscalers—Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud— control two-thirds of the market, and their parent companies are simultaneously suppliers, customers, competitors, and investors of their cloud customers across every layer of the AI technology stack. Drawing on investigations and studies from government agencies across North America, Europe, and Asia, this paper identifies five market features that impede competition: market concentration, vertical integration, conglomerate effects, opaque and differential pricing, and high switching costs. It further identifies two national security risks: society's dependence on cloud infrastructure and the cloud's essential role in today's geopolitics. To address these failures, the paper proposes a six-part blueprint for federal legislation: (A) structural separation; (B) cloud neutrality requirements; (C) data portability and interoperability mandates; (D) designation of cloud computing as a critical infrastructure sector; (E) foreign adversary ownership and control restrictions; and (F) know-your-customer requirements. Each proposal is grounded in the American history of regulating networks, platforms, and utilities, and the paper includes annotated sample legislative text demonstrating how these policies could be enacted. Together, these measures aim to produce a more competitive and secure cloud market aligned with U.S. public policy priorities.

title: Free to Watch, Harder to Love: Subscription Effects on Film Evaluation
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst - Isenberg School of Management and University of New Hampshire

detail.title: Free to Watch, Harder to Love: Subscription Effects on Film Evaluation
detail.abstract: The shift from pay-per-view to subscription video-on-demand (SVoD) has transformed film consumption, yet its consequences for post-viewing ratings remain poorly understood. Viewer ratings are economically consequential: they shape subsequent viewing choices, SVoD platform satisfaction, and act as perceived quality signals that influence producers', distributors', and platforms' strategic decisions. Drawing on behavioral economics and consumer psychology, we argue that the subscription access model itself shapes post-viewing ratings, generating a fundamental theoretical tension. The zero-price effect predicts higher perceived quality when marginal viewing costs fall to zero. Conversely, decoupling payment from consumption may weaken psychological ownership, invoking the endowment effect and reducing viewer engagement and perceived quality. We test these competing predictions using a comprehensive panel of films that became available on major U.S. SVoD platforms between 2016 and 2019, combining availability data with viewer ratings and reviews from an online film community. Using a difference-indifferences design and extensive robustness checks addressing selection, endogeneity, and alternative explanations, we show that subscription availability causally lowers average viewer ratings. Heterogeneity analyses show that this effect is driven by films that impose a high cognitive load on viewers. Mechanism analyses supports the endowment effect pathway: subscription access reduces engagement during viewing, leading to lower ratings. By demonstrating that access models systematically bias perceived quality independent of intrinsic film quality, our findings have important implications for all stakeholders within the film industry.

title: Development and Optimization of a Knowledge Graph-Based Data Management and Intelligent Question-Answering System for New Energy Vehicles
affiliations: Yantai Institute of China Agricultural University, Yantai Institute of China Agricultural University, Yantai Institute of China Agricultural University, Yantai Institute of China Agricultural University and Yantai Institute of China Agricultural University

detail.title: Development and Optimization of a Knowledge Graph-Based Data Management and Intelligent Question-Answering System for New Energy Vehicles
detail.abstract: In recent years, the new energy vehicle (NEV) industry has witnessed remarkable advancements. Nevertheless, owing to its brief large-scale implementation, certain deficiencies persist in both the data management system and the user-oriented Question-Answering(Q&A) system, thereby hindering the comprehensive fulfillment of diverse user information requirements. In light of this, this paper proposes a knowledge graph-based methodology for data management and intelligent Q&A systems in new energy vehicles. The proposed methodology encompasses three principal components: Firstly, a bidirectional knowledge graph is constructed, employing a weighted similarity entity alignment strategy to facilitate the integration of near-synonym entities. The Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers-Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory-Conditional Random Field (BERT-BiLSTM-CRF) model is subsequently utilized to optimize entity relationship recognition under Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) annotation, thereby enhancing the construction quality of both the pattern layer and data layer of the knowledge graph, while simultaneously improving knowledge storage efficiency. Secondly, the Text Convolutional Neural Network (TextCNN) model is implemented to augment the precision of question entity classification, enabling the generation of question triples containing intent and entities, which are then efficiently retrieved from the Neo4j database using the Cypher query language. Finally, the system was implemented using the MVT architecture based on the Flask framework, with D3.js visualization components integrated to enhance Q&A interaction outcomes and improve user experience. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system achieves 98% entity relation recognition accuracy, elevates entity classification accuracy to 93%, while both system stability and compatibility meet design specifications.

title: Assortment Management under the General Multi-Purchase Choice Model
affiliations: CUHK-SZ, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen -School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - School of Information Management and Engineering and

detail.title: Assortment Management under the General Multi-Purchase Choice Model
detail.abstract: We study assortment optimization under a General Multi-Purchase (GMP) choice model in which each consumer possesses a random purchase capacity L and may buy up to L distinct items from an offered set. The model requires only a minimal regularity condition: a product's purchase probability in any assortment is bounded below by the product of its maximal (stand-alone) purchase probability and the probability that a "purchase slot" remains (i.e., that fewer than L items are purchased from the remaining set). The GMP framework subsumes multi-purchase extensions of several canonical single-purchase choice models, including the random consideration set (RCS) model, the negatively associated mixed Multinomial Logit (MMNL) model, and the click-based MNL model. We show that the resulting assortment problem is NP-hard and propose a simple, easily implementable threshold-based heuristic that depends only on maximal purchase probabilities. We benchmark this heuristic against a tractable upper bound and establish tight guarantees: a 1/2 approximation-ratio with deterministic demand and a (1-e-1)/2 ratio under IFR (increasing failure rate) random demand. These guarantees also extend to cardinality-constrained settings. Building on this analysis, we explore extensions to pricing under multi-purchase behavior, joint assortment optimization with customization across segments, and joint information disclosure and assortment planning. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the heuristic delivers consistently strong performance across diverse settings, including cases that violate the IFR assumption.

title: Trust in the Virtual: Deepfake Realism and Consumer Behavior for a Sustainable Future
affiliations: Arkansas State University

detail.title: Trust in the Virtual: Deepfake Realism and Consumer Behavior for a Sustainable Future
detail.abstract: This study develops an analytical framework to examine the interplay between deepfake technology, consumer trust, and regulatory oversight in sustainability marketing. Modeling firm decision-making, consumer trust evolution, and regulatory interventions as a two-period game, the research identifies threshold conditions under which deepfake campaigns yield short-term engagement benefits but ultimately risk long-term brand equity erosion. A numerical experiment simulation validates the model by showing that increased detection probabilities and trust penalties shift consumer behavior and firm strategies toward more transparent marketing. These findings provide theoretical insights and practical guidance for using deepfake technology ethically.

title: Spillover Effects of Gaming Regulation for Minors: Evidence from Game Live-Streaming
affiliations: and School of Management, Jinan University

detail.title: Spillover Effects of Gaming Regulation for Minors: Evidence from Game Live-Streaming
detail.abstract: Governments worldwide increasingly restrict minors’ access to video games to curb excessive use and encourage more productive behavior. Yet little is known about how such restrictions affect minors’ engagement in adjacent digital activities, particularly game live-streaming. Do limits on gameplay reduce overall gaming-related engagement, or do they merely shift attention to related channels? We address this question by studying the 2021 Chinese gaming regulation that sharply restricts minors’ playtime. Using detailed streamer-day data from DouYu, one of China’s largest game live-streaming platforms, and a regression discontinuity in time design, we examine how the policy affects game live-streaming consumption. We find that the regulation leads to a sizable decline in game-streaming viewership, with effects ranging from 15% to 30% across specifications. The effect persists over time, extends to multiple engagement and revenue-related metrics, and is unlikely to be driven by school-calendar effects or changes in streaming supply. Additional analyses exploiting variation in policy strictness suggest patterns consistent with complementarity between gameplay and game-streaming. By documenting spillover effects beyond direct gameplay, this study highlights the importance of considering adjacent digital activities when evaluating and designing regulations aimed at minors’ digital consumption, including emerging policies governing social media use.

title: Does Zillow Deceive Homebuyers? Evidence from a Controlled Experiment
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: Does Zillow Deceive Homebuyers? Evidence from a Controlled Experiment
detail.abstract: This study presents findings from a controlled experiment examining whether consumers understand who they are contacting when they click "Contact Agent" or "Request a Tour" on Zillow's real estate website. Results from 862 respondents-all recent or prospective homebuyers who use online real estate websites-reveal that consumers expect to be connected to the agent associated with the property they are viewing. Incredibly, 99.7% of consumers exposed to Zillow's standard interface were unable to correctly identify who would actually contact them. Even Zillow's additional disclosures failed to meaningfully improve consumer understanding. In contrast, when the interface clearly labeled the contact as the "Listing Agent", 78.9% of respondents answered correctly. These findings were consistent across income levels, indicating that financial sophistication does not protect consumers from this deception. The results suggest that Zillow's interface systematically deceives consumers about a fundamental aspect of the homebuying process. The implications extend beyond individual transactions: as alleged in recently filed lawsuits, consumers are routed to agents who have paid Zillow for these leads and who are heavily incentivized to direct customers to Zillow Home Loans-a mortgage product that (according to a recent study and the lawsuits) can be significantly more expensive than other available mortgages. Consumers should be informed about the value of seeking multiple mortgage offers, and Zillow must be required to cease its deceptive practices.

title: Agent Benchmarks Fail Public Sector Requirements
affiliations: University of Oxford - Oxford Internet Institute, Hertie School - Centre for Digital Governance, University of Oxford - Oxford Internet Institute, Weizenbaum Institute Berlin and University of Oxford - Oxford Internet Institute

detail.title: Agent Benchmarks Fail Public Sector Requirements

JB was supported by the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space of Germany [Grant Number 16DII131]. CS and JB acknowledge funding by the Hertie School’s program "AI and Data Science for the Public Sector", funded by the Dieter Schwartz Foundation. KK was supported by the Clarendon Fund.

detail.abstract: Deploying Large Language Model-based agents (LLM agents) in the public sector requires assuring that they meet the stringent legal, procedural, and structural requirements of public-sector institutions. Practitioners and researchers often turn to benchmarks for such assessments. However, it remains unclear what criteria benchmarks must meet to ensure they adequately reflect public-sector requirements, or how many existing benchmarks do so. In this paper, we first define such criteria based on a first-principles survey of public administration literature: benchmarks must be process-based, realistic, public-sector-specific and report metrics that reflect the unique requirements of the public sector. We analyse more than 1,300 benchmark papers for these criteria using an expert-validated LLM-assisted pipeline. Our results show that no single benchmark meets all of the criteria. Our findings provide a call to action for both researchers to develop public sector-relevant benchmarks and for public-sector officials to apply these criteria when evaluating their own agentic use cases.

title: Robots at Work, Workers at Risk
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: Robots at Work, Workers at Risk
detail.abstract: Robot adoption is expanding at a pace that significantly exceeds global population growth, signaling a structural shift in labor markets. This paper examines the labor-market consequences of this trend using a novel crosscountry dataset on robot revenues. We document robust evidence that robot adoption, particularly industrial automation, is substituted for human labor and is associated with higher unemployment rates. The economic magnitude of this effect is substantial: a one-standarddeviation increase in robot adoption raises unemployment by more than 74.6% of its sample mean. To rationalize these findings, we develop a theoretical model in which robots and labor are imperfect substitutes, with automation reshaping labor productivity and employment outcomes. The empirical results are consistent with the model's predictions and remain robust across alternative specifications. Collectively, our findings highlight that the rapid diffusion of robotics has important implications for employment dynamics, social welfare, and policy design, underscoring the need for forward-looking labor and technology policies in an era of accelerated automation.

title: Learning from Many Experiments: A Hierarchical Bayesian Framework for Decomposing Marketing Treatment Heterogeneity
affiliations: HEC Paris - Marketing, Harvard Business School and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Marketing

detail.title: Learning from Many Experiments: A Hierarchical Bayesian Framework for Decomposing Marketing Treatment Heterogeneity

publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Firms increasingly rely on A/B testing to evaluate marketing strategies, yet most experiments are analyzed in isolation, limiting insight into why effectiveness varies and how repeated exposure shapes outcomes. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework that jointly analyzes randomized marketing interventions to decompose treatment effect heterogeneity into three components: customer responsiveness, campaign design, and contextual timing. The model is scalable, incorporates both observed and unobserved variation, and links estimation directly to policy evaluation with full uncertainty quantification. Using data from large-scale field experiments involving nearly half a million customers, we document three main findings. First, unobserved customer-level heterogeneity accounts for the majority of variation in treatment effects, explaining roughly two-thirds of the total dispersion, considerably exceeding the contribution of campaign design or timing. Second, we find strong evidence of intervention fatigue: responsiveness declines with repeated exposure and recovers only slowly. Third, in a held-out policy evaluation, a model-based targeting strategy improves revenue on average while substantially reducing the share of customers targeted, with gains reaching over 10% in settings where experimental variation is most informative. Approximately 80% of these gains are driven by personalization based on latent customer responsiveness rather than observable characteristics. Together, these results demonstrate how repeated experimentation can be leveraged to explain variation in marketing effectiveness and to support scalable targeting and personalization.

title: Measuring Well-Being beyond GDP: Pollution- and Education-Adjusted Healthy Lifetime Income Estimates for 175 Countries
affiliations: WU Vienna, Vienna University of Economics and Business - Department of Economics, Harvard University - T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Harvard University - T.H. Chan School of Public Health and International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA)

detail.title: Measuring Well-Being beyond GDP: Pollution- and Education-Adjusted Healthy Lifetime Income Estimates for 175 Countries

detail.abstract: We measure well-being across 175 countries using a novel indicator: Pollution-and Education-Adjusted Healthy Lifetime Income (PEHLI). This indicator goes beyond the mere consideration of per capita gross domestic product (GDP) and can be interpreted as the income of the average person in an economy during the years that they spend in good health, adjusted for education and pollution in the given country. Our study addresses how incorporating health, education, and environmental quality reshapes crosscountry wellbeing assessments. Our analysis reveals significant differences in country rankings when compared to GDP-based measures. PEHLI ranks pollution-intensive countries lower and cleaner countries higher. Countries with better education levels in terms of attainment and opportunities also tend to rank higher under PEHLI. Across countries, incorporating health and education widens inequality, while incorporating pollution narrows it slightly; higherlatitude countries generally enjoy greater well-being. By adopting PEHLI, policymakers would gain a comprehensive framework for their decision-making processes that incorporates the well-being dimensions of health, longevity, education, and pollution into a single income-based measure.

title: Pre-Modern Engineering and Project Management: Evidence from South Indian Temple Construction

detail.title: Pre-Modern Engineering and Project Management: Evidence from South Indian Temple Construction
detail.abstract: Pre-modern South India witnessed the construction of large and architecturally complex structures that continue to function structurally and institutionally centuries after their completion. While existing researchers have extensively examined these temples through art historical, religious, and symbolic perspectives, comparatively limited attention has been given to the planning, execution, and management systems that enabled their construction in the absence of modern technology. This working paper examines these temple constructions through an engineering and project management lens, reconstructing the full lifecycle of temple building from initial planning to completion and long-term maintenance. Using case studies of the Brihadeeswarar Temple (Thanjavur), Meenakshi Amman Temple (Madurai), Ramanathaswamy Temple (Rameshwaram), Kailasanathar Temple (Kanchipuram), Nataraja Temple (Chidambaram), and Arunachaleswarar Temple (Thiruvannamalai), the study draws on architectural evidence, inscriptions, and official archaeological records. The analysis highlights systematic design frameworks, skilled labour organization, material and logistics management, institutional governance, and maintenance mechanisms. The findings suggest that South Indian temples represent pre-modern mega-projects characterized by standardized planning, coordinated execution, and durable governance structures, offering insights relevant to contemporary discussions on long-term infrastructure management.

title: Regularized Ensemble Forecasting for Learning Weights from Historical and Current Forecasts
affiliations: George Washington University - Department of Statistics,  and George Washington University - Department of Statistics

detail.title: Regularized Ensemble Forecasting for Learning Weights from Historical and Current Forecasts
detail.abstract: Combining forecasts from multiple experts often yields more accurate results than relying on a single expert. In this paper, we introduce a novel regularized ensemble method that extends the traditional linear opinion pool by leveraging both current forecasts and historical performances to set the weights. Unlike existing approaches that rely only on either the current forecasts or past accuracy, our method accounts for both sources simultaneously. It learns weights by minimizing the variance of the combined forecast (or its transformed version) while incorporating a regularization term informed by historical performances. We also show that this approach has a Bayesian interpretation. Different distributional assumptions within this Bayesian framework yield different functional forms for the variance component and the regularization term, adapting the method to various scenarios. In empirical studies on Walmart sales and macroeconomic forecasting, our ensemble outperforms leading benchmark models both when experts' full forecasting histories are available and when experts enter and exit over time, resulting in incomplete historical records. Throughout, we provide illustrative examples that show how the optimal weights are determined and, based on the empirical results, we discuss where the framework's strengths lie and when experts' past versus current forecasts are more informative.

title: CEO Characteristics and Business Performance: How Leadership Traits Shape Strategy, Culture, and Long-Term Value Creation

detail.title: CEO Characteristics and Business Performance: How Leadership Traits Shape Strategy, Culture, and Long-Term Value Creation

keywords: how CEO traits affect firm performance
CEO decision making and company outcomes

detail.abstract: The role of the chief executive officer occupies a unique position in modern organizations. While firms are complex systems shaped by markets, institutions, and teams, the CEO remains the central figure responsible for setting direction, allocating resources, and interpreting uncertainty. Over decades of research in economics, management, and organizational behavior, scholars and practitioners alike have returned to a persistent question: how much do CEO characteristics actually matter for business performance? Empirical evidence increasingly suggests that CEOs are not interchangeable. Differences in background, cognition, experience, and personal traits systematically influence strategic choices and performance outcomes. In environments characterized by volatility and rapid change, these differences become even more pronounced. Understanding how CEO characteristics shape business performance provides valuable insight for boards, investors, entrepreneurs, and policymakers seeking to improve organizational effectiveness and long-term value creation.

title: Optimal Procurement of Newsvendor Facing Correlated Supply and Demand
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Faculty of Business, Lingnan University, The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Department of Decision Sciences & Managerial Economics

detail.title: Optimal Procurement of Newsvendor Facing Correlated Supply and Demand
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the procurement problem of a newsvendor sourcing from one reliable and multiple unreliable suppliers to meet a stochastic demand. Recognizing systemic factorssuch as macroeconomic trends or global disruptions-make these uncertainties correlated, we examine how the inter-dependencies impact which suppliers should be selected. Methodology and Results: We study a stochastic optimization model that accommodates arbitrary dependence structures among uncertain supply capacities and demand for a newsvendor's procurement problem. To address its inherent nonconvexity, we introduce a novel marginal benefit analysis method that leverages relational stochastic orders (e.g., supermodular and negative association orders) to derive an indicator for supplier advantages. We identify two correlation-driven mechanisms that justify procuring from a supplier beyond cost alone: the demandmatching effect, where a supplier's capacity is positively correlated with demand, and the supply-hedging effect, where a supplier's capacity is negatively correlated with that of others. These effects can make the newsvendor order from high-cost unreliable suppliers, thereby violating the traditional Cost-First Rule. We also show the main findings continue to hold in the risk-averse setting with a CVaR objective. Managerial implications: Our findings suggest that procurement managers should look beyond unit costs when selecting suppliers and instead consider the correlation structure of supply and demand uncertainties. Suppliers that appear inefficient based on cost alone may provide significant value through risk mitigation, and ignoring these dependencies can lead to suboptimal procurement strategies with significant losses.

title: Learning from Success: Sales-Optimized Advertisement Generation in Short Video Marketing
affiliations: Boston University, Boston University and University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business

detail.title: Learning from Success: Sales-Optimized Advertisement Generation in Short Video Marketing
detail.abstract: Short-video advertising has become a dominant form of digital marketing, but most sponsored videos fail to generate revenue. A central cause is the difficulty of crafting an effective shootable script, a multimodal, scene-level blueprint that integrates text, visuals, and selling cues considering both creator and product context. While existing Generative AI tools lower production costs, they are optimized for linguistic fluency rather than commercial effectiveness and fail to internalize the persuasive structures that drive sales. This misalignment limits their value for advertisers and platforms that focus on conversions. To address this challenge, we propose a Sales-Optimized Video Ad Generation Framework (SOVAG), that constructs and optimized shootable scripts. Leveraging a large-scale dataset of sponsored TikTok videos, we first extract structured multimodal representations of human-authored advertising video that aligns real content production and is compatible to downstream generation. We then introduce Sales-Optimized Fine-Tuning (SOFT), which utilizes Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) as an outcome-weighted supervision signal to guide the model toward creative patterns co-occurring with commercial success. This design enables the model to transfer effective narrative structures to underperforming content while remaining robust to the extreme skew of sales data. We conduct comprehensive evaluations, including quantitative benchmarks and human experiments with consumers and creators, demonstrating that SOVAG-generated scripts significantly increase purchase intentions and enhance production efficiency (by 11% and 35% respectively compared to standard SFT). Post hoc interpretability analysis reveals that our framework shapes effective content generation by selectively emphasizing high-impact persuasive features, such as call-to-action and outcome demonstration, that are most strongly associated with revenue. Our work illustrates how design-oriented AI can bridge content production and measurable marketing performance.

title: Balancing Efficiency and Stability in Multi-Rider Ridesharing Systems
affiliations: Florida Atlantic University - Department of Information Technology & Operations Management and James Madison University

detail.title: Balancing Efficiency and Stability in Multi-Rider Ridesharing Systems
detail.abstract: Most ridesharing research focuses on enhancing overall efficiency, such as reducing total travel distance or increasing platform profits. However, an efficient solution may not be ideal for every group of riders. In shared rides, a rider's experience is shaped not only by cost but also by the composition of co-riders, which affects pickup delays, detours, and overall ride quality. As a result, certain groups of riders may envy alternative feasible ride arrangements that could have matched them together and offered a better experience in terms of cost, travel time, or convenience. These groups, who collectively have an incentive to prefer a different feasible match over the one assigned, are referred to as blocking coalitions. The presence of such coalitions leads to instability, making the platform vulnerable to losing riders to competing services that offer more attractive ride options. We propose two optimization paradigms to address stability in multi-rider ridesharing systems. The first approach develops optimization models that directly incorporate stability requirements into the matching process. The second approach introduces a novel side-payment scheme that takes an efficient matching as input and allocates side-payments to selected market participants to reduce or eliminate instability. Our numerical analyses highlight the effectiveness of our proposed approaches to balance efficiency and stability across a variety of scenarios and instability metrics.

title: Can Modern Scholarship Escape AI?
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Can Modern Scholarship Escape AI?

contentFormat.other: Satirical paper that uses the format to make an intellectual point

detail.abstract: As AI use statements become an expected component of scholarly publishing, a deceptively straight forward question arises: is it possible for contemporary scholarship to be conducted without artificial intelligence? This paper investigates the question and arrives at an equally straight forward answer: no. Through a comprehensive AI use disclosure that extends well beyond the usual accounting of chatbot interactions, the paper reveals just how deeply AI is embedded in the infrastructure of modern research — from the machine learning algorithms that surface literature, to the AI-optimized systems that manage energy grids, climate control, and the devices on which scholarship is produced. In doing so, it exposes a fundamental tension at the heart of current scholarship and AI disclosure norms: scholars are being asked to draw boundaries around AI use that no longer meaningfully exist. The paper suggests that the scholarly community's emerging approach to AI transparency, while well-intentioned, rests on assumptions about the separability of human and machine contributions that are increasingly difficult to sustain.

title: A Novel Approach to Trading Strategy Parameter Optimization, using Double Out-of-Sample Data and Walk-Forward Techniques
affiliations: and University of Warsaw - Faculty of Economic Sciences

detail.title: A Novel Approach to Trading Strategy Parameter Optimization, using Double Out-of-Sample Data and Walk-Forward Techniques

keywords: Rolling window optimization JEL Codes: C4

detail.abstract: This study introduces a novel approach to walk-forward optimization by parameterizing the lengths of training and testing windows. We demonstrate that the performance of a trading strategy using the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) evaluated within a walk-forward procedure based on the Robust Sharpe Ratio is highly dependent on the chosen window size. We investigated the strategy on intraday Bitcoin data at six frequencies (1 minute to 60 minutes) using 81 combinations of walk-forward window lengths (1 day to 28 days) over a 19-month training period. The two best-performing parameter sets from the training data were applied to a 21-month out-of-sample testing period to ensure data independence. The strategy was only executed once during the testing period. To further validate the framework, strategy parameters estimated on Bitcoin were applied to Binance Coin and Ethereum. Our results suggest the robustness of our custom approach. In the training period for Bitcoin, all combinations of walk-forward windows outperformed a Buy-and-Hold strategy. During the testing period, the strategy performed similarly to Buy-and-Hold but with lower drawdown and a higher Information Ratio. Similar results were observed for Binance Coin and Ethereum. The real strength was demonstrated when a portfolio combining Buy-and-Hold with our strategies outperformed all individual strategies and Buy-and-Hold alone, achieving the highest overall performance and a 50reduction in drawdown. A conservative fee of 0.1% per transaction was included in all calculations. A cost sensitivity analysis was performed as a sanity check, revealing that the strategy's break-even point was around 0.4% per transaction. This research highlights the importance of optimizing walk-forward window lengths and emphasizing the value of single-time out-of-sample testing for reliable strategy evaluation.

title: The Economics of Galamsey: Why Miners Choose Illegality Over Formal Employment An Institutional Economics Analysis
affiliations: University of Cape Coast Ghana

detail.title: The Economics of Galamsey: Why Miners Choose Illegality Over Formal Employment An Institutional Economics Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper examines the economic rationale behind the decision of artisanal and small-scale miners in Ghana to operate illegally rather than within the formal regulatory framework. Drawing on institutional economics, particularly the work of Douglass North and Oliver Williamson, the paper argues that the persistence of galamsey is not primarily a consequence of individual deviance but rather a predictable outcome of institutional deficiencies. These deficiencies render formalisation prohibitively costly and economically irrational for most miners. Through an analysis of the transaction costs of licensing, the structure of property rights over mineral-bearing land, and comparative income data from formal and informal employment, the paper demonstrates that Ghana's institutional environment creates a systematic incentive structure that favours illegality. Case studies from the Ashanti, Western, and Eastern regions illustrate how these institutional failures manifest at the local level, compounded by foreign capital involvement, corruption, and patronage politics. The paper contributes to the development economics literature on resource governance and informality by offering an institutionalist framework for understanding why enforcement-led approaches to galamsey have consistently failed. It concludes with policy recommendations centred on reducing transaction costs, decentralising licensing, and aligning the regulatory framework with the socioeconomic realities of artisanal miners.

title: Measuring Humanness in the Age of AI: The Fitrah Verification Protocol for Institutional Hiring, Governance, and AI Integration

detail.abstract:
Contemporary organizations confront an authenticity challenge of unprecedented scope. Artificial intelligence systems have developed capacity to simulate human communication, reasoning, and even moral discourse with sophistication that existing verification methods cannot reliably distinguish from authentic human agency. This paper presents the Fitrah Verification Protocol (FVP), a faculty-based assessment methodology that identifies people capable of authentic agency within institutional contexts. 

FVP operates from the principle that human authenticity cannot be faked at scale because authentic agency is rooted in institutional reality: real stakes, real consequences, real relational vulnerability. FVP comprises four assessment stages identifying institutional context, presenting faculty-exercise scenarios, assessing value-choice coherence, and evaluating institutional fit. Rather than assessing surface characteristics or isolated traits, FVP examines faculty-based indicators of authentic human presence—dimensions resistant to simulation because they require institutional substrate to develop.

The protocol addresses two threats: external (bad actors using AI to impersonate humans) and internal (institutional automation systematically eroding human capacity). FVP provides methodology for both hiring and organizational governance, integrating the Fitrah Framework (universal human faculties) with institutional design principles (IACM) to create conditions where authentic agency becomes visible and valued.

Implementation demonstrates that organizations moving from trait-based to authenticity-based hiring and governance witness measurable improvements: authentic leadership development, cultural coherence, retention, and excellence emerging through human contribution rather than optimization pressure.

Operationally, the Fitrah Verification Protocol integrates: the Eight-Faculty ontology of the Fitrah Framework (Paper 1), the signal-to-noise measurement doctrine of Evidence-Based BehavioralCognitive Assessment (Paper 2), and the authority domain architecture of Institutional Authority Constitutional Mechanics (Paper 3). This yields a complete verification system: faculty-based measurement within institutionally-sound governance structures, enabling organizations to distinguish authentic human agency from AI simulation at scale. 

The protocol is ready for institutional implementation, research validation, and integration into hiring, governance, and AI systems design.

title:
Institutional Authority Constitutional Mechanics (IACM):
A Non-Psychological Framework for Diagnosing and Designing Authority Architectures
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Institutional Authority Constitutional Mechanics (IACM):
A Non-Psychological Framework for Diagnosing and Designing Authority Architectures

detail.abstract:
Modern institutions—from government agencies to corporations and AI systems—suffer recurring breakdowns that outlive leadership changes and culture initiatives. Yet most governance literature focuses on mindsets (culture) or individuals (bad actors), overlooking the underlying architecture of authority and decision-making. 

We present Institutional Authority Constitutional Mechanics (IACM), a framework that diagnoses and designs institutional governance as assemblies of authority domains rather than as psychological or cultural entities. IACM reframes the central governance question: not "Who is to blame?" but "How are decisions arranged?"

IACM explicitly abstracts away from individual psychology—intentionally deferring to the EightFaculty ontology and measurement frameworks of the Fitrah Framework (Paper 1) and Evidence- Based Behavioral-Cognitive Assessment (Paper 2)—to focus purely on structural decision-making arrangements. The eight authority domains exist precisely to protect institutional conditions where authentic human faculty expression becomes visible, measurable, and valued, as formalized in the Fitrah Verification Protocol (Paper 4). 

IACM identifies eight irreducible authority domains—Zeus (authorization), Hera (principles), Athena (oversight), Artemis (appeal), Hermes (information), Ares (execution), Nemesis (enforcement), and Hades (termination)—and specifies the minimal set of counter-links (checks and balances) needed to satisfy five stability invariants. 

The framework operationalizes structural pathology as a mismatch: when delegated authority persistently exceeds the system's built-in containment capacity (veto, appeal, shutdown authority). IACM is explicitly artifact-driven: institutions are diagnosed using charters, meeting records, audit logs, and policies—never by speculating about leader motives or culture. 

Historical case analysis demonstrates that institutional failures (NASA Shuttle program, Enron, FTX, Volkswagen emissions scandal) all exhibit missing domains or incomplete counter-links. We propose specific structural remedies: establish independent oversight boards, formalize shutdown authority, implement transparent information flows, create robust appeals mechanisms. 

IACM extends to AI governance by mapping domains to technical controls. Many AI failures simply mirror classical institutional flaws—missing oversight or appeal processes. The thesis is that stable governance requires: every power accompanied by a built-in check, every decision reversible through appeal, every process terminable by designated authority, and all actions traceable and reviewable.

title: Gap Based Learning in Markets

detail.title: Gap Based Learning in Markets
detail.abstract: We consider a broad class of learning algorithms, which we dub gap-based algorithms (GBAs). At a high level, GBA's quantify an algorithm's sensitivity-how quickly they penalize (prune) sub-optimal actions-and tolerance-the threshold level of sub-optimality separating which actions are explored frequently or pruned. As these natural conditions are satisfied by many popular learning algorithms such as Hedge and e t-greedy, GBAs are ubiquitous in both theory and practice. Our main contribution is a set of conditions on the agents' sensitivities and tolerances that guarantee that the corresponding GBA dynamics avoid convergence towards certain Nash equilibria (NE). In particular, let S n (p) denote agent n's set of substitutes-actions that are jointly optimal but unsupported at NE p. In order for the dynamics to converge to p, the sub-optimalities of any a e S n (p) must grow more quickly than agent n's tolerance, where these sub-optimalities can be expressed as a function of their opponents' sensitivities. Conversely, if this sub-optimality grows slowly, then the dynamics cannot converge to p. With this in mind, we give two sets of conditions-one on the algorithms' parameters and the second on the game itself-which guarantee non-convergence regardless of the initial behavior or history of the dynamics. Our results have interesting implications for equilibrium selection in various economic settings such as the first price and uniform price auctions.
