detail.abstract: This project investigates the quality of management practices in manufacturing plants in the Western Balkans. In particular, we focus on modern operations, quality of monitoring, target setting, and incentive management skills applied within manufacturing plants. Our goal was to assess and benchmark the management practices in the Western Balkans region for which very limited information is available so far. We evaluate management practices by defining the concept of “god" and “bad" management practices on a scale from 1 to 5 across key management practices used by organizations across different manufacturing sectors. We do this by using an innovative and rich study design that includes a survey, qualitative interviews, and secondary data. We provide practically relevant findings for policymakers, managers of manufacturing companies, as well as for industrial education and consultancy firms, who can provide potential solutions to improve the effectiveness of management practices.

title: Selling Self-Disruptive Technologies: Identity-Compatible Advantage and the Role-Level Microfoundations of Automation Adoption
affiliations: Harvard Business School and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: Selling Self-Disruptive Technologies: Identity-Compatible Advantage and the Role-Level Microfoundations of Automation Adoption

keywords: Selling and Deploying AI and automation solutions in B2B markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Business School Working Paper No. 26-050

detail.abstract:
Despite massive investment in artificial intelligence and automation, many high‑value technology projects stall after approval or are adopted only symbolically, especially in B2B markets where adoption depends on the endorsement of managers whose roles are disrupted by the technology. We argue that dominant adoption theories focused on firm‑level readiness, usefulness, and institutional pressure overlook a central marketing problem: selling and governing technologies that undermine the approving role itself.

We introduce Self‑Disruptive Technologies (SDTs), offerings that enhance organizational performance while eroding the authority, discretion, or span of control of the role responsible for approving them.  We develop Identity‑Compatible Advantage (ICA), a complementary bundle of seller‑designed solution and governance mechanisms that enables approvers to endorse automation without identity loss and shapes approval, implementation depth, and diffusion under identity threat. Integrating organizational buying, role identity, and innovation adoption theories, we advance propositions that shift attention from organizational resistance to role‑level threat, showing how bundled ICA mechanisms convert symbolic into substantive adoption and accelerate diffusion in B2B AI markets.

title: Research on the Input-Output Efficiency Model of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) in Financial Supply Chains
affiliations: , Independent, Independent, Cornell University, ,  and University of Michigan

detail.title: Research on the Input-Output Efficiency Model of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) in Financial Supply Chains
detail.abstract: This study focuses on the input-output efficiency of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) in financial supply chains, aiming to address the efficiency evaluation dilemma caused by the multi-factor input and multi-objective output characteristics of RPA application. Based on the theory of data envelopment analysis (DEA), the study constructs a three-stage DEA efficiency evaluation model that incorporates environmental variables and stochastic errors. It selects core indicators such as RPA deployment cost, technical maintenance input, transaction processing speed, and capital turnover rate from the dimensions of resource input and benefit output. Empirical analysis is conducted on 32 financial supply chain enterprises. The results show that the model effectively eliminates the interference of external environmental factors, and the evaluation results are more consistent with the actual operation status of enterprises. Moreover, the rational allocation of technical maintenance resources significantly improves the input-output efficiency of RPA. This research provides a scientific evaluation tool for enterprises to optimize RPA application strategies and enhances the operational efficiency of financial supply chains.

title: Hybrid VARIMA-Machine Learning Models for Multivariate Macroeconomic and Energy Forecasting
affiliations: ,  and Independent

detail.title: Hybrid VARIMA-Machine Learning Models for Multivariate Macroeconomic and Energy Forecasting
detail.abstract: Accurate forecasting of macroeconomic and energy time series is complicated by structural instability, strong cross-dependencies, and pervasive nonlinear dynamics. While VARIMA models provide a transparent multivariate framework for linear shock propagation, they often leave economically meaningful structure in forecast residuals. Conversely, machine learning methods offer flexibility but may suffer from instability and limited interpretability in multivariate economic environments. This paper proposes a residual-based hybrid forecasting framework that integrates VARIMA and machine learning in a disciplined and interpretable manner. VARIMA serves as a linear filter capturing common dynamics across macroeconomic, financial, and energy variables, while machine learning models estimate nonlinear corrections from multivariate residuals. Using monthly data from 1999 to 2025, including multiple crisis episodes, we document systematic violations of linear model assumptions through extensive diagnostics. Out-of-sample results show that hybrid models consistently outperform both standalone VARIMA and pure machine learning approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness, particularly during periods of stress. The findings highlight residual-based hybridization as an effective and economically interpretable strategy for multivariate forecasting.

title: Energy Efficiency and Sustainability in 5G Network Deployments
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Energy Efficiency and Sustainability in 5G Network Deployments
detail.abstract: Concerns about the energy and environmental impact of the world's rapid implementation of fifth-generation (5G) mobile networks are growing. Achieving ultra-high data rates, low latency, and massive connectivity requires the construction of extremely dense network architectures, and small cell networks, as well as massive multiple-input (MIMO) technologies, and edge computing. These technologies increase energy consumption and carbon footprints on a global scale (Chochliouros et al.; Williams et al.). This study focuses on the 5G energy and sustainability challenges. This study uses a systematic literature synthesis and a comparative study of the state of the art in energy-efficient literature and applicable frameworks for sustainability to evaluate existing solutions and identify prevailing gaps (Maiwada et al.; Usama and Erol-Kantarci). Based on the results, the authors identify the most significant negative consequences of sub-optimal network performance to cover larger gaps in energy consumption and explain the result of most network buildouts: cardinally optimized energy cost expansion resulting from a disproportionate increase in network capacity. The potential of recent advances such as artificial intelligence (AI) network optimization, traffic-aware resource management, and high-quality service (QoS) integration of renewable energy to resolve these challenges is underscored (Israr et al.; Mughees et al.). The study outlines the need for a comprehensive, multi-dimensional, and holistic approach towards the designing of sustainable 5G networks, adopting an energy-aware network framework and intelligent control machinery, alongside the introduction of corresponding policies and regulations to address the technological and ecological impacts of rapid advancement (Ichimescu et al.; Lorincz et al.).

title: Paying for Good Behavior: What is the Optimal Incentive Structure?
affiliations: Purdue University - College of Agriculture

detail.title: Paying for Good Behavior: What is the Optimal Incentive Structure?
detail.abstract: When policy makers want individuals to adopt behaviors that are individually or socially beneficial (e.g. smoking cessation, healthy eating, healthy activities, etc), one option is to offer monetary incentives. The payoff function for the policy maker in this class of problems may have the ``common values'' property from the principal-agent literature, where the principal benefits when some types of agents perform but not others.  For example, in the realm of healthy eating, the principal may derive more value from unhealthy people improving their diets than people who are already healthy.  When the agent type is unknown  to the principal, Laffont and Martimort (2002) find that pooling incentive schemes can be optimal under a very stringent assumption on the principal's benefit function, which causes the monotonicity condition to be violated.  I show that this assumption can be relaxed and pooling incentives are still optimal, suggesting that the optimality of pooling incentives is fairly robust.  An implication of this finding is that monetary incentives for good behavior can be fairly simple, with no need to structure complex screening menus that try to induce agents to self-select into customized incentive plans.

title: Not in My Backyard, But in My City:Experimental Evidence on What Motivates Citizens to Co-design
affiliations: Incheon National University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Not in My Backyard, But in My City:Experimental Evidence on What Motivates Citizens to Co-design
detail.abstract: Much of the NIMBY literature explains why residents oppose controversial facilities and often treats self-interest as a core driver of local resistance. We shift the focus from opposition to engagement by examining citizens’ willingness to co-design in contested siting contexts. Drawing on a vignette experiment in urban South Korea centered on a proposed mental health rehabilitation facility, we test whether motivational framing shapes willingness to co-design, comparing a proximity-based self-interest frame (“in front of my home”) with a broader community-interest frame (“in my city”), and we assess the role of participation self-efficacy. Results show that the self-interest frame increases willingness to co-design relative to the community-interest frame. Participation self-efficacy also strongly predicts both willingness to co-design and willingness to receive additional information about local public hearings. Public service motivation is positively associated with willingness to co-design but does not condition framing effects. Open-ended responses underscore that perceived capability and procedural confidence frequently determine whether residents engage, often more than civic-minded appeals. Overall, the findings suggest that co-design under local conflict depends not only on aligning interests, but also on strengthening residents’ capacity to participate. We argue that cities aiming to make co-design workable in contentious settings should invest early in efficacy-building interventions, including clear role expectations, accessible participation routes, and low-stakes entry points that allow residents to contribute and see tangible influence on decisions.

title: Crossing the Threshold: Employment Regulation, Firm Behaviour and Labour Market Flexibility in Italy

detail.title: Crossing the Threshold: Employment Regulation, Firm Behaviour and Labour Market Flexibility in Italy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 983
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines how employment protection legislation and firing costs affect firm size growth and workforce composition in Italy (as a ratio of temporary to permanent employment), with a particular focus on recent labour market reforms. The analysis is based on administrative firm-level data from the Italian private sector, with a specific focus on firm outcomes above the 15-employee threshold, where stricter employment regulations apply. Using a linear probability model, we find that firms near this threshold are less likely to grow in terms of employee numbers. Furthermore, the discontinuity in employment protection influences the composition of the workforce, leading to a higher incidence of temporary contracts above the threshold. We apply a difference-in-discontinuities approach to examine the heterogeneity in the threshold effect during a period of labour market reforms. Our results suggest that recent reforms have had negligible effects on the discontinuity in firms’ employment growth. As for the use of flexible contracts, we observe a mitigation of the threshold effect after the regulatory changes.

title: Deep Learning Driven Metaheuristic for Enhancing Vehicle Routing Solutions
affiliations: Athens University of Economics and Business, Athens University of Economics and Business and Athens University of Economics and Business - Department of Management Science and Technology

detail.title: Deep Learning Driven Metaheuristic for Enhancing Vehicle Routing Solutions
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the integration of machine learning techniques with classical optimization methodologies to address the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), a well-known NP-hard problem in logistics. Traditional approaches leverage heuristics and metaheuristics, such as GRASP and VND, but often struggle with adaptability and efficiency at large scale. Recent advancements in deep learning offer new opportunities for enhanced solution quality and computational efficiency. This study proposes a novel hybrid methodology combining Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP), Variable Neighborhood Descent (VND), and a Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE). The GINE model classifies initial solutions as promising or unpromising, enabling selective local search refinement and potential computational savings. Empirical evaluation on benchmark CVRP instances demonstrates that the hybrid GINE-GRASP-VND approach achieves moderate classification accuracy, generalizes beyond training sizes, and shows stronger improvements on large problems. Results suggest the value of machine learning augmentation in metaheuristics but highlight the challenges of feature design and generalization.

title: Analytics for Better Urban Cycling at the City of Toronto
affiliations: University of Toronto, University of Toronto - Department of Civil & Mineral Engineering, University of Toronto and University of Toronto, Mechanical and Industrial Engineering Department

detail.title: Analytics for Better Urban Cycling at the City of Toronto
detail.abstract: Cycling is an effective way to promote healthy lifestyles, improve urban mobility, and combat climate change. However, safety and comfort concerns remain major barriers to cycling uptake globally. To make cycling safer and more inviting, we collaborated with the City of Toronto to develop and implement a suite of analytics tools for urban bike infrastructure planning. First, we propose a descriptive analytics framework that assesses cycling stress-the discomfort cyclists experience-on each road segment and quantifies the network's low-stress cycling accessibility. This framework has been used to evaluate over ten bike infrastructure projects in Toronto and to estimate the infrastructure budget required to meet the city's net-zero target. Building on this framework, we develop an optimization model that identifies optimal locations for new bike lanes. This model is a large-scale bilevel program that cannot be solved with existing techniques. In response, we develop a machine learning-augmented optimization method that is computationally tractable and can generate provably high-quality solutions. From 2022 to 2024, this approach would have matched the performance of Toronto's implemented plan while reducing the required lane length by 25%, saving an estimated 18 million Canadian dollars. As of March 2025, 29.1 km of bike lanes recommended by our model had been approved by Toronto City Council for construction between 2025 and 2027, with an additional 27.6 km under study for future implementation. Finally, we introduce a predictive model and a web application to support broader application of our methods. The predictive model assesses cycling stress based on street-view images, enabling deployment in cities lacking detailed road network data. The web application enables interactive refinement of optimization results, allowing practitioners to engage seamlessly with our tools. As urban centers increasingly prioritize sustainable transportation, this work offers a scalable and user-friendly framework for leveraging analytics to guide impactful infrastructure decisions.

detail.abstract: This article is devoted to the competitive advantages within asset management and brokerage services markets. Strategic management decisions play a crucial role in the operations of modern asset management and brokerage companies. They involve formulating long-term strategies in a competitive market environment to achieve optimal resource allocation and enhance competitive advantage. title:
The Allocation-Insurance Fallacy 
Why Institutions Designed for Efficiency Fail at Protection
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
The Allocation-Insurance Fallacy 
Why Institutions Designed for Efficiency Fail at Protection

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest associated with this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual and theoretical analysis. It does not involve human participants, personal data, experiments, or interventions. As such, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently without institutional or commercial sponsorship.

detail.abstract:
Modern public institutions are predominantly designed to solve allocation problems, managing scarcity through marginal optimization, comparability, and ex post evaluation. This design performs well when risks are frequent, incremental, and broadly predictable. However, many of the most consequential risks faced by contemporary societies-such as pandemics and systemic financial crises-are low-frequency, high-impact events with irreversible consequences. 
This paper identifies a recurring institutional error, termed the Allocation-Insurance Fallacy, which arises when such risks are governed using allocation-oriented decision frameworks. In these contexts, uncertainty is reinterpreted as insufficient evidence, protective capacity appears as inefficiency, and ex ante insurance is gradually eroded despite its critical function. Using a conceptual framework and two illustrative cases-pandemic preparedness and financial stability-the paper shows how institutions can act rationally and in good faith while systematically undermining their own protective role. The resulting failures are not anomalies or policy mistakes, but predictable outcomes of a structural mismatch between decision logic and risk regime.

title: Generative Organizational Learning: Affordances for New Modes of Knowledge Search, Creation, Transfer, and Forgetting with LLMs Batia M. Wiesenfeld NYU Stern School of Business

detail.title: Generative Organizational Learning: Affordances for New Modes of Knowledge Search, Creation, Transfer, and Forgetting with LLMs Batia M. Wiesenfeld NYU Stern School of Business

publicationDetails.detailsText: NYU Stern School of Business Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: New York University Stern School of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Scholars of organizational learning typically focus on how organizations operate in an environment of domain knowledge scarcity, assuming that knowledge abundance is a highly sought after, but fundamentally elusive, goal. In our case study of organizational learning at Northeast Health, we find that generative AI, in combination with actors' goals and organizational institutions, may afford a new form of learning that we call generative organizational learning enabling innovation in the service of organizational goals. In particular, generative catalyzing, iterating, and personalizing may enable abundance rather than scarcity of domain knowledge-both useful and risky. At the same time, actors, institutions, and GenAI's limitations and capabilities may afford processes of generative curating and guardrailing that facilitate knowledge forgetting to limit the abundance of risky domain knowledge. Our model extends the current understanding of organizational learning by exploring how these new affordances enable the development of scalable solutions with GenAI.

title: Generative Pretrained Transformers for Investor-Centric Portfolio Construction
affiliations: Athens University of Economics and Business and Athens University of Economics and Business - Department of Management Science and Technology

detail.title: Generative Pretrained Transformers for Investor-Centric Portfolio Construction
detail.abstract: The objective of this paper is to examine the application of generative artificial intelligence in personalized portfolio construction and evaluate its performance relative to traditional benchmarks. A generative AI model, specifically OpenAI's GPT-4o, was employed to construct investment portfolios for ten virtual investor profiles over a fixed three month investment horizon. The methodology involved prompting the model to create portfolio allocations, followed by performance evaluation using financial metrics including total return, volatility, beta, Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown. All AI-generated portfolios outperformed the S&P 500 index over the investment period, demonstrating stronger risk-adjusted returns and lower drawdowns. These results highlight the potential of large language models to synthesize financial data and produce competitive investment strategies. The study contributes to the growing body of research on AIdriven decision-making in finance and provides a foundation for the development of generative models tailored to asset and wealth management.

title: Defining the Field of Law and Macroeconomics: A Framework from International Monetary Law
affiliations: University of Miami, School of Law and Tulane University - Law School

detail.title: Defining the Field of Law and Macroeconomics: A Framework from International Monetary Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Miami Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Miami School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This Article proposes an analytical framework for defining the contours of the emerging field of law and macroeconomics drawing on the International Monetary Fund’s principle of “macro-criticality.” Such a framework can help steer scholarly debate toward a clearer understanding of the relationship between law and the economy and inform policymaking within that domain. In its native context, the macro-criticality principle limits the IMF’s jurisdiction to policy areas that are critical for member countries’ domestic and external stability. The IMF’s approach distinguishes between a core set of macrocritical policies and other non-core policies that are contextually macrocritical. Over time, the IMF has refined its approach for determining whether and when a policy area falls within the non-core category. Recently such policies have included those related to corruption, climate change, and gender equality. Translating the IMF’s framework to the field of law and macroeconomics suggests that the field has a core subset of topics that include legal and institutional aspects of the main levers that impact the macro-economy, like trade, monetary, exchange rate, financial regulation, and fiscal policies. Beyond this core, the field includes legal and institutional issues and policy areas that can significantly impact macroeconomic performance, even under specific narrow circumstances or at the margins. This framework provides a systematic analytical approach to defining the scope and contours of the field. It also underscores that the field provides an academic home for a number of topics that tend to be lost in the existing array of other legal academic fields and helps draw attention to the IMF itself as an international regulator of domestic macroeconomic policies and performance.

title: Navigating the Unknown: The Sociocultural and Metacognitive Architecture of Wisdom

publicationDetails.detailsText: Annual Review of Psychology, Volume 78. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-020226-034154

detail.abstract: Psychological wisdom research has shifted from characterizing rare exemplars to specifying processes that support sound judgment under uncertainty. Yet it has advanced along two siloed tracks: research on folk theories (cultural tools such as proverbs, heuristics, exemplars, and narratives) and scientific models of mechanisms involved in wise judgment. This review bridges these research tracks using a situated metacognitive lens: folk theories provide candidate attributes or strategies for action, whereas perspectival metacognition-the capacity to recognize epistemic limits, coordinate viewpoints, and track uncertainty and change-regulates their context-sensitive selection and use. We synthesize evidence connecting wisdom-related processes to emotional balance, relational well-being, cooperation, and reduced polarization, while noting boundary conditions. We show how this synthesis sharpens measurement trade-offs, highlighting limits of global self-report and advances in situated assessment. Finally, we summarize work on development and cultivation (from brief prompts to practice-based habit formation), and consider socio-ecological implications in an AI-shaped world.

title: Creative Hybrids: How Generative AI Reconfigures Skill Demand in Design Occupations
affiliations: University of Potsdam - Hasso-Plattner Institut and Goethe University Frankfurt

detail.title: Creative Hybrids: How Generative AI Reconfigures Skill Demand in Design Occupations
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about how creative work is reorganized. While existing debates focus on automation versus augmentation, there is limited empirical evidence on how generative AI reshapes the composition of skills demanded within creative occupations. This study examines changes in skill demand in design occupations following the widespread availability of generative AI in late 2022. Using longitudinal job-posting data from the Job-SDF dataset, we analyze monthly skill demand before and after December 2022. We apply semantic clustering to group skills into coherent capability domains and examine shifts in normalized skill shares to capture compositional changes in employer demand. This approach allows us to identify how the relative importance of different skills evolves over time. The results reveal a systematic reallocation of skill demand within design roles. Demand declines for execution-intensive and technical skills, particularly manual and visual production, while demand increases for creativity, strategic thinking, branding, communication, and coordination-related capabilities. Skill-level analyses support these patterns, indicating that changes are not driven by isolated skills but reflect broader role restructuring. We interpret these findings through the lens of creative hybridization, arguing that generative AI shifts designers' roles away from manual execution toward framing, orchestration, and strategic direction. The study contributes to research on creative work and human-AI collaboration by providing longitudinal evidence on how generative technologies reorganize skill demand within occupations.

title: A Foot in the Door: Seller Preferences for Surcharges

detail.title: A Foot in the Door: Seller Preferences for Surcharges

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval for the experiments in this study was obtained from Newcastle University (#31517/ #43665) and McGill University (# 23-04-048).

detail.abstract: This paper studies holdups in markets where sellers may impose undisclosed surcharges. While prior work has examined price transparency's role in market outcomes, the distinct effect of a transparency norm-separate from a fairness norm-remains unestablished. We formulate a simple model that separates these norms and characterizes their equilibrium implications across different market settings. The model shows that price competition yields higher buyer surplus than ultimatum bargaining and that this surplus increases with transparency concerns but decreases with fairness concerns because of softened competition. Compulsory surcharges cannot be higher in bargaining, as sellers prefer a higher price to a higher surcharge as long as it does not change the buyer's probability of acceptance. Experimental results confirm the transparency norm's influence: Total prices are lower with price competition, and surcharges are lower with ultimatum bargaining. Additionally, surcharges rise when pricing is outside of the seller's control. Estimates of the behavioral parameters reveal that sellers weigh transparency at least as heavily as fairness. The results imply that firms fearing holdups should still procure goods and services in competitive market structures.

title: Supporting Expat Partners' Career Reinvention Implications for Global Mobility Policies, HR Practices, and Integration System
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Supporting Expat Partners' Career Reinvention Implications for Global Mobility Policies, HR Practices, and Integration System
detail.abstract: Despite growing attention to international mobility and global talent management, the career trajectories of expat partners remain largely marginalized within organizational and policy frameworks. Existing research has documented identity disruption, structural barriers to career re-entry, and the role of psychological resources in adaptation processes among expat partners. However, limited attention has been paid to how these insights can be translated into systemic support mechanisms within global mobility programs and host-country integration systems. Building on prior conceptual work on identity reconstruction, career adaptation, and Psychological Capital, this article argues that expat partners' career outcomes constitute a strategic factor influencing assignment success, employee well-being, and long-term organizational performance. The paper critically examines the limitations of current global mobility practices, highlights the role of Psychological Capital as a leverage point for intervention, and proposes a holistic support model integrating organizational, HR, and policy-level responses. By reframing expat partner career reinvention as a shared responsibility rather than a private challenge, the article contributes to global mobility literature and offers actionable implications for organizations and policymakers seeking more sustainable and inclusive international assignment strategies.

detail.abstract: We present a novel application of reversible computing principles to federal and commercial procurement win probability scoring. Reversible computation-where every operation is invertible-provides three simultaneous guarantees required by FAR/DFARS-compliant AI: accuracy via information-preserving transformations, explainability via algorithmic uncomputation (the Bennett Trick), and efficiency via energy recovery at the hardware level. We survey the foundational theory (Landauer, Bennett, Fredkin-Toffoli), catalog the arXiv research landscape and USPTO patent corpus, identify an unoccupied patent gap in reversible Bayesian networks for procurement scoring, and propose a three-layer Reversible Win Probability Engine with measurable hypotheses. Hardware validation from Vaire Computing's Ice River chip (2025) demonstrates 1.77× energy recovery in 22nm CMOS, establishing near-term feasibility for edge-deployed procurement analytics on mobile data centers.

title: Stability in Networked Markets
affiliations: ISO New England, Market Development and University of Notre Dame

detail.title: Stability in Networked Markets
detail.abstract: Networked industries often rely on long-lived infrastructure whose operational availability can be controlled within the trading window. We study a two-sided transferable-utility matching model in which coalitions can withhold access to connections, thereby changing the active network on which trade is settled. This creates a network disruption externality: by altering outsiders' feasible options, a deviating coalition changes the settlement environment itself, so fixed-network core stability need not imply decentralized viability. We define network stability relative to a settlement rule and show that it coincides with the core of a derived network disruption game. Existence is characterized by Bondareva--Shapley balancedness, and a decomposition isolates when instability is driven by disruption rents rather than within-network rematching. Institutionally, a punishment benchmark yields a conservative impossibility test and highlights simple network primitives that guarantee nonexistence for all settlement rules. A design benchmark—disruption internalization—restores stability.

title: Optimizing Airline Logistics Stock Control: The Strategic Role of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)

detail.title: Optimizing Airline Logistics Stock Control: The Strategic Role of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
detail.abstract: This study examines the critical role of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) in enhancing inventory accuracy, supplier reliability, and overall stock control efficiency within airline logistics operations. Employing a mixed-methods approach that integrates quantitative analysis of KPIs with qualitative insights from industry experts, the research identifies key metrics such as Inventory Turnover Ratio, Stock Accuracy Rate, and Supplier On-Time Delivery Rate as pivotal in optimizing stock control. Findings reveal that a KPI-driven strategy significantly improves operational efficiency, reduces inventory holding costs, and enhances supplier performance. A case study of a leading airline demonstrates practical applications of KPI-driven stock management, resulting in increased Inventory Turnover Ratio and improved Warehouse Utilization Rate. The study discusses strategic implications for airlines, highlighting the importance of KPIs in achieving cost savings, operational continuity, and supply chain resilience. Limitations are acknowledged, and recommendations for future research include exploring digital transformation's impact on KPI performance and integrating sustainability metrics into stock control practices.

title: The Nexus of Quantum Technology, Intellectual Property, and National Security: An LSI Test for Securing the Quantum Industrial Commons
affiliations: Stanford University

detail.title: The Nexus of Quantum Technology, Intellectual Property, and National Security: An LSI Test for Securing the Quantum Industrial Commons
detail.abstract:
Our world of power and national security is increasingly probabilistic: like a quantum wavefunction, it encodes multiple plausible futures until policy choices—and shocks—collapse them into outcomes. In quantum mechanics, a “state” is a probability map of possible futures, encoded in complex amplitudes rather than certainties, and remaining in superposition until measurement collapses it into an observable result. Grand strategy in the quantum era shares this ontology. Policymakers cannot forecast a single trajectory for fault-tolerant qubits, quantum sensors at scale, or entanglement distribution across quantum networks; they must prepare for several plausible “eigenstates” of capability, diffusion, and systemic rivalry.

Quantum technologies have moved from laboratory curiosities to strategic infrastructure, with an approaching “event horizon” reflected in recent U.S. strategic assessments—including the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission’s call for a “Quantum First” posture by 2030—and in parallel White House initiatives aimed at securing critical inputs and accelerating trusted innovation. A similar time-compression dynamic is now visible in frontier AI. Recent U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission research further documents that China’s quantum program is centrally mobilized and security-aligned, and that the most consequential advantages may arise not only from computing milestones but also from sensing and cryptanalytic applications, thereby sharpening the need for a deterrence-by-denial governance posture.

In the context of this Article, “responsible quantum technology” (RQT) is accordingly presented as values-based deterrence by denial, implemented through a legal, ethical, and institutional control plane that protects the industrial commons and enhances democratic resilience against authoritarian appropriation and exploitation. It also explains how quantum capabilities may reshape strategic stability and argues that a values-driven deterrence-by-denial posture, illustrated through a Taiwan invasion-denial vignette, is the least escalatory way to preserve crisis stability while denying adversarial gains.

The Article’s central claim is that the United States and its allies should pursue security-sufficient openness, operationalized through a least-trade-restrictive, security-sufficient, innovation-preserving (LSI) test that disciplines both state and private action. The LSI test integrates emerging instruments of economic statecraft, including Project Vault to strengthen the U.S. strategic critical-minerals reserve, a Quantum Criticality Index (QCI) for prioritizing quantum-decisive inputs, the White House Critical Minerals Presidential Order to secure the physical front; and the Genesis Mission–American Science and Security Platform (ASSP) architecture to create secure, closed-loop enclaves for high-sensitivity collaborative R&D.

The Article’s contribution is an implementable coalition playbook, offering administrable, empirically anchored criteria, templates, and differentiated guardrails—including “red-zone” domains where denial is the default—to avoid both over-securitization and under-securitization. Properly applied, LSI reduces the risk of a self-defeating “Silicon Curtain” while establishing standards-first interoperability as a stabilizing eigenstate of the international order and enabling RQT-by-design to shape trusted adoption pathways beyond the coalition, including in the majority world.

title: A National-Provincial Stochastic Mortality Model for China: Methods, Innovations, and Policy Applications
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU), University of Waterloo - Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School and The Hang Seng University of Hong Kong

detail.title: A National-Provincial Stochastic Mortality Model for China: Methods, Innovations, and Policy Applications
detail.abstract: China's rapid population aging creates urgent demand for reliable mortality forecasts to support pension, healthcare, and insurance planning. This paper develops a national-provincial stochastic mortality model that jointly projects mortality for China and its provinces. The model introduces three main innovations: a structural dependence linking national and provincial mortality through a relative Lee-Carter framework; a Poisson-Gaussian error structure with imputation methods to fully utilize sparse and uneven provincial data; and a flexible provincial trend specification that allows either mean-reverting or unit-root dynamics, selected using the Expected Deviance Information Criterion (EDIC) rather than imposing strict long-run coherence. Estimated using a Bayesian estimation procedure that mitigates key limitations in the data, the model shows strong empirical performance and supports several applications, including quantifying provincial inequality in China's pension annuity factors.

title: Dynamic Learning and Optimal Advertising Mechanism for LLM Platforms
affiliations: , Fuqua School of Business and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Dynamic Learning and Optimal Advertising Mechanism for LLM Platforms
detail.abstract: We study advertising on conversational LLM platforms, where in each round of interaction, the platform learns more about a user’s preferences, modeled as an unknown high-dimensional vector. There are multiple advertisers, each with a private valuation and a high-dimensional feature vector, and the quality of an ad match (and hence the advertiser’s utility) is given by the inner product between the advertiser’s features and the user’s preferences. At any point in time, the platform holds a belief about the user’s preferences that lies within a neighborhood of the true preferences. The radius of this neighborhood, which we call the \emph{uncertainty radius}, decreases over time as the platform learns from continued interaction. Waiting allows the platform to improve its estimate of user preferences and potentially identify better matches at the risk of user departure. Thus, the platform faces a trade-off in deciding when and which ad to offer. Solving for the welfare-maximizing policy in this optimal stopping problem is intractable without strong distributional assumptions on belief evolution. Instead, we propose an approximate threshold-based policy based on upper and lower bounds on the continuation value and prove explicit performance guarantees that depend on the platform’s current belief and scale with the uncertainty radius and the heterogeneity of advertisers’ feature vectors, without imposing distributional assumptions. Furthermore, we extend our setting to revenue maximization, where advertisers hold private valuations. We establish a ``virtual welfare equivalence'' in this dynamic setting, showing that the revenue-optimal incentive-compatible mechanism can be obtained by applying the welfare-maximizing policy to appropriately defined virtual valuations. This result generalizes classical optimal auction theory to environments where the information structure evolves, enabling us to derive approximately revenue-optimal mechanisms.

title: The Immortal Roman Empire: How the West cannot Shake its Addiction to Power and Dominance
affiliations: La Trobe University

detail.title: The Immortal Roman Empire: How the West cannot Shake its Addiction to Power and Dominance
detail.abstract: The fall of Rome was an illusion. This paper argues that the imperial project did not die — it transformed. Through colonial expansion, economic hegemony, and the soft power of modern institutions, Western states have preserved the roman logic of domination under new banners: democracy, trade, and international law. Tracing the arc from the Roman Republic through the Pax Romana, European colonial empires, and into contemporary alliances such as the European Union and NATO, this study reveals how Western civilisation remains addicted to power — cloaked in civility but driven by the same strategic impulse: control. Drawing on economic models of instability, institutional legacies, and case studies including Africa’s trade dependency and the EU’s unprecedented €850 billion defence package, this work exposes Rome’s ghost in modern governance. Even those untouched by roman conquest now live under systems forged in her image. The West, it seems, has never truly shaken the eagle from its shoulder.

title: Executives' Intertemporal Choice Preferences and Operational Efficiency: A Textual Analysis Approach
affiliations: Fudan University - School of Management, Singapore Management University, CUNY Queens College and Donghua University

detail.title: Executives' Intertemporal Choice Preferences and Operational Efficiency: A Textual Analysis Approach
detail.abstract: In this study, we investigate how top managers' intertemporal choice preferences (ITCP) shape their strategic decisions and affect firms' overall operational efficiency in future periods. Top managers with short-term-oriented ITCP may perceive future events to be distant and value immediate rewards, thereby behaving myopically at the expense of long-term advantages. Linguistic theory suggests that futuretime-reference (FTR) languages, i.e., the languages that mark the timing of future events, reveal the speaker's tendency to perceive the future as remote. Using FTR languages spoken by CEOs during conference calls to proxy for their ITCP, we find that CEOs with short-term ITCP tend to make myopic decisions in production planning and investment for supply chain relationships, thus deteriorating firms' future inventory turnover, future sales to major customers, and future overall operational efficiency in converting inputs (e.g., inventory) into outputs (e.g., sales). We also document that COOs play a mediating role in the negative association between CEOs' short-term ITCP and firms' future operational efficiency. Our results remain qualitatively the same when we use alternative measures of operational efficiency, change measurement windows, and control for various managerial characteristics. Overall, our study offers a deeper understanding of how top managers' ITCP influence firms' strategic choices and operational practices, uncovering a new cognitive factor that explains differences in firms' long-term operational efficiency.

title: Efficient Market Risk Assessment with Multi-Fidelity Learning: A Case Study on Bermudan Swaptions
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Efficient Market Risk Assessment with Multi-Fidelity Learning: A Case Study on Bermudan Swaptions
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the use of statistical learning models to accelerate financial risk evaluation under stringent regulatory frameworks. We first apply Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) to construct accurate surrogate models for efficiently estimating key risk measures such as Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES). We then propose an extension based on multi-fidelity Gaussian Process Regression (mGPR), combining highfidelity pricing data (from the LGM-1F model) with fast low-fidelity approximations. The approach is validated on portfolios of Bermudan swaptions, which are computationally intensive to value due to their early-exercise features. Numerical experiments show that GPR alone provides substantial speed-ups while maintaining the required precision, and that mGPR achieves further gains, reducing computational costs by up to a factor of four. These results offer a scalable and accurate solution for real-time risk calculations under FRTB requirements. The methodology also opens promising directions for applying multiscale learning techniques to other quantitative finance challenges.

title: The AI-GDP Index: A Market-Based Measure of AI-Driven Value Creation and Creative Destruction
affiliations: Long Island University Post

detail.title: The AI-GDP Index: A Market-Based Measure of AI-Driven Value Creation and Creative Destruction
detail.abstract: The AI-GDP Index is a market-based framework designed to estimate the net economic impact of artificial intelligence by capturing both value creation and value displacement across industries. Existing AI-focused indices primarily track firms expected to benefit from AI adoption, thereby measuring gross technological exposure rather than net economic effects. In contrast, the AI-GDP Index is constructed from two equal-weighted equity baskets: an AI Value-Creation Basket (infrastructure, semiconductors, hyperscale computing) and an AI Disruption-Exposed Basket (software, professional services, and information intermediaries vulnerable to automation). The daily AI-GDP Score is defined as the return differential between these baskets, providing a high-frequency signal of market-implied expectations regarding AI-driven value reallocation. The framework draws on the resource-based view of the firm and Schumpeterian creative destruction to interpret index movements as indicators of technological regime shifts. Preliminary analysis suggests the index reflects changing market assessments of AI's aggregate productivity impact and may serve as a forward-looking indicator of sectoral restructuring. Applications for financial analysis, economic research, and corporate strategy are discussed.

title: Customers on the Board and Inventory Management
affiliations: Hongik University, College of Business, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST),  and College of Business, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: Customers on the Board and Inventory Management
detail.abstract: This study examines the effects of customers on the board (COBs) on inventory management. We argue that the human and relational capital provided by COBs helps improve inventory management. Using a comprehensive sample of customer firms, we show that the presence of COBs enhances inventory turnover and reduces bullwhip effects. Cross-sectional analyses indicate that these effects are more pronounced when COBs provide firm-and industry-specific knowledge (human capital) and when private communication is more valuable for managing contingencies (relational capital). Our findings are robust to potential endogeneity concerns, as evidenced by a variety of analyses, including an instrumental variables approach, propensity score and coarsened exact matching, and entropy balancing. Taken together, we extend prior research by documenting that the presence of COBs has positive effects on inventory management.

title: Modi Doctrine and the Future of Indo-African Ties

detail.title: Modi Doctrine and the Future of Indo-African Ties
detail.abstract: After making his first ministerial visit to Africa over three years ago, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's interest in deepening India's trade relationship and security cooperation with the continent has swelled. Though their trade relationship dates centuries, Indo-African trade stood at just $1 billion 25 years ago. With present bilateral trade valued at over $60 billion, the Modi government hopes to improve the figure to $150 billion by 2023. Though such figures pale in comparison to Africa's trade with China and the European Union, India's standing as a burgeoning investor, donor, and security partner contains considerable appeal for several governments on the continent. Concerns over China's economic and political influence across sub-Saharan Africa has restored fears of quasi-colonialist control, compelling several governments to hedge against the threat via diversification of foreign partnerships. For India, bolstering ties with African governments aligns neatly with BJP government's foreign policy, dubbed the "Modi Doctrine." Among other aims, the Modi Doctrine closely links Indian foreign policy aims with the key initiatives that comprise Modi's economic agenda, including the vaunted "Make in India" campaign, which seeks to encourage manufacturers to establish operations in the country. Furthermore, in an effort to enhance economic cooperation between India and Africa, the Modi government, in conjunction with Japan, outlined a vision three years ago for an Asia-Africa Growth Corridor (AAGC), an agreement that would advance maritime trade links between South/Southeast Asian and African ports.

title: Integrating Self-Attention and Graph Neural Networks with Gradient Surgery for Electricity Price Prediction
affiliations: State Grid Gansu Electric Power Company, State Grid Gansu Electric Power Company and State Grid Gansu Electric Power Company

detail.title: Integrating Self-Attention and Graph Neural Networks with Gradient Surgery for Electricity Price Prediction
detail.abstract: Reliable short-term electricity price forecasts are critical for efficient trading and secure grid operation, yet existing approaches often fail to capture simultaneously the long-range temporal patterns and the spatial couplings induced by network topology. We propose a hybrid forecasting framework that combines a Transformer encoder for temporal representation, a graph neural network for topology-aware spatial modeling, and a PCGrad-based gradient surgery step to reduce interference when training on heterogeneous modalities. The architecture fuses market-level signals (PJM hourly records) with grid-level measurements (PMU data from an IEEE-39 bus model) using a windowed alignment and an attention-based fusion stage. Evaluated on these two public datasets, it attains substantial gains over classical and hybrid baselines: MSE = 0.1439, MAE = 0.1384, RMSE = 0.3965, and R2 = 0.9076 in the fused setting. These results indicate that careful integration of temporal and spatial information with conflict-aware optimization yields a scalable, high-accuracy solution for market forecasting and supports practical applications in smart-grid decision support.

title: Accounting Standards, Banking Regulation, and Financial Intermediation: Evidence from IFRS Convergence and Modern Reporting Limitations

detail.title: Accounting Standards, Banking Regulation, and Financial Intermediation: Evidence from IFRS Convergence and Modern Reporting Limitations

detail.abstract: This study examines the role of accounting standards in shaping banking behavior, financial intermediation, and regulatory oversight within modern financial systems. It analyzes the evolution of accounting from historical cost-based models to IFRS-converged frameworks, with particular emphasis on India's adoption of Ind AS and its implications for bank balance sheets, risk measurement, and market discipline. The paper identifies structural limitations in existing financial reporting models, including inadequate recognition of intangible assets, digital value creation, and ESG-related risks that increasingly affect bank valuation, credit allocation, and regulatory capital assessment. These limitations may weaken supervisory effectiveness and contribute to informational inefficiencies in financial markets. By explicitly linking accounting standards to banking regulation and financial stability, the study contributes to the literature on financial intermediation and regulatory economics. The findings offer policy-relevant insights for regulators and standard setters seeking to enhance the resilience and transparency of financial systems in an increasingly digital and sustainability-oriented economic environment.

title: Understanding the Ridehailing Market
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Operations and Information Management

detail.title: Understanding the Ridehailing Market
detail.abstract: This article reviews the evolution of ridehailing markets and synthesizes the growing academic literature that studies their operational, economic, and regulatory foundations. Motivated by the rapid displacement of traditional taxis by transportation network companies (TNCs) such as Uber and Lyft, the article situates modern ridehailing within its historical and regulatory context and highlights how digital platforms have reshaped labor supply, matching, pricing, and service design. The review organizes prior work around core operational levers—driver supply management, matching technologies, and service differentiation—and examines how these levers jointly determine passenger wait times, prices, driver utilization, and platform performance. The article then turns to market-level outcomes, including competition between platforms, driver multi-homing, congestion, and welfare implications for drivers and passengers, emphasizing how congestion and spatial frictions distinguish ridehailing from canonical two-sided markets. Regulatory responses, including wage floors, worker classification, and caps on driver entry, are discussed alongside their operational trade-offs. Finally, the article considers emerging challenges and opportunities, including the persistence of traditional taxis and the integration of autonomous vehicles. By synthesizing insights across operations management, economics, and transportation research, the article provides a structured framework for understanding ridehailing markets and identifies open questions for future research and policy design.

detail.abstract: We use administrative data to measure sibling spillovers on academic performance before and after the introduction of Free Secondary Education (FSE) in Tanzania. Prior to FSE, students whose older siblings narrowly passed the secondary school entrance exam were less likely to go to secondary school themselves; with FSE, the effect became positive. A triple-differences analysis, using geographic variation in FSE exposure, shows that FSE caused the reversal. Mechanism analyses suggest that changes in parental investments were a more likely channel for this reversal than direct sibling interactions. By alleviating financial constraints, FSE allowed households to distribute educational investments more equitably rather than concentrating resources on high-performing children.

detail.abstract: This study provides new evidence on the functioning of insolvency procedures in Italy, with particular attention to joint composition with creditors. By combining administrative data from Infocamere, INPS, the Central Credit Register, and Cerved, we examine the characteristics of firms undergoing insolvency proceedings, the sequence of events preceding their initiation, and their subsequent outcomes. Only a portion of insolvent firms make use of collective procedures to exit the market, and these firms were typically already in distress for a prolonged period prior to initiating the procedure – even more so those entering judicial liquidation. Firms admitted to the joint composition with creditors, although far fewer in number than those subject to liquidation, tend to be larger and display significant exposure to the banking system. In this paper, we discuss the objectives of joint composition with creditors, its success rate when the goal is business continuity, and the effects of recent regulatory changes. The timeliness of the filing for joint composition with creditors is positively correlated with the probability of successful restructuring and of firm’s return to financial and economic soundness.

title: Short-Circuiting Short-Term Funding
affiliations: Government of the United States of America - Office of Financial Research, Federal Reserve Board of Governors and

detail.title: Short-Circuiting Short-Term Funding

publicationDetails.detailsText: Office of Financial Research Working Paper No. 26-02

detail.abstract: Cyber-induced operational outages can affect the U.S. repurchase agreements (repo) market. Using transaction-level data and institutional cybersecurity ratings, we simulate disruptions to key cash lenders. Our findings indicate that outages at certain institutions can disrupt over $100 billion in funding and raise rates for repo by over 50 basis points. The severity of these disruptions are sensitive to outage timing and duration, with peak settlement times and slower recoveries amplify stress. The results underscore the importance of both cybersecurity preparedness and institutional resilience in limiting financial market disruptions. This study links cyber risk to intraday funding dynamics and rate volatility and offers a framework for assessing and mitigating cyber threats in core funding markets.

title: Integration of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) factors in Mergers and Acquisitions
affiliations: National Law School of India University

detail.title: Integration of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) factors in Mergers and Acquisitions
detail.abstract: The paper examines how environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors are increasingly integrated across the mergers and acquisitions (M&A) lifecycle, transforming them from a peripheral concern into a fundamental driver of deal strategy, valuation, and integration. It first traces the evolution and economics of ESG, arguing that ESG is both legally mandated (in regimes such as the Indian Companies Act and emerging EU frameworks) and economically value‑accretive, with strong empirical evidence linking superior ESG performance to enhanced corporate financial performance, market premiums, and long‑term risk‑adjusted returns. The study clarifies key concepts including ESG ratings, reporting standards (GRI, ISSB/IFRS, CSRD, BRSR, CSDDD), and greenwashing risks, and links ESG to stakeholder theory and fiduciary duty. Using a deal‑flow model spanning pre‑deal, deal, and post‑deal phases, the paper then analyses how ESG shapes target selection, valuation, and ESG‑focused due diligence, showing that acquirers increasingly pay premiums for high‑ESG targets and use M&A to improve their own ESG profiles. It explains how ESG findings are embedded into transaction documentation through representations, warranties, indemnities, pricing adjustments and conditions precedent, while noting that explicit, forward‑looking ESG commitments and protections remain under‑developed in practice. Finally, the paper stresses the underutilised role of post‑merger integration (PMI) in realising ESG synergies, proposing detailed steps to scale ambitions, harmonise metrics, align governance, and embed ESG culture so that ESG operates as a genuine value‑creation lever rather than a mere risk‑mitigation or marketing tool.

title: The Consequentiality-Weighted Wealth Protocol: Resolving the Reliability Crisis in Natural Capital Valuation

detail.abstract: The transition from flow-based GDP to stock-based Inclusive Wealth remains stalled by a "reliability crisis" in non-market valuation. We propose the Consequentiality-Weighted Wealth (CWW) Protocol, which integrates a "Stock-Flow Separation Principle" with a rigorous "Consequentiality Filter" to calibrate shadow prices against binding budget constraints. We validate this protocol across three contexts: Costa Rica's PES program (revealed preference), Norway's Sovereign Wealth Fund (asset conversion), and U.S. Manufacturing defensive expenditures (liability recognition). Results demonstrate that the filter significantly reduces the disparity between Willingness to Pay (WTP) and Willingness to Accept (WTA), aligning valuation estimates with incentive-compatible economic theory. Furthermore, the protocol reveals a material "Reliability Delta" in industrial accounting by isolating unrecorded maintenance liabilities currently absent from standard financial accounts. The CWW Protocol offers a scalable mechanism for operationalizing the SEEA.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Modern Management Practices
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Modern Management Practices
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies influencing contemporary business environments and managerial practices. Organizations across industries are increasingly adopting AI-driven tools to enhance efficiency, accuracy, speed, and strategic decision-making. This study examines the impact of Artificial Intelligence on modern management practices by analyzing its applications across core management functions such as planning, organizing, staffing, directing, and controlling. Using a mixed-method research design, primary data were collected from managers and professionals across manufacturing, service, and technology sectors, supplemented by secondary data from academic literature and industry reports. The findings indicate that AI significantly improves forecasting accuracy, operational efficiency, human resource effectiveness, customer engagement, and financial decision-making. However, challenges such as data privacy concerns, ethical risks, workforce displacement, and skill gaps continue to limit the full potential of AI integration. The study proposes a structured framework for AI adoption in managerial processes, emphasizing ethical governance, workforce reskilling, and strategic alignment. This research contributes to management literature by providing empirical insights into how AI reshapes managerial roles and organizational performance while offering practical recommendations for managers, educators, and policymakers.

title: The Entropic Firm: Bureaucracy as a Thermodynamic Necessity

detail.title: The Entropic Firm: Bureaucracy as a Thermodynamic Necessity

detail.abstract: Standard economic theory attributes the "Coasean Ceiling", the point where firms stop scaling, to agency costs or loss of control. This view treats bureaucracy as a failure of incentive alignment. We argue it is a structural necessity derived from information entropy. Modeling the firm as a Maxwell’s Demon, we demonstrate that the management function is isomorphic to information erasure: a process that imposes an irreducible energy cost (𝑘𝑇) per bit of ambiguity resolved. We introduce the "Thermodynamic Solvency Ratio," a metric identifying when the energy required to filter internal noise exceeds the marginal revenue of production. Finally, we analyze Generative AI as a potential escape from this limit. We conclude that AI represents a topological shift in organizational physics, replacing highcost biological demons with low-marginal-cost silicon counterparts, subject to a binding fidelity constraint regarding probabilistic errors.

title: Decoding the Potential Dysfunctional Emotional Effects of Technology-Enabled Digital Business Models in Individuals
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and IBS Ahmedabad

detail.title: Decoding the Potential Dysfunctional Emotional Effects of Technology-Enabled Digital Business Models in Individuals
detail.abstract: PurposeThe study aims to decode the potential dysfunctional emotional effects of technology-enabled digital business models (DBMs) in individuals, embedded in daily interactions. Digital technostress and appraisal process were introduced as mediating variables to gain insights into the stated nexus.Design/methodology/approachA multidimensional conceptual framework was developed, and data were collected through a structured questionnaire from 541 digitally active individuals selected through purposive sampling across major Indian metropolitan cities. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS 4 was employed to test the proposed hypotheses.FindingsEmpirical results demonstrate that DBMs significantly influence dysfunctional emotional outcomes both directly (β = 0.12, p < 0.001) and indirectly through digital technostress (β = 0.04, p < 0.001), appraisal process (β = 0.03, p < 0.001), and serial mediation pathways (β = 0.01, p = 0.01). The results indicate that the DBMs dimensions designed to increase user engagement and deliver value can concurrently induce dysfunctional emotional states, such as frustration, anxiety, and digital fatigue.Practical implicationsThe proposed multidimensional framework offers significant implications for policymakers, digital platform designers, users and society as a whole. The research findings highlight the requirement of framing robust digital regulatory guidelines and the development of human-centric and emotionally responsible DBMs design structures grounded in validated theoretical perspectives. The insights also underlines the need of an active and conscious user driven digital interventions.Originality/valueThe study develops a comprehensive framework grounded in multiple theoretical perspectives and introduces each construct through novel metaphors. This conceptualization enriches theoretical discourse and introduces a new terminology for understanding the complex phenomenon. Additionally, the research is among the pioneering studies that empirically analyse the role of DBMs in generating dysfunctional emotional effects in individuals beyond professional boundaries in an increasingly digitalised world.

title: Visible Responsibility, Invisible Pollution: Environmental Disclosure and Supply Chain Carbon Leakage
affiliations: Shandong Technology and Business University - School of Economics and Shandong Technology and Business University

detail.title: Visible Responsibility, Invisible Pollution: Environmental Disclosure and Supply Chain Carbon Leakage
detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of global carbon peaking, carbon neutrality goals, and supply chain carbon leakage issues, the actual effectiveness of corporate environmental responsibility disclosure needs to be reexamined from the perspective of the overall supply chain. This study systematically explores the impact and mechanism of environmental responsibility disclosure of listed companies on carbon emissions of upstream and downstream enterprises. Benchmark analysis indicates that the disclosure of environmental responsibility has not led to overall emissions reduction in the supply chain, but instead has pushed up carbon emissions from upstream and downstream enterprises, confirming the existence of hidden emissions in the supply chain under explicit responsibility. The internal mechanism exhibits differential characteristics of scale effect being globally effective, structural effect being upstream exclusive, and technological effect being downstream exclusive. Expansion analysis shows that upstream suppliers are subject to dual suppression of carbon transfer through digital speech and action, while downstream customers are only effective through digital action. Additionally, upstream carbon transfer tends towards long-term stable suppliers, while downstream carbon transfer tends towards non-major and long-term customers. This study provides objective basis for solving the dilemma of carbon transfer in the supply chain and formulating targeted emission reduction policies.

title: Re-Specifying Effectuation through Organizational Decision Boundaries in Generative AI Contexts
affiliations: Arthur D. Little Inc. - Hult International Business School, Harvard University and Central European University

detail.title: Re-Specifying Effectuation through Organizational Decision Boundaries in Generative AI Contexts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Steph Sharma manages her own consulting company, Symbio Strategies and is a Visiting Fellow of Hult International Business School.. Mark Esposito is a professor at Harvard University and Hult International Business School. Yusaf Akbar is a professor at Central European University and Hult International Business School.

detail.abstract: This paper adapts effectuation theory to organizational decision-making contexts in which generative AI participates in the construction of decision inputs, options, and evaluations. While classic effectuation assumes human authorship and control, generative AI alters the conditions under which non-predictive decision logic operates by expanding option generation and redistributing evaluative effort. This creates a theory-phenomenon mismatch that calls for theory adaptation. Drawing on principles of theory adaptation, the paper re-specifies effectuation through organizational decision boundaries that structure authority, admissibility, evaluation, and accountability. It introduces a decision-boundary process framework that distinguishes augmented, hybrid, and delegated configurations and derives propositions linking variation in boundary design to systematic differences in how effectuation principles are enacted at the organizational level. The paper contributes to effectuation and organizational decision theory by showing how non-predictive control, human judgment, and accountability can be preserved when decision inputs are no longer exclusively human. By shifting analytical attention from decision-makers to decision architecture, the framework provides a foundation for empirical research on organizational decision-making under conditions of uncertainty, time compression, and the participation of generative AI.
