detail.abstract:
This paper examines the historical interplay between bankers, privacy, and arcana imperii (the secrets of statecraft) from a legal perspective, with a focus on early modern Europe. It argues that bankers were not only pivotal in shaping the financial and political landscapes of early modern monarchies but also acted as custodians of sensitive information, enabling sovereigns to oversee economic resources and their deployment.

The paper highlights how the role of bankers—from the Italian city-states, through the emergence of Swiss banking secrecy and English common law notions of confidentiality, to later American privacy doctrines—has consistently been oriented towards protecting both individual autonomy and state secrets. Moreover, by conceptualising privacy as the management of “presence”, understood as a spatial and institutional concept, and through a case study of the Spanish Habsburgs’ codification of royal space, the paper demonstrates how financial stability and the protection of arcana imperii were deeply intertwined. Between these poles, bankers emerged as key facilitators—and, at times, masters—of this complex legal and institutional infrastructure.

title: The Politics of AI
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics and Gallup

detail.title: The Politics of AI
detail.abstract:
Using new data from the Gallup Workforce Panel, we document a persistent partisan gap in self-reported AI use at work: Democrats are consistently more likely than Republicans to report frequent use. In 2025:Q4, for example, 27.8% of Democrats report using AI weekly or daily, compared with 22.5% of Republicans. Democrats also report deeper task-level integration, using AI in 16% more work activities than Republicans. Consistent with this, Democrats are employed in occupations with higher predicted AI exposure based on task-content measures and report larger perceived differences in AI-related job displacement risk. However, in regression models the partisan gap in AI use disappears once we control for education, industry, and occupation, indicating that observed differences primarily reflect compositional variation rather than political affiliation per se.

title: Changing Conflict Resolution Institutions in the Ethiopian Pastoral Commons: The Role of Armed Confrontation in Rule-Making

detail.title: Changing Conflict Resolution Institutions in the Ethiopian Pastoral Commons: The Role of Armed Confrontation in Rule-Making
detail.abstract: Pastoralist access and use of common grazing resources in the Horn of Africa increasingly include armed confrontation over diminishing resources and reduced access. This comes about as traditional customary institutions (sets of rules) for commons management become compromised due to the presence of outside influences and actors which significantly change both resource availability, and conceptions about who is subject to traditional rules governing commons-particularly rules associated with exclusion. At the same time a combination of local knowledge regarding what happens to open access commons (degradation), a reluctance to give up control of commons and associated ways of life, and armed conflict as a viable alternative for exclusion rules, provide for combative situations and large costs. While a great deal of valuable work has been accomplished regarding the derivation of effective institutions to better manage commons, situations of armed conflict can seem particularly distant from effective rule-making, because few institutions can endure the stresses of armed conflict. Recent developments in Ethiopia however suggest an unexpected proximity between armed confrontation and the prospect for commons management rule-making. With examples from the Afar, Somali and Karamojong Cluster pastoralists, this paper examines the ingredients for rule-making in combative commons situations. Specific coincident forms of state recognition, donor flexibility, perceptions of the cost of conflict, and the local to international reaction to these, are examined for their utility and limitations in the provision of a facilitating context for institution derivation for commons management.

title: Heaven or Earth? The Evolving Role of Global Shocks for Domestic Monetary Policy
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, World Bank and World Bank

detail.title: Heaven or Earth? The Evolving Role of Global Shocks for Domestic Monetary Policy
detail.abstract:
Business cycles are increasingly driven by global shocks, rather than the domestic demand shocks prominent in earlier decades, posing challenges for central banks seeking to meet domestic mandates and communicate their policy decisions. This paper analyzes the evolving influence and characteristics of global and domestic shocks in advanced economies from 1970-2024 using a new FAVAR model that decomposes movements in interest rates, inflation, and output growth into four global shocks (demand, supply, oil, and monetary policy) and three domestic shocks (demand, supply, and monetary policy). We find that the role of global shocks has increased sharply over time and that their characteristics differ from those of domestic shocks across multiple dimensions. Compared to domestic shocks, global shocks have a larger supply component, higher variance, more persistent effects on inflation, and are more asymmetric (contributing more to tightening than to easing phases of monetary policy). As global supply shocks have become more prominent, central banks have also been less willing to “look through” their effects on inflation than for comparable domestic shocks. The distinct characteristics and rising influence of global shocks—particularly global supply shocks—have significant implications for modeling monetary policy and designing central bank frameworks.

title: The Impacts of AI at Scale: Evidence from Research Scientists
affiliations: University of Southern California - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Impacts of AI at Scale: Evidence from Research Scientists
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of AI on productivity and inequality by focusing on the introduction of AlphaFold2. This AI algorithm can accurately predict protein structures, which were traditionally characterized by structural biologists through experiments. To capture the impact of AI on structural biologists at scale, I implement a difference-in-differences strategy comparing them to life scientists in other fields. While structural biologists did not change their overall number of publications with the availability of AlphaFold2, they experienced a 10% increase in citations to their new projects, a 4% rise in publications in high-impact journals, and a shift from their original research trajectory. However, the emergence of AI intensifies citation polarization between highly cited and less-cited researchers. Consistent with this growing inequality, highly cited scientists are twice as likely to incorporate AlphaFold2 successfully into their research as their less-cited peers. In addition, AI affects the next generation of researchers: the average years of experience of leading authors in protein structure papers increase after the emergence of AI.

title: AI Personality Extraction from Faces: Labor Market Implications
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania, Reichman University, Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Finance and Yale School of Management

detail.title: AI Personality Extraction from Faces: Labor Market Implications
detail.abstract:
Human capital—encompassing cognitive skills and personality traits—is central for labor-market success, yet personality remains difficult to measure at scale. Leveraging advances in AI and comprehensive LinkedIn microdata, we extract the Big 5 personality traits from facial images of 96,000 MBA graduates, and demonstrate that this novel “Photo Big 5” predicts school rank, job matching, compensation, job transitions, and career advancement. The Photo Big 5 provides predictive power comparable to race, attractiveness, and educational background, and is only weakly correlated with cognitive measures such as test scores. We show that individuals systematically sort into occupations where their personality traits are valued and earn higher wages when traits align with occupational demands. While the scalability of the Photo Big 5 enables new academic insights into the role of personality in labor markets, its growing use in industry screening raises important ethical concerns regarding statistical discrimination and individual autonomy.

title: Aggregate Employment and the Rise of Services across Time and Countries
affiliations: University of Toronto and University of Toronto - Department of Economics

detail.title: Aggregate Employment and the Rise of Services across Time and Countries
detail.abstract:
We study the sectoral reallocation of employment over time and across countries, with a focus on the rise of services. We document substantial changes in the ratio of aggregate employment to working-age population across countries that are not systematically related to productivity growth or income levels, yet tightly linked to the rise in services employment. We assess the quantitative contribution of changes in aggregate employment to the rise of services using an otherwise standard model of sectoral reallocation calibrated to time-series for the United States. The calibrated model implies a high elasticity of changes in aggregate employment to services: a one percentage point change in aggregate employment generates on average a 0.7 percentage point change in services employment. The implication is that actual changes in aggregate employment account for one-third of the rise in services, on average across countries, and up to one-half in countries with sustained employment increases.

title: AI, Opinion Ecosystems, and Finance

detail.title: AI, Opinion Ecosystems, and Finance
detail.abstract:
Generative AI use for content generation is associated with divergent outcomes on different financial social media platforms: indications of reasoning enhancement on Seeking Alpha, and of belief distortions on WallStreetBets. On Seeking Alpha, adoption is associated with information frictions. AI-assisted postings tilt toward analysis/credibility, and their sentiment positively predicts future returns. Use of AI is associated with more informative retail order flow and lower bid-ask spreads. In contrast, AI adoption on WallStreetBets follows surges in retail buying, and AI-assisted content is associated with emotionality and sentiment contagion. Such content precedes higher trading volume, greater volatility, and more lottery-like return distributions.

detail.abstract:
With the goal of curbing electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS) use among youths, 40 states and the District of Columbia have adopted restrictions on nicotine vaping at elementary and secondary (K-12) schools. This study is the first to estimate the effect of K-12 school vaping restrictions (SVRs) on ENDS use among youth. Using data from several nationally representative data sources and a generalized difference-in-differences approach, we find little evidence that school indoor vaping restrictions reduce youth ENDS use. With 95% confidence, we can rule out SVR-induced youth vaping declines of more than 3.5%. Descriptive evidence suggests that students may respond to SVRs by substituting to smaller vaping devices and vaping in school locations that are less easily detectable by school employees (e.g., bathrooms and locker rooms). In contrast, we find that comprehensive vaping restrictions covering school campuses, workplaces, restaurants, and drinking establishments are associated with a 1.5-2.6 percentage-point reduction in teen nicotine vaping. This result is concentrated on the initiation margin of use and is consistent with the hypothesis that broader place-based restrictions increase the costs of youth ENDS use.

title: Progress or Backsliding? Changes in the Gender Wage Gap for Business Professionals
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Progress or Backsliding? Changes in the Gender Wage Gap for Business Professionals
detail.abstract:
In the United States, much of the gap in earnings between men and women is due to the persistent gap for high wage earners. This paper explores changes in the gender wage gap for MBAs graduating from a large public university over 30 years. We document large gender wage gaps on average, which grow in the course of men’s and women’s careers. Comparing graduates at identical career stages across time periods to address composition concerns, we show that the raw gender wage gap has shrunk by 33 to 50 percent over the last two decades. Additionally, the temporal pattern of the gap has fundamentally shifted: while gaps only emerged over time in earlier decades, significant gaps now emerge immediately. Convergence in labor supply factors, particularly hours worked, explains much of the narrowing gap, alongside shifts in industry composition. However, unexplained wage gaps persist for recent graduates from the very start of their careers, suggesting different underlying mechanisms across cohorts. These findings highlight both progress in gender wage equity among business professionals and concerning patterns that emerge earlier in careers than in previous decades.

title: Searching for Fish in Trees (緣木求魚)? Economic Development when Context Matters
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), University of British Columbia (UBC) and University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy

detail.title: Searching for Fish in Trees (緣木求魚)? Economic Development when Context Matters
detail.abstract:
In this chapter, we develop a framework for analyzing the determinants of economic development and their implications for policy. We distinguish between classical determinants—such as inputs into education and health, access to credit, and geography—and non-classical determinants—including cultural values, social norms, beliefs, identity, and social organization. We classify these determinants along two policy-relevant dimensions: whether they can be clearly ranked in terms of their contribution to development (vertical versus horizontal) and whether they can be directly altered through policy intervention (manipulable versus non-manipulable).We show that even for classical determinants, policy impacts are often hard to predict and are mediated by local social and cultural context. These issues are more pronounced for non-classical determinants, which are more complicated to change through policy intervention and more difficult to rank in welfare terms. In some cases, traits commonly viewed as obstacles to development may be well-adapted to local conditions or even supportive of economic performance, a possibility we refer to as “reverse vertical.” Building on Hirschman’s (1967) distinction between trait-making and trait-taking policymaking, we argue that interventions that attempt to directly transform non-classical determinants often rest on fragile assumptions about ranking and manipulability and risk generating unintended or adverse effects. By contrast, many of the most successful development episodes of the past several decades relied on policies that took existing social and cultural traits as given and designed institutions, technologies, and incentives that worked within those contexts rather than attempting to overturn them.

title: Field Experiments in the Science of Science: Lessons from Peer Review and the Evaluation of New Knowledge
affiliations: Northeastern University (USA)

detail.title: Field Experiments in the Science of Science: Lessons from Peer Review and the Evaluation of New Knowledge
detail.abstract:
Scientific evaluation and peer review govern the allocation of resources and certification of knowledge in science, yet have been subjected to limited causal investigation. This chapter synthesizes randomized experiments embedded in live peer-evaluation systems at journals, conferences, and funding agencies, restricting attention to published studies. I organize this evidence using a Q–A–R–S framework that decomposes peer review into attributes of submissions (Q), authors (A), reviewers (R), and evaluation systems (S), and interpret outcomes through a view of the core problem of scientific evaluation as assessing new knowledge using the existing stock of knowledge.The chapter treats experimental design choices as objects of analysis, assessing what existing interventions can—and cannot—identify given their designs and settings, the institutional constraints they face, and opportunities for higher-leverage experimentation. I show that randomized experimentation embedded in peer review spans the full Q–A–R–S space, albeit sparsely, and yields uneven but informative insights across different margins.Based on the full body of evidence, I advance several novel claims: (1) system interventions often affect participant behavior with little impact on core evaluative judgments; (2) core evaluations are most clearly shaped by who reviews and their expertise; and (3) peer review functions more reliably as a “filter” of poor submissions than as a fine-grained “ranker” of acceptable submissions. Overall, the evidence points to a functioning institution operating under binding epistemic and organizational constraints, rather than to systemic failure. I identify channels for improving the speed, cost, and reliability of scientific evaluation institutions.Substantial scope remains to redesign embedded experiments to increase inferential power, generalizability, and cumulative insight, while reducing disruption and more tightly linking to institutional innovation and policy changes.

title: Early Learning Across Decades: Advances in Measuring Head Start Effectiveness

detail.title: Early Learning Across Decades: Advances in Measuring Head Start Effectiveness
detail.abstract:
The Head Start program, launched in 1965 and targeted to children from disadvantaged backgrounds, remains the largest early childhood care and education (ECE) program in the United States and the only one deployed at the federal level. As such, the Head Start literature spans several decades and now allows for synthesis of findings from different contexts, time periods, and research designs. This paper provides a comprehensive assessment of the rigorous evidence measuring Head Start’s effects on children, their families, and society. The focus is on how (1) the contrast between program and counterfactual conditions, (2) takeup of the program among eligible populations, and (3) treatment–effect heterogeneity inform interpretation and applicability of key findings. The paper presents implications of the evidence for the modern-day Head Start program and an adjacent, policy-relevant research agenda.

title: International Currency Dominance
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

detail.title: International Currency Dominance
detail.abstract:
We present a micro-founded monetary model of the world economy to study international currency competition. Our model features "unipolar'' equilibria, with a single dominant international currency, and "multipolar'' equilibria, in which multiple currencies circulate internationally. Long-run equilibria are highly history-dependent and tend towards the emergence of a dominant currency. Governments can compete to internationalize their currencies by offering attractive interest rates on their sovereign debt, but large economies have a natural advantage in ensuring the dominance of their currencies. We calibrate the model to assess the quantitative importance of these mechanisms and study the international monetary system's dynamics under several counterfactual scenarios.

title: Screen More, Sell Later: Screening and Dynamic Signaling in the Mortgage Market

detail.title: Screen More, Sell Later: Screening and Dynamic Signaling in the Mortgage Market
detail.abstract:
We develop a dynamic model of asset origination with unobservable screening effort and signaling of loan quality through delayed sale by extending Vanasco (2017). The theory predicts a positive relationship between screening effort and the strength of the signal. We test this central prediction using U.S. mortgage data, measuring screening effort by mortgage processing time. Consistent with the theory, loans that take longer to process are sold with longer delay and are less likely to default, even though observably riskier loans are processed more slowly. Our calibration reveals that the subprime mortgage market operated in a parameter range with endogenous fragility.

title: Interest Rates and Equity Valuations
affiliations: University of Chicago and University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business - Finance Group

detail.title: Interest Rates and Equity Valuations
detail.abstract:
A large body of work has sought to measure the effect of interest rates on equity valuations. The challenge in doing so is that both are endogenous, and their comovement depends on the forces driving interest-rate changes. To address this problem, we develop and estimate a decomposition that splits movements in real rates into three structural drivers: changes in expected growth, risk, or “pure discounting.” We show that only pure discount-rate shocks transmit one-for-one to equity valuations, with little or negative transmission of growth and risk shocks. Implementing our decomposition with a global panel of growth expectations and asset prices, we find a weak unconditional relation between valuations and real rates but a strong relation with the pure discounting component, which explains 80% of cross-country valuation changes since 1990. In the U.S., we find that 35% of the interest-rate decline is attributable to pure discounting, implying that only a fraction of the change in rates has passed through directly to equities. We use the decomposition to revisit evidence on the role of interest rates in explaining price variation, and to study higher-frequency returns, cross-sectional rate exposures, duration-matched equity premia, and reactions to monetary policy.

title: Extractive Taxation and the French Revolution
affiliations: University of Amsterdam, University of Neuchatel and Harvard Business School

detail.title: Extractive Taxation and the French Revolution
detail.abstract:
In this paper, we provide systematic evidence in support of the long-standing hypothesis that taxation was an important driver of the French Revolution. We first document that areas with heavier taxes experienced more riots between 1750 and 1789 and voiced more complaints against taxation in the cahiers de doléances of 1789. After showing that these effects are driven by indirect taxes, we exploit sharp spatial differences in the salt tax and the traites—the two principal indirect levies—to implement a regression discontinuity design (RDD).We find that unrest was higher on the high-tax side of the border. These effects intensified over time, peaking in the 1780s, and were stronger where fiscal disparities were larger and Enlightenment ideas more widespread. We further show that adverse weather shocks amplified unrest in high-tax municipalities. We then document that taxation fueled the spread of unrest during the Grande Peur—the wave of revolts that swept France in July 1789 and culminated in the abolition of feudal privileges. Finally, we link taxation to revolutionary politics in Paris, documenting that deputies from heavily taxed constituencies were more likely to frame the tax system as oppressive, support the Revolution, demand the abolition of the monarchy, and vote for the king’s execution.

title: The Innovation Race: Experimental Evidence on Advanced Technologies
affiliations: Harvard University - Business School (HBS), Goethe University Frankfurt, Bank of Italy, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The Innovation Race: Experimental Evidence on Advanced Technologies
detail.abstract: We present a large-scale field experiment test of strategic complementarities in firms' technology adoption. Our experiment was embedded in a Bank of Italy survey covering around 3,000 firms. We elicited firms' beliefs about competitors' adoption of two advanced technologies: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and robotics. We randomly provided half of the sample with accurate information about adoption rates. Most firms substantially underestimated competitors' current adoption, and when provided with information, they updated their expectations about competitors' future adoption. The information increased firms' own intended future adoption of robotics: a 1 pp increase in the share of competitors expected to adopt advanced technologies causes an increase of 0.704 pp in the firm's own robotics adoption. We do not observe a significant effect on AI adoption, but we cannot rule out modest effects either. Our findings provide causal evidence on coordination in innovation and illustrate how information frictions shape technology diffusion.

title: A decade of data: Trends in child protection system activity and expenditure in Australia between 2014-15 and 2023-24
affiliations: Deakin University - Melbourne Burwood Campus, Deakin University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Western Sydney University, Deakin University - Geelong Waterfront Campus and Australian Catholic University

detail.title: A decade of data: Trends in child protection system activity and expenditure in Australia between 2014-15 and 2023-24
detail.abstract: Background: Child protection systems are critical in responding to and resolving child maltreatment concerns. Mapping trends in system activity and expenditure can highlight opportunities to better support vulnerable children and families.Objective: To describe national and state/territory trends in child protection system activity and government expenditure in Australia.Participants and Setting: All children aged <18 years who had contact with Australian state/territory child protection systems between 2014-15 and 2023-24.Methods: We conducted a descriptive analysis of publicly reported population-level data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and the Productivity Commission. Child protection system activity indicators included investigations of alleged maltreatment notifications, substantiated investigations, care and protection orders, and out‑of‑home care (OOHC) placements. Expenditure included the total and per child costs of child protection system activity to the government.Results: National child protection activity remained largely stable from 2014-15 to 2023-24, despite notable variation across states/territories. Over 50% of children with any prior history of investigation for alleged maltreatment were re‑investigated, each year. Substantiated notifications for emotional abuse rose from 43.1% to 57.0% over the period, while government spending on child protection services nearly doubled from AUD 5.4 billion in 2014-15, to AUD 10.2 billion in 2023-24.Conclusions: Despite increased national investment in child protection, overall system activity has remained stable, with notable variation across states/territories. High rates of re‑investigation point to persistent unmet needs among children and families. These results highlight the value of earlier, preventive support to create more sustainable pathways and reduce reliance on mandated statutory responses.

title: Circular Bioeconomy: Always the same hijacking? Revisiting Pearce and Turner’s Genealogy in Light of Georgescu-Roegen’s Bioeconomics
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Circular Bioeconomy: Always the same hijacking? Revisiting Pearce and Turner’s Genealogy in Light of Georgescu-Roegen’s Bioeconomics
detail.abstract: This paper critically revisits the genealogy of the circular economy concept, highlighting a conceptual “hijacking” in its reinterpretation by Pearce and Turner (1990). Through a close reading of foundational texts and Georgescu-Roegen’s bioeconomic perspective, we analyze how the circular economy shifted from a critique of mechanistic epistemology to a celebrated pillar of ecological economics. Our findings reveal a striking reversal: Pearce and Turner frame circular economy as an innovative paradigm aligned with strong sustainability, whereas Georgescu-Roegen saw it as emblematic of standard economics. This semantic drift obscures thermodynamic constraints and perpetuates myths of technological and economical optimism. We argue that current narratives promoting a “circular bioeconomy” risk reinforcing these misconceptions. Addressing this hijacking requires renewed attention to material limits, entropy, and the normative foundations of ecological economics.

title: Addressing Conflict through Collective Action in Natural Resource Management
affiliations: International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), , International Water Management Institute (IWMI), , Independent, International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), Independent and Environmental Law Institute

detail.title: Addressing Conflict through Collective Action in Natural Resource Management
detail.abstract: The food security crisis and international “land grabs” have drawn  renewed attention to the role of natural resource competition in the livelihoods  of the rural poor. While significant empirical research has focused on diagnosing the links between natural resource competition and (violent) conflict, much less has focused on the dynamics of whether and how resource competition can be transformed to strengthen social-ecological resilience and mitigate conflict. Focusing on this latter theme, this review synthesizes evidence from cases in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. Building on an analytical framework designed to enable such comparative analysis, we present several propositions about the dynamics of conflict and collective action in natural resource management, and a series of recommendations for action. These propositions are: collective action in natural resource management is influenced by the social-ecological and governance context; natural resource management institutions affect the incentives for conflict or cooperation; and, the outcomes of these interactions influence future conflict risk, livelihoods, and resource sustainability. Action recommendations concern policies addressing resource tenure, conflict resolution mechanisms, and social inequalities, as well as strategies to strengthen collective action institutions in the natural resource sectors and to enable more equitable engagement by marginalized groups in dialogue and negotiation over resource access and use.

title: Land Rights in Darfur: Institutional Flexibility, Policy and Adaptation to Environmental Change
affiliations: and University of Khartoum

detail.title: Land Rights in Darfur: Institutional Flexibility, Policy and Adaptation to Environmental Change
detail.abstract: With environmental change set to affect the developing world in significant ways, examination of the process of adaptation is increasingly being brought to the fore. Common to all forms of adaptation in rural livelihoods will be a process of change in resource use and the resource rights that will either facilitate or subvert adaptation. This paper looks at Darfur and the repercussions from the multi-year drought and land degradation that led to forms of adaptation that involved change in relationships between groups over land resources. The analysis looks at how changes in land resource rights relationships have been dealt with historically, as adaptation developed. Approaches involving highly flexible customary institutions were used to effectively manage the change in land resource rights relationships inherent in adaptation, and considerable opportunity existed for positive interaction between customary and statutory law. Initial success at adaptation was followed by interventions by the Sudanese government to manage these relationships for specific objectives that worked against adaptation. This resulted in competition, animosity, confrontation and the subsequent collapse of the institutions, legitimacy, and trust necessary for successful management of land resource rights change. These national policies debilitated the adaptation opportunities and instead led to profoundly negative repercussions in relationships about land in Darfur, eventually becoming a primary driver in the current war. This highlights both the importance of land resource rights relationships to adaptation and how these relationships can be changed (positively and negatively) by specific practices and policies.

title: ESG Performance as a Catalyst in the R&D Investment-Firm Performance Paradox: Evidence from High-Tech Industries *
affiliations: , Bocconi University and Bocconi University - Department of Policy Analysis and Public Management

detail.title: ESG Performance as a Catalyst in the R&D Investment-Firm Performance Paradox: Evidence from High-Tech Industries *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: Horizon Europe research and innovation programme (Hi-Prix), Grant Agreement Number: 101095593

publicationDetails.detailsText: This paper is currently under review. Please do not cite, circulate, or reuse without permission.

detail.abstract: This study advances the debate on the strategic role of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance by examining its moderating effect on the relationship between research and development (R&D) investment and firm performance. While prior research has largely examined R&D investment and ESG performance independently, often within single-country or single-industry contexts, this study uses an integrative, multi-theoretical perspective drawing on agency theory, stakeholder theory, and resource-based theory. Using a panel dataset of 6,600 firm-year observations from high-tech industries across Europe and the US (2016-2023), our results show that R&D investment exerts a negative short-term but positive lagged impact on firm performance. ESG performance directly enhances firm performance and significantly moderates the R&D-performance relationship by mitigating short-term inefficiencies and agency costs. These findings remain robust across alternative variable specifications, lag structures, and dynamic panel estimations using the system GMM approach. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the moderating effect of ESG performance is more pronounced in the information technology sector and among European firms, while comparatively weaker in the healthcare, communication services, and in the US. Disaggregated analysis further shows that environmental and governance dimensions are particularly effective in offsetting the short-term costs of R&D investment, while the social dimension is less influential, underscoring the multidimensional nature of ESG performance. Overall, our study provides insights into ESG performance as a strategic enabler that enhances the effectiveness of R&D investment and clarifies when and how R&D investment creates value in the short term.

title: How managed lake-level fluctuations affect waterfront property values: evidence from a regulated lake system
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How managed lake-level fluctuations affect waterfront property values: evidence from a regulated lake system
detail.abstract: Climate change is increasing hydrologic variability and management trade-offs. This study examines how managed lake-level fluctuations are capitalized into waterfront property values within a regulated lake system in Wisconsin, USA. By linking residential property transactions from 2013–2024 with high-frequency hydrologic and lake water-quality data, we estimate two-way fixed-effects hedonic models that isolate the economic impacts of deviations from expected seasonal lake levels under existing management rules. The results reveal a strongly asymmetric market response to lake-level fluctuations. Property values decline significantly when lake levels rise above expected seasonal conditions, while moderate low-water deviations are associated with higher prices. A positive lake-level deviation of 0.25 ft reduces sale prices by approximately 10 percent, and a 0.50 ft deviation lowers prices by about 20 percent. Distributional analysis indicates that capitalization losses are concentrated among higher-value waterfront properties, highlighting unequal exposure to hydrologic risk. Monte Carlo simulations further suggest that stabilizing positive lake-level deviations within ±0.25 ft increases the aggregate value of lakefront housing by approximately $5.5 million (2013 USD), equivalent to an average gain of roughly $15,000 per property. By demonstrating how property markets internalize hydrologic risk in a nonlinear and policy-relevant manner, this study contributes evidence on the economic consequences of freshwater management under climate variability. While the analysis focuses on a single regulated lake system, the underlying mechanism of capitalization of managed hydrologic variability is relevant to many dam-regulated and rule-based freshwater systems facing increasing climate risk.

title: Political Polarization, Institutional Investor Power, and the Viability of Climate-Change Shareholder Activism
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics and University of Oxford - Said Business School

detail.title: Political Polarization, Institutional Investor Power, and the Viability of Climate-Change Shareholder Activism
detail.abstract: This paper considers the effects of two emergent phenomenon on corporate governance: the increasing polarization of investors' attitudes towards sustainability issues, and diversified blockholders, e.g., universal owners, replacing atomistic small shareholders as the pivotal voters in proxy voting contests. We show that polarized views and strategic voting break the relationship between vote outcomes and voters' preferences. Proposals, motivated by sustainability values, not share value maximization, can pass even when the majority of proxy votes are controlled by agents who do not share these values. Increasing the fraction of voters adhering to sustainability norms can reduce the probability that proposals advancing sustainability goals pass.

title: Regulatory Migration to Europe: ICO Reallocation Following U.S. Securities Enforcement
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and Kathmandu University

detail.title: Regulatory Migration to Europe: ICO Reallocation Following U.S. Securities Enforcement
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether a major U.S. regulatory clari9ication coincided with cross-border spillovers in crypto-asset entrepreneurial 9inance. We study the Securities and Exchange Commission's July 2017 DAO Report, which clari9ied the application of U.S. securities law to many initial coin offerings (ICOs), and analyze how global issuance activity adjusted across regions. Using a comprehensive global dataset of ICOs from 2014 to 2021, we construct a region-month panel and evaluate issuance dynamics around the announcement. We document a substantial and persistent reallocation of ICO activity toward Europe following the DAO Report. In panel regressions with region and month 9ixed effects, Europe experiences an average post-2017 increase of approximately 14 additional ICOs per region-month relative to other regions, net of global market cycles. The results are consistent with cross-border regulatory spillovers in highly mobile digital-asset markets.

title: Component-wise Latent Class Choice Model
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: Component-wise Latent Class Choice Model
detail.abstract: Understanding individual preference heterogeneity is a central challenge in discrete choice modeling. While the Latent Class Choice Model (LCCM) offers interpretable segmentation by grouping individuals with similar tastes, it imposes a restrictive structure in which all utility coefficients vary jointly within a single latent class. When heterogeneity arises independently across multiple attribute dimensions, this structure requires a combinatorial number of classes, leading to parameter redundancy, information dispersion, and statistical inefficiency.To address these limitations, we propose the Component-wise Latent Class Choice Model (CLCCM). The CLCCM decomposes the utility function into analyst-defined components, each governed by its own latent class structure. Rather than assigning individuals to a single monolithic class, the model allows distinct class memberships for each utility component, with overall preference profiles formed as the Cartesian product of component-specific memberships. This structure parsimoniously captures multidimensional heterogeneity while preserving interpretability. We further develop a generalized EM algorithm with component-wise updates that guarantees monotonic likelihood improvement and stable estimation.Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the CLCCM achieves superior statistical efficiency, more accurate recovery of utility coefficients and memberships, and more stable convergence than conventional LCCM specifications spanning the same heterogeneity space. An empirical application to discrete choice experiment data on breast cancer screening shows that the CLCCM uncovers interpretable behavioral segments associated with specific parts of the utility function that are conflated in standard models. Overall, the CLCCM provides a flexible and scalable framework that balances interpretability and efficiency for modeling multidimensional preference heterogeneity in applied choice analysis.

title: Moral Consumers and the Environment
affiliations: University of Copenhagen and Stockholm School of Economics

detail.title: Moral Consumers and the Environment
detail.abstract: We develop a unit-demand model for environmentally costly goods and moral consumers who have a Kantian desire to "do the right thing". This moral desire is reflected in each consumer's buying strategy, which accounts for the environmental cost she would incur if, with some probability, other consumers were to follow her strategy. We first establish the existence and uniqueness of a Nash equilibrium strategy profile for heterogeneous finite populations of such moral consumers. Next, we study optimal taxation of such goods and find that with moral consumers, it matters whether they understand the tax system. If they do, then the optimal tax is the Pigovian, regardless of the distribution of moral values in the consumer population and their uncertainty about the environmental cost. If they do not understand the tax system, the optimal tax is lower, and the more moral the consumer population, the lower it is. Last, we consider a quota system like the European emissions trading system. We show that any binding quota neutralizes the effect of morality when consumers are aware of the quota system.

title: Are Government Bonds Safe in Times of War and Pandemic?
affiliations: , Stanford University, Columbia University Graduate School of Business and University of Texas, Austin - Department of Finance

detail.title: Are Government Bonds Safe in Times of War and Pandemic?
detail.abstract:
We analyze real returns on U.S. and U.K. government debt during major wars and the COVID-19 pandemic over the past three centuries. Wars are associated with sharply negative real returns on outstanding government debt, with returns falling far below economic growth, in contrast to peacetime periods when returns exceed growth. Elevated surprise inflation and financial repression account for a cumulative 31% wedge between returns and growth over four years of war, implying that bondholders bear a substantial share of wartime fiscal costs. During wartime, government bonds also systematically underperform risky assets.

title: DAP-Whisper: A Robust Audio-Visual Speech Recognition System via Distribution-Aware Prompting and Consistency-Gated Modulation
affiliations: Northwestern Polytechnic University (NPU), Academy of Military Sciences - Defense Innovation Institute, Academy of Military Sciences - Defense Innovation Institute,  Tianjin Artificial Intelligence Innovation Center,  Tianjin Artificial Intelligence Innovation Center, Academy of Military Sciences - Defense Innovation Institute, Northwestern Polytechnic University (NPU) and Academy of Military Sciences - Defense Innovation Institute

detail.title: DAP-Whisper: A Robust Audio-Visual Speech Recognition System via Distribution-Aware Prompting and Consistency-Gated Modulation
detail.abstract: Large-scale pre-trained models like Whisper have established a new paradigm for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). However, their unimodal nature renders them vulnerable to non-stationary environmental interference and unpredictable distribution shifts in unconstrained scenarios. Existing multimodal adaptation approaches typically rely on static fusion mechanisms, which apply a uniform injection strategy regardless of the input's degradation profile. This rigidity creates a fundamental mismatch between fixed parameters and dynamic noise manifolds. To address this limitation, we propose DAP-Whisper, a parameter-efficient framework that reformulates multimodal adaptation as a continuous interpolation problem within a learned manifold simplex. Specifically, we design a Quality-Aware Distribution-Adaptive Prompting (Q-DAP) mechanism, which dynamically synthesizes instance-specific parameters by interpolating orthogonal basis vectors, ensuring precise alignment with real-time acoustic shifts. Furthermore, to mitigate the epistemic uncertainty arising from visual corruption, we introduce a Consistency-Gated Modulation (CGM) mechanism that acts as a reliability valve to prevent negative transfer. Extensive experiments on the LRS3 benchmark demonstrate that DAP-Whisper outperforms state-of-the-art static baselines.  Specifically, with the Whisper-Medium backbone, it drives the WER down to 3.36% under 0dB noise, while exhibiting superior resilience against joint audio-visual degradation.

title: Shopping From Home
affiliations: , Stanford University - Department of Economics, Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business and Northwestern University

detail.title: Shopping From Home
detail.abstract: Conducting a new survey on the Nielsen Consumer panel we examine the impact of working from home (WFH) on shopping, finding three key results. First, WFH changed shopping modes, increasing online shopping and the fraction of trips to stores on weekdays. Second, WFH increased total spending through increased product quantity and range, tilting expenditure towards food and general merchandise and away from health and beauty products. Finally, WFH increased prices paid by shoppers and lowered price elasticities due to a move towards higher-cost products and lower deal usage. The change in prices paid is concentrated among married households, driven by a redistribution of shopping responsibility within the household, especially when the new remote worker is male. We find that remote workers engage in more shopping trips but fewer minutes of shopping. Our results suggest that shifting to remote work increases prices paid for groceries by about 1%, highlighting how WFH is impacting households, retail and inflation.

title: Early Birds Get the Vol: Morning Volatility Uncertainty and Variance Risk Premium
affiliations: University of Liverpool - Management School (ULMS) and University of Liverpool - Management School (ULMS)

detail.title: Early Birds Get the Vol: Morning Volatility Uncertainty and Variance Risk Premium
detail.abstract: We document that morning volatility-of-volatility (VVIX), measured at 10:00 EST during the U.S.-European market overlap, strongly predicts next-day variance asset returns. Predictive power peaks with t-statistics reaching 5.6 and adjusted R 2 of 2.6%, but diminishes after 11:00 EST. Trading strategies exploiting this pattern generate Sharpe ratios exceeding 2.0, remaining economically meaningful even after transaction costs. Crucially, intraday returns display a flat relationship with morning VVIX on high volatility uncertainty days, while close-to-close returns exhibit strong predictability. These findings are difficult to reconcile with standard risk premium theories but are consistent with limited attention and slow-moving beliefs about volatility.

title: Geopolitics in the Evaluation of International Scientific Collaboration
affiliations: Center for Science of Science and Innovation, University of California, San Diego (UCSD), University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - 21st Century China Center and Northwestern University - Northwestern Institute for Complex Systems (NICO)

detail.title: Geopolitics in the Evaluation of International Scientific Collaboration
detail.abstract:
This study provides evidence that geopolitical considerations systematically shape funding evaluations of international collaboration proposals. We examine this dynamic in the consequential context of U.S.–China collaboration. Across two large-scale randomized experiments with U.S. policymakers and U.S.-based scientists, we find substantial and consistent penalties for proposals involving China-based collaborators. Policymakers express much greater unconditional support for proposals with Germany-based collaborators than for otherwise identical proposals with China-based collaborators (68% vs. 28%). Crucially, this penalty is not confined to policymakers: scientists themselves exhibit a sizeable 18 percentage-point gap (48% vs. 30%), despite professional expectations of merit-based evaluation. Much of the difference reflects a shift from unconditional to conditional approval rather than outright rejection. These penalties are remarkably consistent across scientific fields and respondent characteristics, with little evidence of heterogeneity, indicating that they reflect geopolitical rather than domain-specific concerns. Overall, the findings suggest that geopolitics influences gatekeeping judgments in government funding, with broad implications for peer review, scientific norms, and the future of international collaboration in an era of intensifying geopolitical competition.

title: The Perils of Over-Ambition: A Critical Analysis of Ghana's 2026 Budget, Unrealistic Revenue Projections, And the Risks of Economic Overreach
affiliations: University of Buckingham

detail.title: The Perils of Over-Ambition: A Critical Analysis of Ghana's 2026 Budget, Unrealistic Revenue Projections, And the Risks of Economic Overreach
detail.abstract: The 2026 Budget Statement of Ghana with the theme of Resetting for Growth, Jobs and Economic Transformation is the most ambitious budgetary blueprint of the country in the history of the Fourth Republic. It also plans the introduction of the 30-billion programme of the 24-Hour Economy and mega-projects of oil-palms and the 500-million-US-dollar mega-plan, the abolition of the COVID-19 levy, and a significant project in education and health recapitalisation drive to date. The whole apparatus is founded on the revenues figures that are not only heard to sound rosy, but displayed to be inconsistent with the Ghana 2025 out-turn and 30 years of historical evidence on tax-elasticity. As indicated in the article through the official 2026 Budget Statement, 2025 midyear and 4th quarter revenue returns, and the panel of crosscountry fiscal-performance data, the 33 per cent growth in non-oil tax revenue, 130 per cent growth in oil receipts and 63 per cent growth in grants cannot be realised under the existing macro conditions. This may imply a financing gap (of 71 billion of fresh domestic borrowing) would bring the cash deficit to 6 per cent of GDP, triggering renewed debt distress and crowd-out social expenditure. We put our findings into perspective with the literature on political-economy relating to optimism bias (Flyvbjerg 2013), commodity-price volatility (Reinhart and Rogoff 2010), and the African tax capacity (Adu and Marbuah 2021). The paper concludes with a progressively-evidence-based reform agenda: (i) conservative revenue forecasts using a three year moving average; (ii) A parliamentary Revenue-Stabilisation Buffer (to be financed by windfall oil and port surpluses); (iii) A gradual rollout in phases (priority given by ex-ante ERR and gender employment elasticities); and (iv) An independent Parliamentary Revenue-Scorecard to be achieved before committing expenditure undertakings in more than three years. In their absence, the 2026 Ghanaian reset is susceptible to becoming another boom-bust cycle capable of annihilating the hard-acquired progress in 2023-2025 in macro-stabilisation.

title: Impacts of Compound Pollution on Winter Wheat Yield Through Machine Learning-Driven Ozone Projections Under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
affiliations: Hebei University of Environmental Engineering, Hebei University of Environmental Engineering and Hebei University of Environmental Engineering

detail.title: Impacts of Compound Pollution on Winter Wheat Yield Through Machine Learning-Driven Ozone Projections Under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of global climate warming, the threat posed by surface ozone pollution to agricultural production is becoming increasingly severe. To accurately predict future changes in ozone concentration, this study first compared multiple machine learning models and found that the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model performed best in the prediction task. The model demonstrated exceptional accuracy on the test set, with a coefficient of determination (R²) reaching 0.996, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.42 μg/m³, and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.882 μg/m³.Simulations based on the XGBoost model revealed significant differences in ozone concentration changes in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region from 2021 to 2100 under different Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). Specifically, under the high-emission scenarios of SSP370 and SSP585, ozone concentrations increased by 20.7 μg/m³ (11.6%) and 23.8 μg/m³ (13.4%), respectively, with the increase under SSP585 being 6.3 times that under SSP126 and twice that under SSP245. This highlights the exacerbating effect of high-emission pathways on ozone pollution.The rise in ozone concentration directly threatens crop yields. This study further employed the AOT40 algorithm to quantify winter wheat yield losses, finding that under high-emission scenarios (SSP585 and SSP370), the average loss rate reached 11.6%, with the area of high-risk regions significantly exceeding the loss levels under sustainable development pathways, posing a severe threat to food security.To investigate the driving factors behind yield losses, the study utilized geographic detector analysis and found that PM2.5 distribution was the most critical factor affecting winter wheat yields, with all factor interactions exhibiting synergistic enhancing effects. The relative contribution values (q) for "PM2.5 ∩ temperature," "PM2.5 ∩ nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)," and "temperature ∩ NO₂" reached 0.91, 0.91, and 0.86, respectively. This indicates that the combined effects of compound pollution and high-temperature stress are the core mechanisms driving yield losses, providing a basis for formulating emission reduction policies.

title: The Economic Impact of Mass Deportations
affiliations: University of Michigan, University of Michigan - Department of Economics, University of Notre Dame and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Economic Impact of Mass Deportations
detail.abstract:
This paper quantifies the effects of large-scale deportations on wages, prices, and real incomes in the United States. We impute the legal status for each worker in the American Community Survey by combining detailed individual information with group-level visa records. In 2024, 3.2% of US workers were unauthorized, but some regions and sectors were heavily dependent on unauthorized immigrant labor. We develop a dynamic quantitative framework with multiple regions, sectors and occupations, heterogeneous workers, and endogenous capital accumulation to study the economic impacts of removing unauthorized workers. We derive analytical expressions relating region- and occupation-specific real wages and sectoral relative prices to changes in the supply of immigrant workers, observable factor shares, and combinations of structural elasticities. Following the removal of 50% of unauthorized immigrants, in the short run average native real wages rise 0.15% nationally, driven by an increase in the capital-labor ratio. In the long run, however, native real wages fall in every state, and by 0.33% nationally, as capital gets decumulated in response to a lower population. Consumer prices in the sectors intensive in unauthorized workers – such as Farming – rise by about 1% relative to the price of the average consumption basket, while most other sectors experience negligible relative price changes.

title: Quantifying Privacy-Driven Shifts in the Spatial Representativeness of Smartphone Mobility Data: Evidence from Chicago
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: Quantifying Privacy-Driven Shifts in the Spatial Representativeness of Smartphone Mobility Data: Evidence from Chicago

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The analysis involved only data that was fully unidentified, aggregated, and had no access to identifiable private information, nor did it entail any interaction with individuals. As such, Institutional Review Board approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by funding from the National Science Foundation Smart and Connected Communities (SCC) Planning Grant Award # 2125488. We would like to thank the Planning Grant Steering Committee for its continued support and guidance for this research.

detail.abstract: Smartphone-derived location-based services (LBS) data are increasingly used to analyze travel behavior, accessibility, and spatial mobility patterns, yet their representativeness is uncertain due to opaque and rapidly evolving data-generation processes. In recent years, platform-level privacy interventions have altered how and when mobile devices generate traceable location signals, with potential implications for transport research relying on these data. This study examines changes in the spatial and demographic representation of smartphone mobility traces in the Chicago metropolitan area between 2021 and 2022, a period coinciding with major privacy changes to the iOS operating system. Using a combination of market share analysis, difference-indifferences modeling, and an integrated spatial-statistical validation, we document a pronounced decline in the visibility of iOS devices within a large commercial LBS dataset, alongside spatially uneven patterns of representation. Contrary to common assumptions about underrepresentation in mobility data, higher-income, denser, and younger census tracts exhibit lower tracking rates relative to other areas. These patterns persist after accounting for overall growth in device counts and are consistent with a platform-mediated behavioral barrier to data capture. Rather than isolating a single causal mechanism, the findings illustrate how privacy governance can reshape the mobility datagenerating process in ways that produce non-random spatial biases. The results underscore the need for transport geographers and urban researchers to critically assess how platform policies, user behavior, and vendor data pipelines jointly influence the populations and places that remain visible in smartphone-based mobility analyses. This evidence base helps move the debate beyond general cautionary notes to quantified, policy-relevant diagnostics of how privacy architecture shapes who is visible in LBS data, and where.

title: Coca’s Return and the American Overdose Fallout
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), Department of Economics, University of Oregon - Department of Economics, Old Dominion University - Economics and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Coca’s Return and the American Overdose Fallout
detail.abstract:
Colombian coca cultivation fell dramatically between 2000 and 2015, a period that saw intense U.S.-backed eradication and interdiction efforts. That progress reversed in 2015, when peace talks and legal rulings in Colombia opened enforcement gaps. Coca plantation has since increased to record levels, which coincided with a sharp rise in cocaine-related overdose deaths in the U.S. We estimate how much of that rise can be causally attributed to Colombia’s new coca boom. Leveraging the unforeseen coca supply shock and cross-county differences in pre-shock cocaine exposure, we find that the surge in supply caused an immediate rise in overdose mortality in the U.S. Our analysis estimates on the order of 1,000–1,500 additional U.S. deaths per year in the late 2010s can be attributed to Colombia’s cocaine boom. Implicit annual loss in American statistical life values about $48,000 per hectare of cultivation in Colombia. If left untamed, the current level of coca cultivation (over 230,000 ha in 2022) may impose on the order of $10 billion per year in costs via overdose fatalities.

title: Does Social Media Identify the Optimistic Bias of State-Controlled Media? Evidence from China
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen - School of Management and Economics, University of Sothern California and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)

detail.title: Does Social Media Identify the Optimistic Bias of State-Controlled Media? Evidence from China

publicationDetails.detailsText: forthcoming at Journal of Law and Economics

detail.abstract: State-controlled media, which is subject to political influence, tends to exhibit optimistic bias. In contrast, social media, which relies on the collective wisdom of crowds and generates information anonymously, is less likely to reflect politically induced optimistic bias. This paper investigates whether social media can serve as a benchmark for identifying the optimistic bias of statecontrolled media. Using articles from state-controlled newspapers and posts from online stock forums in China that discuss the same firms on the same days from 2009 to 2016, we find that social media can effectively identify the politically induced positive tone bias in state-controlled media. Furthermore, our stock return analysis shows that the market perceives state-controlled media as less informative when it is identified as optimistically biased, providing additional evidence that social media can serve as a reliable benchmark for detecting reporting bias.

title: American Investment in Chinese Renminbi
affiliations: Columbia University, Yale School of Management, New York University (NYU) - New York University, Stanford Graduate School of Business and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Economics

detail.title: American Investment in Chinese Renminbi
detail.abstract:
This paper uses microdata on U.S. mutual fund and ETF portfolios from SEC Form NPORT to study American investment in Chinese Renminbi (RMB)–denominated bonds. We show that, even as total foreign holdings of Chinese bonds rebounded in 2024, U.S. holdings of RMB bonds fell sharply and that most of this decline reflects funds exiting RMB positions entirely. These patterns point to a shift in the composition of China’s foreign investor base away from U.S. institutional investors and illustrate how publicly available microdata can inform work on international currency use.

title: The H-1B Wage Gap, Visa Fees, and Employer Demand
affiliations: Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS)

detail.title: The H-1B Wage Gap, Visa Fees, and Employer Demand
detail.abstract:
The H-1B program lets firms hire high-skill foreign workers for a six-year term. The annual number of visas allocated to for-profit firms is capped at 85,000 and there is excess demand for those visas. The analysis merges data from the Labor Condition Application where firms attest that H-1B hires do not adversely impact natives, the I-129 Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker where firms request to hire a specific person, and the American Community Surveys. On average, H-1B workers earn 16 percent less than comparable natives. The payroll savings suggest that firms may be willing to pay a one-time fee to obtain an H-1B visa. The data are examined using a labor demand model to simulate how a fee alters the hiring decision. Depending on the level of excess demand, the unobserved productivity gains or costs from an H-1B hire, and the rate of job separations, the revenue-maximizing fee is between $118,000 and $264,000, has little or no impact on the number of H-1Bs hired, and generates between $6.2 and $22.4 billion in revenues. The fee would also change the skill composition of the H-1B workforce, making it more skilled.

title: Automation Is Not a Sufficient Statistic A Two-Frontier Task Model of Robots, AI, and Inequality
affiliations: Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos

detail.title: Automation Is Not a Sufficient Statistic A Two-Frontier Task Model of Robots, AI, and Inequality
detail.abstract: The standard task-based framework organizes automation along a single continuum. This paper introduces a second frontier: production requires both physical and cognitive tasks, each with its own automation threshold. The main result is a masking theorem: a single automation index that conflates robot and AI exposure assigns the wrong sign to the skill premium effect. Two economies with identical aggregate automation can exhibit opposite inequality dynamics depending on which frontier advances. The key asymmetry is reinstatement: robot adoption creates roughly five times more new complementary tasks than AI does, because physical automation generates maintenance, supervision, and quality-control roles that non-college workers fill, while cognitive automation concentrates new tasks in high-skill niches. Cross-sectional evidence from 445 U.S. commuting zones confirms both predictions: among seven automation measures, Webb Robot exposure is the only one that compresses the skill premium, while all six others widen it. Separating robot and AI exposure triples the explained variance relative to pooling. The sign pattern reverses after 2019 as robot diffusion plateaus, consistent with the model's prediction that opposite-sign effects are a transitional phenomenon of active frontier movement.

title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5m Neighborhoods
affiliations: , , Dartmouth College - Department of Economics, University of Chicago and Harvard University

detail.title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5m Neighborhoods
detail.abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards, and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the U.S. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy.

title: The Resilience of Rule Compliance in a Polarized Society
affiliations: University of Bonn, University of Nottingham, University of Bonn, Max-Planck-Institut für Verhaltenökonomik and University of Bonn

detail.title: The Resilience of Rule Compliance in a Polarized Society

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the European Research Council [grant number ERC-AdG 101020453 PRINCIPLES] and the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under Germany’s Excellence Strategy [EXC 2126/1-390838866].

detail.abstract: Democratic societies depend on citizens following rules even when those rules are set by political opponents. Rising polarization may threaten this behavior. We test the impact of polarization on rule compliance in the United States across three pre-registered waves (May and November 2024; April 2025; n = 8,340) using the "coins task", which is a non-political, generic rule-following task, where breaking the rule increases payoffs. Participants were randomly assigned to follow rules set by the experimenter, a political co-partisan, a political opponent, or a non-partisan US citizen. Rule compliance ranged from 52.3% to 57.8%, and equivalence testing indicates no meaningful differences across waves or partisan rule-setter identities. However, greater affective distance from partisan rule setters is associated with lower compliance and weaker descriptive and normative beliefs about rule-following. These findings suggest that rule compliance is resilient to the rule-setter's identity. While affective polarization may erode this behavior somewhat, substantial compliance remains: the human tendency to follow rules, even when incentivized to break them, survives the "stress test" of partisan rule-setting in highly polarized times.

title: Why Adult Learning Systems Fail To Signal: Institutional Separation, Credential Gaps, And The Case For Job-Embedded Competency Degrees Evidence From South Korea’s Lifelong Education System

detail.title: Why Adult Learning Systems Fail To Signal: Institutional Separation, Credential Gaps, And The Case For Job-Embedded Competency Degrees Evidence From South Korea’s Lifelong Education System

keywords: and the Case for Job-Embedded Competency Degrees lifelong learning

detail.abstract:
Adult learning systems in many countries aspire to support occupational mobility, yet in practice they often gravitate toward leisure and cultural enrichment rather than job-relevant skill formation. This paper uses South Korea’s lifelong education system as an illustrative case of a broader structural phenomenon we term signaling failure in adult learning—a condition in which participation in formal continuing education produces credentials that are insufficiently legible to employers (Kim et al., 2025), thereby undermining the investment rationale for adult learners seeking occupational transitions.

Drawing on labor market signaling theory (Spence, 1973) and human capital theory (Becker, 1964), this paper develops the IS-CG-LE analytical framework (Institutional Separation → Credential Gap → Leisure Equilibrium) to link administrative bifurcation to a self-reinforcing non-vocational equilibrium. It extends Spence’s model by introducing multi-layered signal guarantors, arguing that the absence of tri-party endorsement (education, government, and industry) is the cause of signaling failure. Finally, it proposes the Job-Embedded Competency Degree (JECD) as an institutional design instrument to bridge the credential gap and realign adult learning with labor market demands.

title: Will Payment Innovations Transform the International Monetary System?
affiliations: Banque de France and Banque de France

detail.title: Will Payment Innovations Transform the International Monetary System?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Banque de France

detail.abstract: In this paper, we analyze the effects of the rise of new payment technologies on the international role of the dollar and on the functioning of the international monetary system. The analysis highlights an ambiguous impact of new payment technologies, which are among the main factors that could lead to a significant change in the functioning of the international monetary system in the short term. While the rise and widespread adoption of instant payment systems are likely to contribute to the emergence of a multipolar monetary system, the efficiency of such a system will depend on the ability to interconnect the different systems so as to avoid the pitfall of financial fragmentation. Conversely, the rise of stablecoins, given their current features 1 is likely to increase the role of the dollar, potentially ensuring its near-total domination. Only the possibility of issuing alternative payment instrumentseither in the form of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) or stablecoins backed by other currencies-would be likely to limit the effects of extreme dollarization. Other drivers of change-political and geopolitical factors, or portfolio diversification motives-are more likely to operate over the longer term. They nevertheless run up against powerful network externalities, which tend to favor the continued dominance of the dollar.

title: Fast Core Identification
affiliations: Cornell University

detail.title: Fast Core Identification
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a fast eigenvector-based methodology for optimal matching for any number of agents and objects in the system. The methodology helps separate agents who are likely to be in the core from those not in the core in a novel way and in linear time (O(n)) using hardware acceleration for selected components. The proposed technique is well suited for complex large-dimensional problems like housing choice and school choice, among others. The process retains all the properties of Top Trading Cycles (TTC), namely Pareto efficiency, individual rationality, and strategy-proofness.

title: Resilient-to-Fragile Transition and Excess Volatility in Supply Chain Networks
affiliations: Sorbonne Université, Macrocosm, Utrecht University and Capital Fund Management

detail.title: Resilient-to-Fragile Transition and Excess Volatility in Supply Chain Networks
detail.abstract: We study the disequilibrium dynamics of a stylised model of production networks in which firms use perishable and non-substitutable intermediate inputs, so that adverse idiosyncratic productivity shocks can trigger downstream shortages and output losses. To protect against such disruptions, firms hold precautionary inventories that act as buffer stocks. We show that, for a given dispersion of firm-level productivity shocks, there exists a critical level of inventories above which the economy remains in a stable stochastic steady state. Below this critical level, the system becomes fragile, i.e., it becomes prone to system-wide crises. As this resilience-fragility boundary is approached from above, aggregate output volatility rises sharply and diverges, even though shocks are purely idiosyncratic. Because inventories are costly, competitive pressures induce firms to economize on buffers. Although we do not explicitly model such costs, we argue that the resulting behaviour of individual firms drives the system close to criticality, generating persistent excess macroeconomic volatility-in other words, "small shocks, large cycles"-in line with other settings where efficiency and resilience are in tension with each other (Hynes et al., 2022; Moran et al., 2025). In the language of phase transitions, the resilient-to-fragile transition is continuous (supercritical): the economy exhibits a well-defined stochastic equilibrium with finite volatility on one side of the boundary, while beyond it the probability of a collapse in finite time tends to one. We characterize this transition primarily through numerical simulations and derive an analytical description in a high-perishability, high-connectivity limit. Finally, we show that the ability to rapidly reallocate demand across alternative suppliers shifts the critical boundary and can eliminate the fragile regime, underscoring the macroeconomic importance of inventory policies and supplier diversification for production network resilience.

title: ICE Arrests across Trump's First and Second Terms: Variation in Targeting, Method, and Geography
affiliations: , University of California, Berkeley and

detail.title: ICE Arrests across Trump's First and Second Terms: Variation in Targeting, Method, and Geography
detail.abstract:
Deportation is often framed as a necessary tool to protect public safety by removing people who commit crimes. We use newly available, and externally validated, administrative data containing all US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests from September 2015-October 2025. Beyond demonstrating national trends in immigration arrests by method and composition over time, we are also able to compare, for the first time, apprehensions spanning the start of the two Trump administrations, both of which focused on mass immigration enforcement. Our results reveal that the reality of immigration enforcement diverges sharply from the public narrative: while arrests spiked at the outset of both Trump presidencies, there were significant declines in the percentage of arrested individuals with criminal convictions, with especially marked declines in 2025. Examining potential mechanisms reveals that this is driven by a change in ICE tactics, but even conditional on tactic, as arrests rose, the percent with a criminal record declined. Moreover, we find substantial heterogeneity over time and across ICE Areas of Responsibility. Taken together, our results highlight a substantial gap between political rhetoric and reality.
