title: Bias in Shipping Returns
affiliations: Bayes Business School (formerly Cass), City, University of London, Bayes Business School and University of Essex - Essex Business School

detail.title: Bias in Shipping Returns
detail.abstract: We use a hand-collected dataset to document that vessels are sold more rapidly when the sale realizes a substantial capital gain. This has important implications for measuring returns on shipping assets. We demonstrate that it generates a "quit-while-ahead" bias which significantly raises the IRRs recorded for individual vessels and shipping funds. We show that the underlying cause is an endogeneity bias that will also be present in other annualized return measures. To avoid this, and an additional convexity bias, returns must be calculated over predetermined horizons. It is important that investors do not rely on biased data when choosing their strategic asset allocations, or selecting individual assets or fund managers.

title: Can A Holistic Coaching and Referral Programme Enhance Well-being and Employability Amongst NEET Youth?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Can A Holistic Coaching and Referral Programme Enhance Well-being and Employability Amongst NEET Youth?
detail.abstract: Global youth NEET rates declined from 22.8% in 2005 to 20.4% in 2025 (ILO, 2025) yet have stagnated or worsened in some regions. While most upper middle-income countries reduced NEET rates over two decades, South Africa experienced a notable increase. In response, the Basic Package of Support (BPS) for youth was piloted. Grounded in understanding the multidimensional nature of poverty and its role in constraining opportunity, the BPS draws on global evidence showing that interventions addressing multiple barriers-especially underlying vulnerability factors-tend to yield stronger outcomes (Kluve et al. 2019; Apunyo et al. 2022). The existing literature is dominated by evidence from high-income countries and focuses largely on skills training and employment outcomes, offering limited insight into how multi-component programmes address the vulnerabilities that contribute to NEET status. Using concurrent triangulation mixed methods design, this article addresses these gaps with evidence from a middle-income context. It evaluates a multi-component intervention and assesses broad outcomes, including mental health, wellbeing, social support, and connections to learning and earning opportunities. It also examines how changes in these domains relate to shifts in underlying vulnerabilities, providing insight into mechanisms supporting sustained improvements. Findings show improvements in wellbeing, including quality of life, mental health, perceived support, stress management and service access. By the completion of four coaching sessions, almost 40% of participants reconnected to learning or earning opportunities. These results demonstrate meaningful reductions in barriers to opportunity and have important implications for youth programming and policy in contexts grappling with persistent youth unemployment and high NEET rates.

title: Does the Low-Carbon City Pilot Policy Promote Green Innovation Collaboration? Evidence from Knowledge Embeddedness and Complexity
affiliations: Tsinghua University and University of Chicago

detail.title: Does the Low-Carbon City Pilot Policy Promote Green Innovation Collaboration? Evidence from Knowledge Embeddedness and Complexity
detail.abstract: Environmental policies are increasingly expected to promote not only emission reduction but also high-quality green innovation. While existing studies show that China’s Low-Carbon City Pilot (LCCP) policy increases green innovation output, little is known about whether and how it reshapes the structure of innovation collaboration across and within cities. Drawing on the extended Porter Hypothesis, this study examines the impact of the LCCP on green innovation collaboration by focusing on inter-city embeddedness and intra-city complexity. Using a balanced panel of 250 Chinese prefecture-level cities from 2006 to 2022, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences approach and construct patent-based indicators to capture cross-city collaborative integration and within-city technological diversity. The results show that the LCCP significantly increases both inter-city embeddedness and intra-city complexity. Digitalization and environmental regulation intensity positively moderate these effects, and the joint implementation of the Innovation City Pilot (ICP) and the LCCP generates strong complementary impacts. The effects are more pronounced in eastern and large cities, in key environmental protection cities, and in directly designated pilot cities, while weaker in resource-based regions. This study contributes to the literature by moving beyond innovation quantity to examine how environmental regulation reshapes innovation collaboration networks, providing new evidence on the collaborative mechanisms through which low-carbon policies foster green technological upgrading.

title: Time-of-Use Pricing and Peak Shifting in Residential EV Charging: A Quasi-Experimental Study from China
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, VU University Amsterdam, Zhejiang University and Beijing Jiaotong University

detail.title: Time-of-Use Pricing and Peak Shifting in Residential EV Charging: A Quasi-Experimental Study from China
detail.abstract: The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) has intensified peak load pressures on electricity systems. Time-of-use (TOU) pricing aims to alleviate this pressure by incentivizing intertemporal load shifting, yet causal evidence on its effectiveness, drawn from real-world, high-frequency charging data, remains scarce. This study employs a difference-in-differences (DID) model to evaluate the impact of TOU pricing on residential EV charging behavior, utilizing high-frequency hourly data from over 20,000 users in Shandong Province, China. Findings reveal that TOU pricing significantly reduces peak-period charging while increasing off-peak consumption, indicating a pronounced intertemporal substitution effect. Despite reduced peak demand, total charging volume marginally increases due to lower charging costs. CES model estimates detect weak self-price elasticity between peak and off-peak periods but significant cross-price elasticity. Welfare analysis indicates that TOU pricing enhances consumer surplus. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that users with higher peak-hour dependence and greater consumption volatility exhibit stronger adjustments. Overall, the findings demonstrate that TOU pricing not only mitigates peak load stress but also promotes EV usage and supports the electrification of transport. These results underscore the institutional value of TOU mechanisms in facilitating vehicle-grid integration and advancing coordinated development between the energy and transport sectors.

title: The OnlyFans Economy: Intellectual Property's Pivot from Scarcity to Authenticity

detail.title: The OnlyFans Economy: Intellectual Property's Pivot from Scarcity to Authenticity
detail.abstract:
Generative AI is destabilizing the foundational assumption of intellectual property law: that creation is difficult, expensive, and requires legal inducement. When machines produce text, images, and code at near- zero marginal cost, the utilitarian justification for copyright and patent protection begins to collapse. This Essay argues that what emerges in its place is a regime organized not around the scarcity of creation, but around the scarcity of verification – a shift from an incentive paradigm to a source identification paradigm dominated by trademark, rights of publicity, and platform-controlled authentication infrastructure. OnlyFans provides a revealing case study. Despite AI-generated pornography flooding the market, the platform paid over $5.8 billion to human creators in 2024. Consumers pay not for content, which AI can approximate, but for provenance – the verified knowledge that they are interacting with a specific, authenticated person. This Essay identifies a "triple-lock" structure underlying this economy: verified identity draws consumers in, proprietary infrastructure ensures access requires staying inside the walled garden, and aggressive copyright enforcement destroys unauthorized copies that would otherwise undermine authenticity's value.

Applying a Law and Political Economy lens, the Essay argues that this emerging regime systematically advantages those who already possess recognized brands, legal departments, and capital for proprietary infrastructure – while offering little to individual creators who lack pre- existing fame. It concludes by proposing that the Library of Congress serve as a public "digital notary," preventing the infrastructure of authenticity from becoming a private toll road.

title: The Need for Trade Secret Legislation and its Multifaceted Impact on Commercial Law

detail.title: The Need for Trade Secret Legislation and its Multifaceted Impact on Commercial Law
detail.abstract: The protection of trade secrets is pivotal in fostering innovation, maintaining competitive advantage, and ensuring the efficiency of markets. This dissertation examines the hypothesis that the introduction of targeted legislation aimed at safeguarding trade secrets within the Indian legal framework will exert a substantial influence on business practices, innovation dynamics, and legal strategies, consequently bolstering market competitiveness and efficiency. Through comprehensive analysis and synthesis of existing literature, legislative frameworks, and case studies, this study explores the current landscape of trade secret protection in India and other countries and identifies the requirement of a specific trade secret law. By delving into comparative studies and drawing insights from jurisdictions with robust trade secret laws, it delineates the potential benefits of enacting tailored legislation tailored to address the unique challenges faced by Indian businesses. Ultimately, this dissertation seeks to provide insights regarding the formulation and implementation of trade secret legislation in India. By elucidating the multifaceted implications of robust protection mechanisms, it endeavors to contribute to the advancement of a more resilient, competitive, and innovation-driven Indian economy.

title: The Efficacy Filter and Pharmaceutical Patent Evergreening: Section 3(d) in India and a UK Perspective

detail.title: The Efficacy Filter and Pharmaceutical Patent Evergreening: Section 3(d) in India and a UK Perspective
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the role of Section 3(d) of the Indian Patents Act as a distinctive “efficacy filter” designed to curb pharmaceutical patent evergreening. Evergreening, commonly achieved through secondary patents on new forms, formulations, or uses of known drugs, risks extending monopoly protection without delivering commensurate therapeutic benefits. Through a doctrinal analysis centred on the Supreme Court of India’s landmark decision in Novartis AG v Union of India, the paper evaluates how Section 3(d) raises the patentability threshold by requiring a demonstrable enhancement in therapeutic efficacy for certain pharmaceutical derivatives.

The paper further assesses the international legality of Section 3(d), arguing that it is compatible with the TRIPS Agreement and reflects the public-health flexibilities affirmed by the Doha Declaration. Drawing comparative insights from the United Kingdom, the analysis considers whether a Section 3(d)-style efficacy threshold could be integrated into the UK patent system. While direct statutory transplantation is constrained by the European Patent Convention, the paper argues that the underlying principle of rewarding only clinically meaningful innovation remains relevant to UK patent doctrine. Ultimately, the paper contends that India’s efficacy-based approach offers a valuable conceptual framework for recalibrating pharmaceutical patent standards to better balance innovation incentives with access to medicines.

title: Employee Stock Ownership Plans and Corporate Earnings Performance: A Dynamic Perspective Using a Quantile Regression Approach
affiliations: School of Accounting, Finance and Economics, University of Waikato and National Cheng Kung University

detail.title: Employee Stock Ownership Plans and Corporate Earnings Performance: A Dynamic Perspective Using a Quantile Regression Approach
detail.abstract: This paper re-investigates the effect of Employee Stock Ownership Plans (ESOP) on profitability. Given the extensive research on the topic of ESOP, this paper contributes to the literature in using the quantile regression method (QR method) to better examine the relationship between ESOP and profitability, since prior studies of a variety of forms of employee ownership have yielded inconsistent results with regard to whether firms with these plans have better or worse performance, on average, than firms without them. The QR method has the advantage of tracking the dynamic relationship among variables, and it avoids the weakness of focusing on central behavior given the probability distribution of variable. In this paper, the empirical results show that by using S&P 500 10-year data since 1998, taking ESOP has a significantly positive impact on firm performance for companies which are in growth or decline stage. However, if firms already reach its mature stage, the relationship between ESOP and corporate earnings is insignificant. Factors which are likely to influence corporate performance, such as firm size and debt ratio, are taken into account in this work, and the previous results still hold.

title: Let's Stop Pretending: A Case for Recognizing Undevelopable Economies
affiliations: University of Portsmouth

detail.title: Let's Stop Pretending: A Case for Recognizing Undevelopable Economies
detail.abstract: Why do some nations absorb decades of international aid, technical assistance, and institutional reform programs yet remain trapped in cycles of stagnation? This article introduces the concept of "undevelopable economies"-contexts where development is not merely delayed, but structurally foreclosed by self-reinforcing institutional dysfunction. Unlike existing classifications such as "fragile," "failing," or "least developed" states-which imply the potential for progress given appropriate reforms-the notion of undevelopability challenges this foundational optimism. It identifies political-economic systems in which institutions persist precisely because they reproduce elite power, suppress accountability, and neutralize reform, even under sustained external intervention. The "developed-developing" spectrum has long organized the global economic imagination, implying a linear, if uneven, progression toward modernity for all nations. This article challenges that binary logic by introducing a third category that exists outside this continuum. In undevelopable economies, the institutional foundations for development are not merely weak but structurally foreclosed-actively resistant to the transformative trajectory the spectrum assumes. Grounded in institutional and critical theory, this paper argues that the conventional spectrum is not just incomplete but misleading. It obscures political realities where development is systematically blocked, not delayed. Through comparative analysis of Somalia, Haiti, and Venezuela, we illustrate three pathways of institutional foreclosure-substitution, stagnation, and perversion-that operate outside the spectrum's logic. Recognizing this "undevelopable" condition is not fatalistic but diagnostic. It calls for a paradigm shift: from pursuing progress along a presumed path to engaging with the political limits of development itself. This reclassification demands new ethical and strategic foundations for international engagement, moving beyond a linear model of change to a more sober, politically grounded understanding of global inequality.

title: Ambivalent Attachments: Place, Precarity and Survival in Lesotho’s Rough Neighbourhoods
affiliations: University of Cape Town, University of the Free State, Sol Plaatje University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Ambivalent Attachments: Place, Precarity and Survival in Lesotho’s Rough Neighbourhoods
detail.abstract: This paper critically rethinks the concept of place attachment through an ethnographic study of Sea Point, a longstanding informal settlement in Maseru, Lesotho. While dominant theories of place attachment often frame it as an emotional or voluntary bond with place, the experiences of Sea Point residents challenge this assumption. In contexts marked by tenure insecurity, infrastructural neglect, and spatial illegibility, attachment emerges less from affection and more from survival. We conceptualise Sea Point as a rough neighbourhood; a space of durable hardship produced through infrastructural deficit and socio-legal uncertainty, showing how place attachment is forged through endurance and constraint rather than voluntary belonging. Drawing on ethnographic participant observations, in-depth interviews and life histories, the study reveals how residents remain tethered to place not through choice, but through constraint, embedded social networks, and the absence of alternatives. Building on the work of Tuan, Roy, Simone, and Bayat, the paper proposes “ambivalent attachment” as a key conceptual contribution, capturing the simultaneous endurance and aspiration, fatigue and care, that define urban life under informality. It argues that informality is not a planning failure but a structuring condition of urban governance in the Global South, producing attachments that are negotiated, contingent, and deeply political. The paper moves the field from emotional bonding toward a critical understanding of how attachment is shaped by exclusion, survival strategies, and everyday forms of resilience.

title: Corruption Perceptions and Political Misogyny
affiliations: Dublin City University Business School and University College Dublin (UCD)

detail.title: Corruption Perceptions and Political Misogyny
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between corruption and attitudes towards women in positions of political leadership. Using Afrobarometer data, we examine whether personal experiences with corruption, local corruption rates, and individual perceptions of corruption influence support for the belief that only men should serve as leaders. Overall, we find no significant association between corruption indicators and gender-biased attitudes in the general population. However, our analysis reveals that among women, higher perceived corruption is significantly associated with lower support for male only leadership. These findings suggest that women may respond to perceived corruption by rejecting traditional leadership norms, potentially viewing male dominated systems as complicit in institutional failure. In contrast, men's attitudes appear either unaffected or more resistant to change in response to corruption perceptions.

title: Game-Theoretic Option Pricing
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Game-Theoretic Option Pricing
detail.abstract: We present a game-theoretic derivation of the implied volatility smile as an equilibrium object arising from a Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) formulation of option pricing under model uncertainty. The riskneutral measure Q is interpreted as the market's optimal adversarial strategy against a trader, while the physical measure P governs growth, learning, and realised dynamics. We show that the Black-Scholes equation arises as a degenerate Isaacs limit corresponding to Gaussian completeness, and that leptokurtic physical dynamics necessarily induce curvature in the implied volatility surface. Using the Variance Gamma (VG) family, we give explicit closed-form expressions for cumulants, Esscher-tilted pricing equilibria, and the resulting smile. Finally, we show that within this equilibrium class the physical measure can be recovered from the option surface up to a single scalar risk-premium parameter.

title: The Dark Night Rises: The Impact of Switch-Off Policies on Crime
affiliations: University Paris-Saclay, INRAE, AgroParisTech, Paris-Saclay Applied Economics

detail.title: The Dark Night Rises: The Impact of Switch-Off Policies on Crime
detail.abstract: In recent years, a growing number of French municipalities have adopted policies to switch off public lighting at night, in an effort to decrease energy consumption and mitigate light pollution. While these policies offer environmental and financial benefits, their impact on public safety, and crime in particular, remains unknown. This paper provides the first empirical assessment of the effect of public lighting switch-off on crime in France between 2017 and 2023. To do so, I combine administrative data on reported crimes at the municipality-year level with a novel database on public lighting switch-offs at the national level, and exploit the random temporality of policy implementation, using a staggered difference-in-differences. I find that, contrary to frequent arguments put forward by opponents of this kind of policies, switching off public lighting has no significant impact on most types of crimes and a small impact on burglaries. Increased burglaries that can be imputed to nighttime switch-offs are around 0.35 burglaries per 1,000 dwellings in treated municipalities over the study period. Further analysis shows that this effect is largely driven by high-density municipalities. Overall, even if further research is needed to confirm these results at the sub-municipal level, the findings of this study offer new evidence on the marginal impact of switch-off policies on crime, providing valuable insights to the ongoing debate on sustainable lighting strategies.

title: Implications of Negative Real Interest Rates on the Nigerian Economy
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria and Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: Implications of Negative Real Interest Rates on the Nigerian Economy

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This study establishes an empirical analysis of the macroeconomic effects of Nigeria's persistently negative real interest rates. Unlike advanced economies that may deliberately employ negative rates as a stimulative tool, Nigeria's negative rates are an involuntary consequence of inflation consistently outpacing the nominal Monetary Policy Rate (MPR). Employing a Non-Linear Autoregressive Distributed Lag (NARDL) model on quarterly data from 2010 to 2024, the research investigates the asymmetric short-and long-run impacts of real interest rate shocks on key macroeconomic indicators such as output, inflation, and investment flows. The findings reveal a critical policy trade-off: positive real interest rate shocks are significantly disinflationary but growth-retarding in the short run, while negative shocks stimulate output at the cost of higher inflation. In the long run, positive rates foster stability and attract Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), whereas negative rates are contractionary and deter FDI. The transmission to stock market performance and portfolio investment is found to be weak. The study concludes that the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) must prioritize achieving a positive real interest rate environment to effectively anchor inflation expectations and build macroeconomic credibility, despite the shortterm growth sacrifices. This necessitates maintaining the MPR sufficiently above the inflation rate, complemented by structural reforms to enhance policy transmission.

title: Sovereign Exposure to the Global Financial Cycle and Unconventional Monetary Policy in Emerging Markets

detail.title: Sovereign Exposure to the Global Financial Cycle and Unconventional Monetary Policy in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: During the Covid-19 pandemic, several emerging market central banks announced unprecedented sovereign bond purchase (SBP) programs. This paper investigates whether such announcements mitigated the exposure of domestic sovereign bond markets to the Global Financial Cycle (GFC). Our findings reveal that SBP announcements significantly reduce the sensitivity of long-term sovereign bond yields to the VIX, our high-frequency proxy for the GFC. This suggests that central bank communication about unconventional monetary policy can act as a stabilizing signal to markets, partially insulating economies from global shocks. We further develop a theoretical model to explain this effect, emphasizing how the announcement of state-contingent sovereign bond purchases shapes investors' expectations regarding sovereign default risk and inflation, thereby amplifying or dampening global financial spillovers.

title: Weather Index Vehicle Insurance
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics and University College Dublin

detail.title: Weather Index Vehicle Insurance
detail.abstract: Scientific research shows that weather factors significantly influence driving behavior. This paper proposes a weather-index-based auto insurance theoretical framework, focusing on two key environmental triggers: temperature and rainfall. Unlike traditional compensation-based auto insurance, the proposed index-linked scheme compensates policyholders who avoid driving when weather conditions exceed predetermined thresholds. Policyholder behavior patterns are categorized into four key strategies, with detailed explanations of the two most prominent strategies. Equilibrium conditions under fair insurance are derived, and the expected utility of policyholders seeking to maximize wealth in the face of external weather shocks is simulated. Through special incentive compatibility mechanism theory and empirical data, the paper demonstrates that weather-indexed auto insurance has a higher expected utility versus traditional insurance contracts.

title: Currency Board vs Currency Union: A Theme Park Analogy for Bulgaria’s Transition to the Euro
affiliations: Nazarbayev University

detail.title: Currency Board vs Currency Union: A Theme Park Analogy for Bulgaria’s Transition to the Euro
detail.abstract:
In 2026, Bulgaria transitioned from a currency board arrangement to fully adopting the euro
and becoming its 21st member state. Many have questioned the suitability of the euro and have
argued that it would create higher inflation. Traditionally, interest rate parity is used to argue
that a currency board and a currency union are very similar monetary regimes. This paper
provides an alternative mechanism. It uses a unique theme park analogy based on the supply of
local and anchor currencies to show that the two regimes are indeed functionally equivalent
and would thus lead to very similar inflation outcomes.

title: Empirical Precision and Theoretical Depth across the Sciences
affiliations: ETH Zürich - KOF Swiss Economic Institute

detail.title: Empirical Precision and Theoretical Depth across the Sciences
detail.abstract: The sciences differ in the precision of their empirical tests. A central determinant of this precision are the applied auxiliary hypotheses, which can encompass everything from theories to apparatus to data analysis. If they are subject to large variation within and between studies, the obtained results will vary, too. This paper investigates how the ways to handle auxiliary hypotheses differ across the sciences. This covers, for example, the possibility to separate and test auxiliary hypotheses, to reveal them through intervention, or to construct the experimental setup to exclude false ones. The paper focuses on a comparison of physical work in the laboratory in the natural sciences to data work with computers in the social sciences. The interaction with physical experimental setups allows natural scientists to better test, manipulate, and neutralize auxiliary hypotheses. In contrast, the collecting, processing, and analysis of data in the social sciences faces severe difficulties in choosing the right auxiliary hypotheses. Too many of them seem equally true. Social scientists thus struggle with numerous researcher degrees of freedom in their studies. Consequently, the natural sciences can better narrow down false auxiliary hypotheses than the social sciences, which allows them to achieve more precise empirical results and in turn reach deeper levels of theoretical development.

title: The Cuban Model and its Application in Mexico
affiliations: Instituto Tecnológico Autónomo de México (ITAM)

detail.title: The Cuban Model and its Application in Mexico
detail.abstract: The Cuban Model represents the ways in which the State aims to control the flows of human time (work, leisure) and value of goods and services. It assumes the government has the capacity to control those flows directly and to discipline deviations. It aims to control directly capital and land assets, the organization of industry, and the decisions of use of time by individuals. To control deviations, it relies on compensating the armed forces and suppressing expression and elections. Its success sustaining in power a party clique makes it attractive to other authoritarian regimes in Latin America. which have attempted its total or partial adoption.

title: JudgeGPT: When Progress Meets Precedent
affiliations: UC Berkeley School of Law, UC Berkeley School of Law and Independent

detail.title: JudgeGPT: When Progress Meets Precedent

publicationDetails.detailsText: UC Berkeley Public Law Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: University of California, Berkeley School of Law, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted to appear in Berkeley Technology Law Journal, Volume 40, No. 4

detail.abstract:
This article examines how artificial intelligence technologies are being integrated into the judicial systems of three jurisdictions: Brazil, China, and the United States. Organized around three primary domains of judicial activity —core judicial functions, court management, and interfacing with the public — it provides a comparative perspective on the role of governance, data infrastructure, and local conditions in the realization of AI’s promise to improve court efficiency and access. 

Responsive to a litigation rate that is among the highest in the world, Brazil has become a leader in judicial AI by leveraging a strong, centralized governance structure and a unified commitment to digital records. Courts are developing proprietary generative AI systems to carry out core functions, utilizing bespoke tools to help with case management, and operating under a sophisticated risk-based governance framework for evaluating use cases. In China, initiatives like the country's “smart court” and Same Type Case Reference system in combination with government aspirations in AI and judicial legitimacy have similarly led to a far-reaching court adoption of automation and AI. This includes national and local initiatives that in certain contexts use intelligent software to find cases, generate draft judgments, and offer streamlined and automated options to the public. In the U.S., the judiciary has taken a more cautious and fragmented approach, driven by concerns raised by early experiences with risk assessment tools, an emphasis on due process and judicial autonomy, and a decentralized system of judicial governance. This has so far resulted in a landscape that reflects local innovation, piloting, and experimentation to a greater extent than any top-down mandate. As efforts to centralize and coordinate across the US judiciary take shape, the likelihood of greater technological and procedural legal interoperability—essential for more systematic reform—will also increase.

title: Rethinking Private Ordering: The Financial Disclosure Quandary
affiliations: Duke University School of Law

detail.title: Rethinking Private Ordering: The Financial Disclosure Quandary

publicationDetails.detailsText: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Series Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Private ordering is the delegation of regulatory authority to the private sector. The United States and other governments often use private ordering in business and finance. The goal is to engage experts from the private sector who have greater expertise than typically available within a government agency. Domestically and worldwide, private ordering is most widely used for financial disclosure. To this end, governments commonly delegate to the accounting profession responsibility for recording and summarizing a firm's business and financial transactions and analyzing, verifying, and reporting the results. Because investors in securities issued by firms rely on the disclosure, this represents the delegation of securities-law authority from government agencies, including the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission ("SEC"), to the private sector. The legitimacy of this private ordering has been challenged, however, by questions whether financial statements of publicly-listed companies accurately reflect reality. Infamous accounting failures, including the collapses of Enron and Lehman Brothers, suggest that financial disclosure--and thus, the private ordering of such disclosure--may be flawed. Furthermore, the private-sector body acting for the accounting profession, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), has been criticized for its slow pace of promulgating important new accounting standards and a belief that conflicts of interest are preventing it from adequately addressing investor needs. This Article reexamines the private ordering of financial disclosure, including whether it continues to work effectively and, if not, how it can be improved. The analysis also takes a cross-border perspective, comparing U.S., U.K., and EU financial disclosure.

title: Conflicting Interests of Authorities in Platform Policy? A Comparative Analysis of Legal and Regulatory Frameworks in the field of VAT, Customs and Competition law
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Law and Erasmus University Rotterdam

detail.title: Conflicting Interests of Authorities in Platform Policy? A Comparative Analysis of Legal and Regulatory Frameworks in the field of VAT, Customs and Competition law
detail.abstract: This article explores the growing tension between EU tax/customs enforcement and competition law in the context of digital platforms. While platforms such as online marketplaces are increasingly tasked with collecting VAT and, under proposed reforms, import duties as 'deemed suppliers' and 'deemed importers,' these obligations may inadvertently reinforce market concentration. Larger platforms are better equipped to handle complex compliance duties, while smaller competitors face disproportionate burdens that may hinder entry and innovation. The paper provides a comparative legal analysis of VAT, customs, and competition law frameworks, examining how compliance duties can lead to vertical integration, self-preferencing, and exclusionary practices. It also discusses possible regulatory solutions, including thresholds, transitional regimes, and exemptions for limited facilitation models. The article ultimately questions whether the same rules that aim to secure public revenue might conflict with the goal of maintaining open, competitive digital markets.

title: The Causal Effect of Debt on Interest Rates
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Independent, Independent and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: The Causal Effect of Debt on Interest Rates

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: This paper uses a natural experiment to measure the causal effect of an expected debt-financed fiscal stimulus on interest rates. We find that a 1 percentage point increase in the expected US debt-to-GDP ratio leads to an increase of about 1-2 basis points in the longer-run neutral rate (r *) and about 2-3 basis points in the 10-year Treasury term premium. Our results validate estimates from a common time-series approach that regresses long-term forward interest rates on long-term projections of government debt, where the exclusion restriction does not apply.

title: Paying for Peers? Parental Willingness to Pay for School Composition and Quality in Switzerland
affiliations: Swiss Coordination Centre for Research in Education (SKBF),  and University of Bern

detail.title: Paying for Peers? Parental Willingness to Pay for School Composition and Quality in Switzerland
detail.abstract: Switzerland features strong socio-economic segregation and no formal school choice, making residential relocation the only channel through which parents can access preferred schools. Identifying how parents value school attributes is therefore essential but challenging, given that choices bundle multiple characteristics. We address this by conducting a discrete choice experiment with nearly 2,700 parents with school-aged children, allowing us to estimate willingness to pay (WTP) for individual and combined school attributes. We find that a substantial minority of parents value academic quality so highly that their preferences are effectively price-insensitive. Among price-sensitive parents, academic quality remains central, but they also exhibit positive WTP for schools with fewer students with special educational needs and fewer non-native-speaking peers. Interaction effects are strong: WTP for reductions in special-needs peers is highest if the school is among the academically strongest. Accounting for attribute interactions further reveals marked heterogeneity, with parents clustering into seven distinct preference types.

title: Financial Market Interdependence, Contagion and Jumpy Risk Exposure
affiliations: Ghent University and European Stability Mechanism

detail.title: Financial Market Interdependence, Contagion and Jumpy Risk Exposure

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Stability Mechanism Working Paper No. 76
publicationDetails.journalName: European Stability Mechanism (ESM) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We develop a factor model to jointly measure financial market interdependence and contagion effects. Countries’ exposure to the common factor is composed of a slow-moving trend, measuring cross-market linkages during ‘normal times’ and a regime-switching component, measuring excess sensitivity often indicative of contagion. When estimating the model using daily excess returns for 19 European stock markets over the period 1995–2025, we find a decreasing degree of interdependence after the Great Recession. Moreover, we identify contagion days in multiple countries, often linked to well-known market events. Finally, allowing for regime changes in the factor loadings can help improve forecasts of downside risk.

title: The Quest for Adaptive Inference: Comparing FC-TVPVAR and LSTM-TVPVAR in High-Dimensional Volatility Scenarios

detail.title: The Quest for Adaptive Inference: Comparing FC-TVPVAR and LSTM-TVPVAR in High-Dimensional Volatility Scenarios
detail.abstract: Dynamics of financial contagion are rapidly and drastically transforming by altering the investment preferences and the increasing diversification in the investment environment coupled with successive global events lead to more complex and non-linear relationships between the traditional and emerging markets. In this regard, this study explores the dynamic, asymmetric, and non-linear volatility transmissions among the DeFi, commodity, energy, technology, and clean energy markets by incorporating Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) into the Time Domain of Time Varying Parameters Vector Auto Regression (TD-TVPVAR) model to eliminate the shortcomings of the previous studies. Results compare the outputs of the Frequency Extension of TVPVAR (FC-TVPVAR) and LSTM-TVPVAR methods and verify the achievements of the new novel methodology, which allocates the total transmission among the selected markets in a more unbiased way. Consequently, optimized LSTM-TVPVAR results identify Bitcoin, gold, and oil prices as the most significant sources of risk, while clean energy market is determined to be the only significant receiver. In addition, results highlight DeFi, energy, and commodity prices as strong hedgers against the technology and clean energy prices. Finally, robust prediction accuracy and fitness of the incorporated model are validated by performance metrics and the stability and contributions of the new methodology are verified by the bootstrapping tests.

title: The Crypto-Equity Nexus: A Novel Simulation of Risk Transmission Channels

detail.title: The Crypto-Equity Nexus: A Novel Simulation of Risk Transmission Channels
detail.abstract: Crypto currency market is swiftly transformed and integrated into the financial system by developing substantial interdependencies with the financial and non-financial markets in the long and short-run. In this regard, this study explores the dynamic, asymmetric, and non-linear volatility transmission across the equity and decentralized finance (DeFi) markets through simulating the dependencies in order to eliminate the bias and drawbacks of the traditional models by employing an optimized and original methodology composed of Deep Neural Network (DNN) and Time Varying Parameters Vector Auto Regression (TVP-VAR) models. Results identify substantial transmission from Bitcoin (BTC), Nasdaq 100 (NASDAQ), Shanghai Stock Exchange (SSE), and New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) indices to BNB, Euronext, Tether (TET), and Ethereum (ETH) and reflect the significant impact of the global important events on the financial contagion. Model assessment results confirm the robust accuracy, fitness, reliability, and validity of the model, as well as the success of parameter optimization.

title: Beyond Linear Models: Evaluating Tree-Based, Instance-Based, and Deep Learning Methods for Carbon Market Forecasting

detail.title: Beyond Linear Models: Evaluating Tree-Based, Instance-Based, and Deep Learning Methods for Carbon Market Forecasting
detail.abstract: Transition to the zero-carbon economy is intensely driven by market mechanisms and carbon pricing plays a pivotal role in determining the pace and success of this transition. In this context, it is extremely significant to unravel the underlying carbon price drivers and develop precise carbon price prediction models. Accordingly, this study proposes a comprehensive and comparative research through developing original and optimized machine and deep learning models for carbon price feature screening and prediction tasks, and evaluates the accuracy and reliability aspects of the applied models. Results identify substantial impacts of the energy prices and stock returns on the carbon price volatility and determine the coal price, United Kingdom 10-year bond yield, and the Standard and Poor's 500 index as the leading carbon price drivers. Finally, assessment and validation results highlight the robust precision and reliability features of the Extra Trees (ET), K-nearest Neighbor (KNN), and Deep Neural Network (DNN) methods.

title: Embedding and Surfacing Skills in Higher Education Curriculum and Pedagogy
affiliations: University of New South Wales, , University of New South Wales and University of New South Wales

detail.title: Embedding and Surfacing Skills in Higher Education Curriculum and Pedagogy

declarations.funderStatement: The UNSW ADA Skills Passport project is funded by the UNSW Provost’s Office and the Faculty of Arts, Design & Architecture. We would also like to acknowledge the contributions of UNSW colleagues, including the UNSW ADA Education Innovation team, the UNSW Pro Vice-Chancellor Education Portfolio (Education Solutions) team, and the UNSW IT Partnership and Engagement team, as well as UNSW ADA students, alumni, and educators, and industry stakeholders, to the development, exploration, and validation of this project.

detail.abstract: This paper discusses the growing importance of skills in higher education and examines how skills can be more deliberately embedded and surfaced in curriculum design and teaching practice. It begins by clarifying how skill is defined and understood in higher education, acknowledging diverse terms and interpretations in the literature. The paper highlights the growing value of enduring human skills across higher education systems, especially in an era of rapid technological change and advances in artificial intelligence, while noting challenges for students in identifying and articulating their skills. The discussion then turns to two critical dimensions of skill integration. At the curriculum level, the paper explores strategies to surface skills in academic programs. In parallel, it emphasizes effective teaching and assessment of these skills in the classroom. By raising these key issues and reflecting on existing practices, the paper highlights the challenges and implications for higher education institutions. It concludes that a more deliberate, holistic approach to skills development is needed and calls for collaborative efforts to enhance students' and graduates' skills to meet the demands of an uncertain world.

title: A Non-Debt Financial Architecture for Household-Level Structural Transformation: Evidence from an 18-Year Field Prototype in an Emerging Economy

detail.title: A Non-Debt Financial Architecture for Household-Level Structural Transformation: Evidence from an 18-Year Field Prototype in an Emerging Economy
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Inner-Output Model (IOM) as a non-debt financial microarchitecture for household-level structural transformation in Emerging Market and Developing Economies (EMDEs). Based on an 18-year longitudinal field prototype in a periurban, land-constrained environment, the study demonstrates how coordinated interaction among time, labor, land, and biological assets can generate sustained cash flow, progressive land expansion, and long-term asset accumulation without reliance on credit, subsidies, or public transfers. The prototype achieved positive cash flow within 30 days, durable poverty exit within 100 days, and multi-cycle asset compounding while maintaining zero debt exposure across economic, price, and climate shocks. Through rule-based sequencing of multiple asset classes-labor, land, productive capital, and biological systems-the IOM converts household capacity into a self-financing, balance-sheet-stable production system. This provides direct evidence that structural transformation can occur at the household level through system design rather than financial leverage. The paper further maps these micro-level dynamics into portfolio-relevant primitives for Public Development Banks (PDBs) and Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs). By treating the IOM as a standardized, licensable coordination architecture rather than a credit instrument, development institutions can mobilize fiscally neutral pipelines of household asset formation, employment absorption, and land-based resilience without increasing sovereign or household indebtedness. In high-informality, high-debt environments, this enables development finance to shift from loan deployment to balance-sheet engineering. By reframing development finance as the design of scalable, multi-asset household systems rather than the expansion of credit, the IOM provides a new micro-foundation for debt-free growth, climate-resilient livelihoods, and long-term economic sovereignty in the Global South.

title: Mapping Spatial Network and Driving Factors of Non-Contact Drug Crimes: Insights from Postal Drug Trafficking in Chinese Cities
affiliations: Ningxia University, Northwest University, Northwest University, University of Colorado Boulder and University of Alabama

detail.title: Mapping Spatial Network and Driving Factors of Non-Contact Drug Crimes: Insights from Postal Drug Trafficking in Chinese Cities
detail.abstract: Postal drug trafficking is a non-contact crime with significant implications for combating cross-regional drug trafficking and maintaining social stability. This study, utilizing postal drug trafficking case data from the China Judgments Online website from 2015 to 2019, applies natural language processing (NLP) and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression models to analyze the offenders’ profiles and crime spatial patterns. Findings show that perpetrators are typically young to middle-aged males with low education, unemployment, and criminal records, often involved in administrative violations like drug use and gambling. Most crime incidences distributed in Sichuan, with a pattern of "higher in the west and north, lower in the east and south". Drug trafficking flows primarily in the southwest and Pearl River Delta, with Chengdu and Guangzhou as key hubs. The crime stages include preparation, contact establishment, crime execution, and post-crime activities. Unemployment rates, crime rates, distance to Myanmar’s drug source areas, rural education levels, and express delivery volume influence the crime rate. These findings offer empirical evidence for the prevention and control of postal drug trafficking.

title: Parsimony, Agnosticism, and Estimability of Dynamic Discrete Choice Games
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Parsimony, Agnosticism, and Estimability of Dynamic Discrete Choice Games
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the statistical price of agnostic estimation in dynamic discrete games with equilibrium multiplicity. When the mapping from structural primitives to equilibrium behavior is locally flat, economically distinct models generate observationally indistinguishable outcomes, sharply increasing estimation difficulty. Equilibrium multiplicity compounds this problem by expanding ambiguity over equilibrium selection and endogenously destroying smoothness through switching across equilibria. Together, these forces dramatically inflate data requirements. For empirically relevant sample sizes, reliable agnostic estimation is often infeasible. The paper develops a reduced-form diagnostic that detects when this occurs, reframing the structural versus reduced-form debate around statistical feasibility rather than methodological preference.

title: Financial Innovation, Endogenous Money Velocity, and Monetary Policy Transmission

detail.title: Financial Innovation, Endogenous Money Velocity, and Monetary Policy Transmission

keywords: and Monetary Policy Transmission Financial innovation

detail.abstract: This paper studies how financial innovation alters monetary policy transmission by endogenizing money velocity. We extend a standard New Keynesian framework by allowing velocity to depend on digital payment adoption, financial deepening, and interest rate spreads. This generates an innovation-augmented IS curve in which financial innovation increases the effective interest rate elasticity of aggregate demand and shifts the mapping between policy rates and output. We test the empirical relevance of this mechanism using World Bank annual data from 20 countries (10 developed and 10 emerging economies) from 1995-2023, a period characterized by rapid digital payment diffusion. To mitigate endogeneity concerns, we employ an instrumental variable approach using lagged internet penetration as an instrument for digital payment adoption. The results show a robust positive association between digital payment adoption and output growth, consistent with an endogenous-velocity channel. The effect is significantly stronger in emerging economies. The findings imply that monetary transmission varies systematically with the level of financial innovation, and that policy rules calibrated under stablevelocity assumptions may become unreliable in highly digitalized economies. We propose a modified Taylor rule that incorporates a financial innovation index.

title: Interest Rates vs Unemployment Risk: What Drives Automobile Purchases?

detail.title: Interest Rates vs Unemployment Risk: What Drives Automobile Purchases?
detail.abstract: Textbook theory predicts that durable spending moves with interest rates, but in practice households respond far more to unemployment risk. Using U.S. macroeconomic data and household surveys, I show that subjective unemployment expectations are much stronger predictors of durable expenditure than interest rates. When households expect rising unemployment, they delay purchases because the utility cost of waiting a few quarters is small. I build a heterogeneous agent model with durable and non-durable goods that directly incorporates surveybased expectations. My model employs directed search and continuous shocks that enable usage of the sequence space jacobian (SSJ) toolkit. The model implied variance decomposition attributes roughly 80 percent of fluctuations in durable expenditure to unemployment risk-50 percent uncertainty (second moment) and 30 percent expected income (first moment)-and 20 percent to interest rates. The results demonstrate that combining measured expectations with a realistic heterogeneous agent framework delivers sharply different conclusions than the representative-agent, full-information benchmark.

title: The Information Effect of U.S. Monetary Policy on Global Corporate Credit Risk
affiliations: The University of Sydney - Discipline of Finance, University of Sydney Business School and Columbia University

detail.title: The Information Effect of U.S. Monetary Policy on Global Corporate Credit Risk
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of U.S. interest rate changes on corporate credit risk for non-U.S. firms. Using a global sample of firms across 45 countries, we document a negative relationship between changes in the U.S. federal funds rate and credit default swap (CDS) spreads for foreign firms, challenging the conventional view that higher interest rates increase default risk. Our findings suggest that U.S. rate hikes convey positive information signal about future economic conditions, reducing perceived credit risk. To address endogeneity concerns, we use news policy shocks of Nakamura and Steinsson (2018) and forward guidance shocks of Gürkaynak, Sack, and Swanson (2005) as instruments, confirming that the information component of monetary policy plays a critical role. The effect is more pronounced in countries that are more economically and politically aligned with the U.S. and in those with more opaque information environments. These findings highlight the global informational spillovers of U.S. monetary policy and their implications for investors, policymakers, and corporate risk management.

title: EUDR and Deforestation in Brazil: Are Producers Anticipating the European Deforestation-Free Regulation?
affiliations: FEA-USP, University of Nottingham, Universidade Federal de Viçosa (UFV) and NOVA University Lisbon - Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities ( FCSH- UNL)

detail.title: EUDR and Deforestation in Brazil: Are Producers Anticipating the European Deforestation-Free Regulation?
detail.abstract: The European Union Deforestation-Free Regulation (EUDR, Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023) is set to enter into force in early 2027, after two postponements. This regulation was enacted in July 2023 and aims to reduce the deforestation footprint of the EU for a given selection of goods: soya, coffee, cattle, rubber, cocoa, wood, and palm oil, along with their derived products. Although the regulation's effects have yet to become legally binding, its impacts on deforestation and land use should occur earlier, given that it prohibits EU countries from importing these goods if produced on land deforested or degraded deforested land after December 2020. In this context, this paper analyzes from legal and economic perspectives whether preceding and anticipatory effects, respectively, of this regulation exist, focusing on deforestation and land use in Brazil. We deploy an impact analysis, anchored by a legal analysis, that measures the EUDR's impact on deforestation and land use patterns. Our model employs novel data on municipalities' production directed toward exports, singling out exports of selected goods to the EU. These novel data and methods allow for conclusions indicating that the EUDR has not yet produced any identifiable effect on deforestation or land use.

title: Miscalibrated Mergers
affiliations: California State University, San Bernardino - Department of Accounting & Finance

detail.title: Miscalibrated Mergers
detail.abstract: In this paper, I study how managerial miscalibration, defined as an overestimation of signal informativeness, affects merger decisions. I develop a real options model with learning in which an acquirer endogenously chooses both the timing and the terms of the merger bid. Miscalibration causes the acquirer to overreact to new information, increasing the volatility of its beliefs and, as a result, raising the threshold at which it optimally initiates the bid. The model predicts that merger activity is delayed relative to a benchmark with correctly calibrated beliefs. The model generates clear implications for deal outcomes. Miscalibration shapes which mergers are ultimately completed because of the valuation disagreement at the time of the bid. Accepted deals are those in which the acquirer holds a lower valuation of the merged firm than the market, leading to overpayment and negative announcement returns for the acquirer alongside positive returns for the target. By focusing on miscalibration separately from other facets of overconfidence, the paper highlights a distinct behavioral mechanism that is central to understanding merger activity and managerial decision making.

title: U.S. Dollar Invoicing and GVC Participation: A Two-Way Interaction
affiliations: American University

detail.title: U.S. Dollar Invoicing and GVC Participation: A Two-Way Interaction
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the bidirectional relationship between dollar-invoiced trade and bilateral global value chain (GVC) participation using a two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental variables approach. Empirical results reveal a robust and negative feedback loop: greater reliance on the US dollar for trade invoicing constrains deeper integration into GVCs, while increased GVC participation reduces dependence on the dollar as an invoicing currency. These relationships vary with exchange rate volatility, highlighting complex policy trade-offs under conditions of currency uncertainty. The findings contribute to an understanding of how dominant currency use and GVC participation interact, with implications for exchange rate management and trade policy design in an increasingly interconnected global economy.

title: Younger Firms and CEOs Allow More Work from Home
affiliations: University College London, ITAM - Business School, Stanford University - Department of Economics, Stanford University, Stanford University, Ifo Institute and Princeton University

detail.title: Younger Firms and CEOs Allow More Work from Home
detail.abstract:
We establish three facts about work from home (WFH) in the United States. First, employees WFH more often at younger firms – almost twice as often at firms founded after 2015 than at firms founded before 1990. Second, employees working under younger CEOs have higher levels of WFH. The average WFH rate is 1.4 days per week when the CEO is under 30, compared to 1.1 days when the CEO is 60 or older. Third, the self-employed WFH more than twice as often as wage-and-salary employees. These facts highlight the importance of organizational and managerial attributes for the prevalence of WFH.

title: Clustered Network Connectedness: A New Measurement Framework, with Application to Global Equity Markets
affiliations: SKEMA Business School, University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and Koc University

detail.title: Clustered Network Connectedness: A New Measurement Framework, with Application to Global Equity Markets
detail.abstract:
Network connections, both across and within markets, are central in countless economic contexts. In recent decades, a large literature has developed and applied flexible methods for measuring network connectedness and its evolution, based on variance decompositions from vector autoregressions (VARs), as in Diebold and Yilmaz (2014). Those VARs are, however, typically identified using full orthogonalization (Sims, 1980), or no orthogonalization (Koop, Pesaran, and Potter, 1996; Pesaran and Shin, 1998), which, although useful, are special and extreme cases of a more general framework that we develop in this paper. In particular, we allow network nodes to be connected in "clusters", such as asset classes, industries, regions, etc., where shocks are orthogonal across clusters (Sims style orthogonalized identification) but correlated within clusters (Koop-Pesaran-Potter-Shin style generalized identification), so that the ordering of network nodes is relevant across clusters but irrelevant within clusters. After developing the clustered connectedness framework, we apply it in a detailed empirical exploration of sixteen country equity markets spanning three global regions.

title: Revising the Use of F-Tests in Weak Instrument Practice: Point Estimation and Beyond
affiliations: , University of Cambridge - MRC Biostatistics Unit and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Revising the Use of F-Tests in Weak Instrument Practice: Point Estimation and Beyond
detail.abstract: To analyse the performance of estimators under weak instruments, we adopt the local-tozero weak instrument asymptotics studied in Staiger and Stock (1997) and Stock and Yogo (2005). The commonly used F > 10 rule-of-thumb criterion is motivated by the relative bias, a metric comparing the performance of the OLS and 2SLS estimators. This metric fails to account for the variance of the 2SLS estimator when comparing its performance to that of the OLS estimator and hence assumes that 2SLS is always superior to OLS in performance, even when there is no confounding present, since the bias of 2SLS is always smaller than OLS. We show that, as a result, significant problems due to weak instruments can still persist even if the F > 10 rule-of-thumb is satisfied. To remedy this, we propose different metrics for comparing the performance of 2SLS with that of OLS and propose alternative criteria based on these alternative metrics as more targeted measures of instrument strength. A key challenge with these new metrics is that, unlike the relative bias, they depend on the amount of confounding present between the endogenous variable and outcome. We also make supplementary contributions such as rigorously proving that the relative bias in Stock and Yogo (2005) is monotonically decreasing in the concentration parameter for any fixed K ≥ 3.

title: Contract Design and Insurance Demand

detail.title: Contract Design and Insurance Demand
detail.abstract:
We introduce experimental variation in the insurance contracts offered to rice farmers in China to study how contract design affects insurance takeup. We compare a single-contract offering with menus that include multiple contracts differing in premiums and payouts. Expanding the contract menu substantially increases take-up, primarily through higher adoption of the basic, lowest-cost contract. Additional experimental variation in relative prices and information provision shows that these effects are driven by context effects arising from relative price comparisons within the menu, rather than information inference. The findings highlight contract menu design as an effective supply-side tool for expanding insurance coverage.

title: Indebted Supply and Monetary Policy: A Theory of Financial Dominance
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University, Sciences Po and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Indebted Supply and Monetary Policy: A Theory of Financial Dominance
detail.abstract:
We develop a New Keynesian model with financial frictions to study how corporate capital structure shapes static and dynamic monetary policy tradeoffs through the supply side. Ex post, when corporate leverage is high, monetary tightening contracts both demand and supply. As a result, the Phillips curve is highly non-linear and state-dependent, and the “natural rate” Rn ensuring price stability increases with corporate leverage. Yet the tradeoff between inflation targeting and tightening supply constraints implies that the optimal ex-post policy is to set a rate Ropt < Rn that can decrease with leverage. Ex ante, firms’ market-timing incentives lead them to increase leverage when rates are low, which creates an intertemporal tradeoff: monetary easing supports current demand but hurts future supply, which makes easing partially self-defeating. The optimal ex-ante monetary policy features a prudential motive for leaning against leverage even when the divine coincidence holds in the current period.

title: The Effect of Exposure: Evidence from Spatial Choices in Nairobi
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Harvard University and The World Bank

detail.title: The Effect of Exposure: Evidence from Spatial Choices in Nairobi
detail.abstract:
How much do people dislike opportunities they have never been exposed to, and why? We study how exposure affects work location decisions of casual workers. We offer short-term employment and randomize training locations to induce novel exposures. Participants sacrifice 22% of the median daily wage to avoid working in a location never visited before; one hour-long visit eliminates this premium. Workers anticipate two thirds of the effect exposure has on their later preferences. Results are most consistent with perceived fixed costs of exposure rather than sorting or quality uncertainty. Unfamiliar neighborhoods are also less likely to enter workers' consideration sets.

title: Class Mobility in the Era of Rising Inequality: A Synthetic Dynasty Analysis
affiliations: University of Chicago - Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility, University of Chicago, University of Chicago and University of Chicago - Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility

detail.title: Class Mobility in the Era of Rising Inequality: A Synthetic Dynasty Analysis
detail.abstract:
This paper studies contemporary trends in class mobility using a new approach based on the “synthetic dynasties” represented in Markov chains. This approach yields several novel measures of movement and memory, which respectively capture how class positions differ from one generation to the next and how the influence of class origins dissipates across generations. Applying these methods to data from the U.S., we find that overall levels of movement and memory have remained largely stable across cohorts born between 1945 and 1990. This stability, however, masks offsetting class-specific trends. Among those from the upper and lower classes, movement has declined and memory has increased. In contrast, among the middle classes, movement has risen and memory has weakened.

title: Loan-funded Loans: Equity-like Liabilities inside Bank Holding Companies
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and Tulane University

detail.title: Loan-funded Loans: Equity-like Liabilities inside Bank Holding Companies
detail.abstract:
Leveraging regulatory data on fund flows within bank holding companies (BHCs), we characterize internal loans as a critical funding source for commercial banks. Although recorded as bank liabilities, parent-to-bank internal loans function as contingent support that resembles capital. We show that internal-loan funded banks do not hoard liquidity; instead, they originate larger and longer-maturity loans at lower spreads, initiate more relationships with marginal borrowers, and retain larger shares in syndicated deals. Internal-loan-funded lending is followed by higher short-run profits but higher future nonperforming loan ratios. We further show that organizational structure shapes internal lending: in BHCs with both bank and nonbank operations, nonbank affiliates crowd out internal lending to banks and discipline banks’ use of internal funds, and these BHCs exhibit higher overall performance. To identify our tests, we exploit the passage of the Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act and the announcement of the Basel III Accord, using instrumental variables and discontinuity-design approaches. Our findings highlight an equity-like internal debt channel that shapes monetary policy transmission, risk-taking, and the role of organizational structure in banking.
